title: Tiling lab (pattern blocks)

k1.why: Filling a sailboat, cat and star with real pattern blocks at 1-inch scale is pure hands-on puzzling with no reading; five-year-olds happily turn pieces to fit corners. 'Ask an adult to trace' for the two-ways task is the only fiddly bit.

g23.why: Getting stuck filling a board with blue rhombi and then discovering why (odd count, too many up-triangles) is a real, child-findable aha. Problem 3 (six boards, blues then purples, three numbers each) drifts into repetitive recording and can be trimmed.

g45.why: Finding the six rhombus tilings and the flip map is engaging, but the ribbon-code pages (L/R codes, matching tables, circling RL pairs) become reading- and recording-heavy, and ten problems mostly ask for written explanation. A capable adult is needed to keep the letters tied to the blocks.

best_moment: A 2-3 child realises the blue rhombus always covers one up and one down triangle, so board A can never be filled no matter how they turn it.
biggest_problem: The grades 4-5 path piles ribbon codes, tables and written explanations onto a lovely flip-map discovery, so the second half becomes paperwork.
one_change: Cut the 4-5 ribbon section to one problem (trace the ribbon with string, read its code, rebuild a tiling from a code) and let children spend the saved time flipping real blocks between tilings.

title: Pattern blocks encore: blocking game and fewest pieces

k1.why: Placing blues in a turn-taking game and filling pictures with fewest/most pieces is all hands; kids can play many fast games and 'beat the grown-up'. Deciding who 'can always win' is beyond most five-year-olds, but the playing itself carries the hour.

g23.why: The rhombus-placement game on symmetric boards gives a genuine surprise (second player wins by copying) that children can discover and test against the adult. The trapezoid up/down counting in Problems 4 and 7 is drier and more recording-driven.

g45.why: The game and its centre-move exceptions give real strategy, and seeing a rhombus filling as a stack of cubes in a box corner is a memorable gasp. The flip-distance and odd-cycle proofs and the trapezoid-move problem ask a lot of written explanation, so expect few children to reach them.

best_moment: A child spots that copying every move on the opposite side always wins, then beats the adult with it; or a 4-5 child builds the cube pile and suddenly sees the flat rhombi as 3D.
biggest_problem: Several problems (trapezoid up/down tallies, later flip proofs) shift from building to counting and explaining, which is where attention will drop.
one_change: Front-load the game and the cube-pile reveal for every band and move the trapezoid up/down tally problems to an optional page.

title: Lamp lab (flip both ends of a line)

k1.why: Flipping two counters at the ends of a line is a clear physical move, but matching small start/target pictures and planning which line to press is abstract for five-year-olds; an adult will read every prompt and steer. The early targets are easy enough to give some success.

g23.why: Problems 1-7 are short, mostly easy 'make this picture' puzzles that may feel samey; the payoff (the impossible islands puzzle and the bridge that fixes it) arrives at Problem 8. The pointer/flipper/checker roles help, but the rule is easy to break by flipping one lamp.

g45.why: The upper catalog asks real questions (which targets are possible, all solution sets, fewest moves, ring records) and the even-per-island rule is a nice discovery, but 'find every set of lines' on six-node graphs is search-and-record heavy without much play.

best_moment: Trying and failing to move the light across to the other island, then realising every press changes two lamps so the lone light can never go out.
biggest_problem: The impossibility surprise that makes the week sing comes late, after many easy and similar-feeling puzzles.
one_change: Put the islands puzzle (and a 'can you make just one lamp on the square?' puzzle) early, so children hit the impossibility within ten minutes and spend the rest explaining and inventing.

title: Shuffle machines (permutations)

k1.why: The chair launch is great fun and moving cubes down arrows is doable, but each turn is a two-step procedure (all down, then slide up) repeated many times with a tally, so it leans toward rote simulation. Drawing their own machines for a target number of turns is the best part but needs adult help.

g23.why: Predicting from coloured loops and finding the 5-slot machine that takes 6 turns is a nice surprise, but there are many machines to run and record, and Problems 6-8 (composition, all 6-slot orders, 7-slot maximum) ask for long explanations.

g45.why: Predicting return times without cubes, the 'slowest machine' race and doing perfect card shuffles by hand give real puzzles and a surprising result (52 cards return after 8 shuffles). Composition and inverse problems are abstract but optional.

best_moment: Children discover that a 5-slot machine takes 6 turns, more turns than cubes, because the pair and the trio only line up at 6.
biggest_problem: Most of the hands-on time at K-1 and 2-3 is executing turns and tallying, so the activity can feel like a simulation chore before any pattern appears.
one_change: Do more machines as human chair-switching (whole body, everyone counting) and have tables predict first, so physical simulation is short, social and always paired with a guess.

title: Stars and wheels (star polygons, Caesar cipher)

k1.why: Hopping a counter around big dots and watching a star appear is appealing, and the dots are large, but the same task repeats on rings of 4, 5, 6, 7 and children must also draw straight lines on small rings. The picture-ring 'secret hop' pages are a nice change but abstract.

g23.why: Drawing stars on 8-12 dot rings with guesses is satisfying, and making a real code wheel and sending secret messages is exactly the kind of thing 8-year-olds love. Cutting the wheels takes about 10 minutes, which the guide plans for with spares.

g45.why: Cracking codes with unknown settings, the crack race, predicting pieces on big rings and the cardioid coda give variety and real reasoning; the gcd rule is reachable by experiment.

best_moment: Cracking a partner's coded message on your own spinning wheel, or seeing a five-pointed star draw itself from a simple hop.
biggest_problem: The K-1 packet repeats one procedure across many rings with little new to notice each time.
one_change: Give K-1 a simple picture-wheel 'secret message' game earlier and drop two of the repetitive ring pages.

title: Tower cities (visibility / skyscraper puzzles)

k1.why: Building rows of 1-2-3 cube towers, putting your chin on the table and counting what you see is concrete and a bit silly in a good way; the hidden-row game behind a folder is a real game they can play themselves.

g23.why: Building 3-by-3 cities with coloured towers and solving and inventing edge-number puzzles is genuinely absorbing; colour-by-height makes checking easy. Problems 6-7 (count all 12 cities, totals always 22) are more bookkeeping but optional.

g45.why: 4-by-4 skyscraper puzzles are a proven, addictive puzzle type, and making minimal-clue puzzles for a partner adds challenge. The counting problems (24 and 120 rows sorted in a table) are dry and will be skipped by many.

best_moment: A partner lifts the folder and the guessed row matches the hidden one, or a child realises you can never see just one tower from both ends.
biggest_problem: Preparation is heavy: about 96 pre-built towers and over 240 cubes, likely more than a 30-minute job for one parent.
one_change: Have children build their own towers as the first five minutes of play (or reuse a stored kit) rather than asking a parent to pre-build every tower.

title: Code breaking (yes/no questions, mastermind)

k1.why: Guessing a hidden pattern block with yes-or-no questions is a great kitchen-table game for five-year-olds. The counter code game needs the adult to keep the secret and do all the copying and scoring, and 'can you always be sure' questions are beyond most of them.

g23.why: Children like code games, but the scoring procedure (copy the test behind a folder by column number, place triangles, count) is error-prone and a wrong score spoils the game; the two-colour codes are small enough that deduction can feel thin.

g45.why: The 1-16 number game and finding a method for 3- and 4-counter codes are solid, and the lower-bound 'why not fewer' arguments are real reasoning, but the play is slowed by the folder-and-copy scoring ritual and a referee role.

best_moment: Pinning down a hidden block in exactly three questions after realising each good question cuts the blocks in half.
biggest_problem: The keeper's copy-and-score routine is a fragile procedure that eats time and produces wrong scores, which breaks the deduction that is the whole point.
one_change: Simplify scoring: the keeper looks over the folder at the test and places one triangle per match directly on the breaker's side, with no copying, and add a third colour for 4-5 so the deduction is richer.

title: Take-away games (subtraction Nim)

k1.why: Taking 1 or 2 counters, losing to the grown-up and hunting for the secret is a fast, competitive game five-year-olds will replay; the track helps them see 'land on 3, 6, 9'. Colouring the squares is light.

g23.why: The 1-3-4 rule has a non-obvious pattern (0, 2, 7, 9...) that children can find by playing and colouring, and testing Lena's and Omar's claims gives real reasoning. Rounds are short so tears and boredom are manageable.

g45.why: Many rules, the repeating patterns, 'take as many as you can is wrong', misère and two-pile copying give plenty of depth; Race to 100 against the organizer is a reliable hook. Fourteen problems is more than anyone needs.

best_moment: A child finally beats the grown-up because they figured out to leave 3, 6 or 9 counters.
biggest_problem: Later problems shift from playing to colouring tracks, which can feel like filling in charts once the pattern is found.
one_change: Keep every colouring problem paired with a 'play the adult from a pile you choose' challenge so the charts are always used to win something.

title: Rook race and Nim

k1.why: Sliding a token to the star and taking counters from two piles are simple moves, and discovering that copying wins from 7 and 7 is a real aha a first grader can find and use against the adult. Seating so the star is in the same corner for both matters.

g23.why: Colouring the 8-by-8 board and seeing the diagonal, then realising the board is just two piles, is a satisfying surprise; three-pile searches in Problems 8-9 get long but are optional.

g45.why: Finding the binary-stack rule for Nim and using it to beat the organizer from a big start is a classic thrill; the queen game is a good stretch. Explaining why the rule always works will need adult conversation.

best_moment: A child beats the adult from piles of 7 and 7 by copying every move, or a 4-5 child wins from 13, 9, 7 using the stacks rule.
biggest_problem: The three-pile search problems (all starts up to 6 or 7) can turn into systematic listing before the rule is found.
one_change: Replace the 'find all starts' listing with 'beat the organizer from these five starts', letting the rule emerge from wanting to win.

title: Bouncing paths (paper pool)

k1.why: Walking the ball on a taped floor grid and guessing the stopping corner is excellent, but tracing diagonal paths on paper and keeping the right direction after each bounce is error-prone for five-year-olds, and the ruler-cut-fold-hold-to-light Problem 7 is a fine-motor stretch.

g23.why: Tracing tables, predicting the corner and the prediction game against a partner are engaging, and noticing that 4 by 6 behaves like 2 by 3 is a findable aha. Folding the unfolded strip to see the bounce is a lovely but fiddly extra.

g45.why: The rule (lowest terms, parity decides the corner, p+q-2 bounces) is a great target, but filling a 36-table chart by tracing is a long chore even split three ways, and the folding sheet needs careful cutting and marker work.

best_moment: Children stand at the corner they guessed while a classmate walks the floor grid as the ball and everyone shouts 'bounce'.
biggest_problem: The 4-5 path relies on tracing dozens of tables to fill a chart before the pattern appears.
one_change: Give 4-5 a partly filled chart (or let each child trace only the tables that test a conjecture) so time goes to predicting and explaining instead of tracing.

title: Bridges (Euler walks)

k1.why: Walking a token over printed bridges and picking up counters is a concrete game that 5-year-olds can run themselves, and getting stuck and trying again is the activity. The floor-tape town launch and the build-a-town fallback give movement and choice; the adult only reads the problem once.

g23.why: Pairs walk, get stuck, retry and write the walk as letters. Counting bridges per island leads to a rule they can state themselves and then use to predict towns before walking. Problem 8, where they build a town to a spec for a partner, is a good puzzle-making task.

g45.why: Königsberg, the odd-island argument, the impossible exactly-one-odd-island question, Lee's loop-splicing walk and the fewest-extra-counters route are all real reasoning that stays grounded in counters. The referee role keeps the third child involved.

best_moment: Realising that the stuck towns all have more than two islands with an odd number of bridges, then correctly predicting a new town without walking it.
biggest_problem: The packets are long (12-13 pages), and the counter-per-bridge setup and reset take real time, so pairs can spend a lot of the hour resetting counters rather than thinking.
one_change: Cut each packet to the core 4-5 problems, and have children mark the starts they have tried with a pencil dot so the reset loop stays short.

title: Chip-firing with a sink

k1.why: The page opens with a dense paragraph of rules, and every problem is a table of sharing words and final piles that an adult must scribe. The investigation's answer, that order never matters, is a non-event for a 5-year-old, and K-1 P6 adds chips one at a time eleven times.

g23.why: Firing chips is a pleasant physical move, but every page repeats the same experiment: finish a start in two orders and fill a table row. The finding is always the same, so the surprise wears off after the first table. P6 is 24 add-and-stabilize runs.

g45.why: Older children can carry out the firings and appreciate why the finish is unique. P5's termination proof and P6's order-independence proof are real mathematics, but they will need a strong adult to supply the weight-function idea, and the tables are still long.

best_moment: A child's 12-chip pile cascades around the board, and the finish matches the partner's even though they fired in a completely different order.
biggest_problem: The activity is mostly recording firing words and final piles in tables, to confirm an invariant whose payoff is that nothing changes.
one_change: Drop most of the tables and replace them with one striking challenge: two children race different orders on the same big pile and bet on whether they will match. Then pose a goal-seeking puzzle, such as which start ends at a target pile.

title: Catalan pairings, paths and trees

k1.why: Pairing six dots on a circle with strings without crossings is a good hands-on puzzle with a findable answer (5). The odd-dots impossibility is a nice aha. Fourteen eight-dot pairings and drawing chords on the small recording circles are too long and too fiddly for most 5-year-olds.

g23.why: Enumerating six-dot rainbow pairings is good. The U/D path code is a clear, concrete bridge, and spotting illegal codes is a nice puzzle. But P6, drawing all 14 eight-dot pairings, is a long drawing chore, and the matching tasks are mostly transcription.

g45.why: Ordered trees and walk codes are a real bijection puzzle, and the legal-code rules are good reasoning. But trees start abstract on paper with no physical material. P6 asks children to count 42 and 132 trees, which is hopeless by hand unless an adult steers them to the recurrence.

best_moment: Noticing that the counts of different objects come out the same (1, 2, 5, 14), or that a pairing's string code turns into a mountain path that never dips below ground.
biggest_problem: Much of the work is drawing complete collections of 14 near-identical small diagrams, which turns into tedious bookkeeping before the interesting matching appears.
one_change: Stop each band's enumeration at 5 objects, and spend the saved time on the code puzzles: a mystery code to decode, and a broken code to spot.

title: Route packing and bottlenecks

k1.why: Tracing coloured routes on small arrow boards and blocking all travel with markers are concrete, findable puzzles, and the closure game in P6 adds real play. But the one-route-per-arrow rule is easy to break unnoticed, and coloured pencil cannot be undone.

g23.why: Children can find maximum route sets and minimum blocking sets, and may notice that the two numbers match. The complete list of 8 blocking pairs and the add-an-arrow puzzle are good tasks. The proofs that a collection cannot be larger will mostly come from the adult.

g45.why: The max-flow/min-cut duality is a real aha. But the change-walk (augmenting path with backward steps) adds a new rule set that many 10-year-olds will find confusing. P7 is a general theorem proof most will not reach.

best_moment: Finding that the most routes that fit always equals the fewest markers that stop every route.
biggest_problem: Routes drawn in pencil on paper are hard to revise, and nothing physical stops a child from reusing an arrow. So the key constraint is policed by an adult rather than by the material.
one_change: Use physical route pieces (yarn or coloured strips laid on arrows, one per arrow) so routes can be moved and the one-route-per-arrow rule is enforced by the material.

title: Polygon triangulations and flips

k1.why: Drawing straight diagonals with a straightedge on one-inch recording pentagons and hexagons, then flipping lines with tracing paper, is beyond most 5-year-olds' motor control. The adult ends up drawing, and the triangle-count question has little pull at this age.

g23.why: Finding the 5 pentagon fillings is satisfying. Discovering that the flip map of a pentagon is itself a pentagon is a genuine surprise. The 14 hexagon fillings and the tracing-paper flips are long and fiddly.

g45.why: Shortest flip routes to a fan and the connectivity proof are substantial, reachable reasoning. The odd-cycle question is a good twist. Children spend a lot of time redrawing octagon triangulations by hand.

best_moment: Drawing the join map for the five pentagon fillings and seeing that it makes a pentagon.
biggest_problem: Every move requires precise redrawing of small diagrams, so drawing labour crowds out the thinking, especially for younger children.
one_change: Use a physical board, such as pegs or dots on a whiteboard polygon with sticks or wiki sticks for diagonals, so a flip is lifting one stick and placing another rather than redrawing on tracing paper.

title: Nearest-site regions (Voronoi)

k1.why: Comparing string lengths to label crosses is doable but slow. But 'divide the sheet' asks a 5-year-old to draw an accurate perpendicular-bisector boundary on a blank frame, which needs abstraction and precision they lack, so the adult will draw it.

g23.why: Folding to find the fair line between two dots is a nice trick, and three or four sites give a reasonable puzzle. But the dry 'dots and regions' framing and accurate line drawing make it more of a construction exercise than a game.

g45.why: The inverse puzzles are genuinely good: place dots so A owns exactly the shaded triangle, and decide whether new dots can steal R but not P and Q. Convexity and the question of whether adding a dot can ever help an old one give real reasoning.

best_moment: Placing three new dots so that A's region snaps exactly onto the shaded triangle.
biggest_problem: The core action is accurate geometric drawing on a blank frame, with no story or game to make children care who owns which place.
one_change: Give it a story and a body launch, such as kids as ice-cream stands in the room with a 'which stand is closest?' walk-around. Lead with the inverse placement puzzles rather than ruler construction.

title: Three-colour triangles (Sperner)

k1.why: Placing R/B/Y counters on a six-dot board and trying not to make a rainbow triangle is simple and concrete, and failing every time is a real surprise. With only four little triangles the boards are small enough, though the side rules are an extra thing to remember.

g23.why: Trying to avoid an all-three triangle on bigger boards is a good hook. But the doors-and-routes argument (routes cross edges, must exit two-door triangles) piles on rules, and writing letters on many dots is slow.

g45.why: The odd-count conjecture comes from children's own failed attempts. The door pairing argument is a proof 10-year-olds can follow and check by tracing. P6's broken side rule shows why the hypothesis matters.

best_moment: After several tries to avoid a rainbow triangle, a child realises it is impossible and that the count is always odd.
biggest_problem: For 2-3, the jump from 'try to avoid it' to marking doors and drawing routes adds a rule-heavy representation before children want an explanation.
one_change: Make the opening a two-player game: one player places counters trying to avoid a rainbow triangle while the other hunts for one. Introduce doors only after the group asks why it never works.

title: Machine memory (finite automata)

k1.why: Moving a marker along R/B arrows is a fine board-game move for P1. But listing every 4-card row (P2), finding distinguishing rows (P3, P6) and designing machines (P4-5) are abstract tasks that a 5-year-old will watch an adult do.

g23.why: Designing a machine for 'saw a red' or 'last card blue' is a good puzzle, and the groups-of-three cycle is satisfying. P1 is 16 rows times two machines of rote running, and the 'fewest circles, explain why' lower bounds will mostly be adult-led.

g45.why: Building divisible-by-k machines and spotting the cycle pattern is engaging. The distinguishing-histories lower bound is deep and reachable for strong 10-year-olds, but it is a verbal proof with little hands-on payoff.

best_moment: Building a machine that correctly says YES to every row with a multiple of three reds, and testing it on a friend's long row.
biggest_problem: After the first page, the activity shifts from operating a machine to abstract design and proofs of minimality, with no game element to sustain it.
one_change: Add a 'guess my machine' game: one child secretly builds a two- or three-circle machine, and the others feed it rows and try to work out what it detects.

title: Hidden changes (error-correcting codes)

k1.why: The secret sender-changer-receiver game behind a folder is a role-play kids enjoy, and trying to fool the receiver is fun. But P2's listing of every possible outcome, P4's every key and P5's every row are enumeration that adults will record.

g23.why: Playing the game and then designing keys that the changer cannot beat is a good puzzle with an adversary. Finding every four-counter key (P4) and the two-change extension get heavy.

g45.why: The shortest key for four pictures, why three pictures cannot fit in four positions, and the 'differ in 3 places' rule are excellent puzzles that grow straight out of the game and allow real proofs.

best_moment: The changer secretly flips a counter, and the receiver still names the right picture, then finds the one flip that would have fooled a bad key.
biggest_problem: The game is the fun, but most printed problems switch to exhaustive listing of rows and keys, which is bookkeeping for younger children.
one_change: Keep children in game mode longer: a team designs a key, and the other team plays changer trying to break it. Score breaks, and let the 'every row' listing come only when a dispute needs settling.

title: No card inside another (antichains)

k1.why: Comparing whether one card's pictures are all on another is a doable check, but the goal of avoiding inclusion is a negative rule with no game or story. Recording collections means drawing cards, so 5-year-olds are unlikely to stay engaged past Problem 1.

g23.why: Searching for the largest legal hand from a physical deck is a decent puzzle. The chain-row bound is clever but adult-guided, and listing every collection is tedious.

g45.why: Maximal-versus-maximum and the six-card two-symbol answer with a matching six-row proof are real mathematics that 10-year-olds can check. The activity is fairly dry, and classifying every largest collection is bookkeeping.

best_moment: Getting stuck at a collection that cannot take another card, then finding a bigger one elsewhere.
biggest_problem: There is no game or tension: children sort cards against an abstract rule, and the payoff (a size bound) is invisible to younger children.
one_change: Turn it into a two-player game, where players take turns adding a card to a shared pile without breaking the rule and the last to move wins. The size question then arises naturally.

title: Averaging boards

k1.why: Problem 1, sharing a copied 0-stack and 4-stack into equal piles with cubes, is a real concrete move a 5-year-old can do. But 'one pile per joined shape, including empty ones' is subtle, linked circles that must work at once are beyond most K-1 children, and Problem 2 asks them to record about ten triples in tiny boxes.

g23.why: Adding and halving to fill a circle is easy. Filling chains of linked circles by guess-and-adjust is a decent puzzle, but kids will mostly be doing arithmetic checks. 'A circle can't beat every square' is close to obvious, so it doesn't land as a surprise.

g45.why: Filling linked boards (some needing thirds) is a fair puzzle. Most of the packet, though, asks for proofs 'for every finite board' (maximum principle, uniqueness), and kids will reach those through adult talk rather than their own discovery.

best_moment: On a chain of circles between 0 and 6, finding that the values have to step up evenly (2, 4) for everything to balance.
biggest_problem: The rule that every circle must work at the same time turns each board into solving a linear system by trial, and the theorem it leads to feels obvious to kids, so the work is checking with no gasp.
one_change: Make it a balance or 'fair neighbour' game with one free circle on a long chain and a hidden target, so kids predict before checking, and drop the 'every finite board' proof pages to adult notes.

title: Shortest route touching a line

k1.why: K-1 children can bend a string around one contact point, but the guide admits a contact 1.5 cm off is only 1-3.5 mm longer, so string can't tell them which is shortest. Seven near-identical 'find the shortest' boards leave them guessing, holding taut string on dot centres, with no tool to settle the question.

g23.why: Folding or tracing to reflect B and drawing a straight line is a real aha, and straightedge work suits the age. But kids rarely invent the fold themselves, so an adult usually supplies it, and the remaining pages are repetitive construct-the-route boards.

g45.why: This is the classic Heron problem, and the reflection proof is within reach. The locus and restricted-segment problems give it depth. The concrete string phase is short and inconclusive, and once kids have the trick the boards become routine constructions.

best_moment: Folding the paper on the line and seeing that the best bent route becomes one straight line to the reflected dot.
biggest_problem: The physical experiment can't tell routes apart, so the discovery depends on an adult revealing the reflection trick, and most pages repeat the same construction.
one_change: Open with a big-difference board and a 'river and well' story so string comparisons actually decide something, then use a mirror or fold reveal as the single surprise and cut the number of near-duplicate boards.

title: Meeting regions (Radon)

k1.why: Children have to juggle splitting four labels into two groups, using every label once, drawing hulls, shading, and finding a shared point. That is too many rules for a 5-year-old, and drawing triangles through small dots on record boards is fiddly, so the adult ends up doing the split while the child watches.

g23.why: Finding a split for a given placement is a decent puzzle, and the placement game (try to beat your partner) has real pull. But listing all seven splits on many small boards is a chore, and drawing hulls accurately slows things down.

g45.why: The adversarial game, placing four dots to defeat your partner and always failing, gives a real 'why can't I win?' moment. The contrast with three dots, and explaining the guarantee, suits this age.

best_moment: A child places four dots sure the partner can't split them, and the partner finds the crossing anyway.
biggest_problem: The packet buries the game under split enumeration and record boards, and the rules page is dense for younger children.
one_change: Lead every band with the 'beat your partner' placement game using movable markers and a rubber band, and keep the complete-list enumeration as an optional 4-5 extension.

title: Sorting machines

k1.why: Sliding dot cards past a bar so the smaller one goes up is a simple physical move, and 'find a start that breaks the machine' is concrete. But keeping track of all six starts, and building machines that sort one set but fail another, needs adult bookkeeping. Most K-1 children will run starts the adult chooses.

g23.why: Building a three-lane sorter with fewest bars and hunting for failing starts is satisfying. But the four-lane tasks mean running many starts (24 orders, or 16 zero-one starts) through the mat, which turns into a repetitive simulation.

g45.why: Finding the five-bar four-lane sorter is a good challenge, and the zero-one shortcut is real depth. The threshold, swap-record and lower-bound pages are abstract and heavy, though, and still need lots of hand runs.

best_moment: Finding the one starting order that sneaks through a machine unsorted.
biggest_problem: Testing a machine means running many starts card by card, so the minute-to-minute work is simulation and recording, and the kit takes about 40 minutes to cut and tape the first time.
one_change: Run it as a floor game with kids as the cards walking the lanes, and frame the main task as 'build a machine your partner can't break' with a challenger choosing starts, so kids test only the starts that matter.

title: Three random decks (nontransitive)

k1.why: Circling the bigger number in nine pairs is easy, and drawing from bags is fun. But the three comparison tables are 27 near-identical circles, and the cycle surprise needs an adult to point it out. The later construction problems (swaps, two-card decks) are beyond most K-1 children.

g23.why: Playing the bag game, then finding that A beats B, B beats C and yet C beats A, is a genuine gasp. Building their own cycles with 1-6 and 7-9 is a puzzle they'll want to keep at, and 'can six wins in a row make you sure?' sparks good arguments.

g45.why: Kids get the cycle surprise, then construction puzzles with all-arrangements searches, then a clean proof that two-card decks can't cycle. Each step builds on a hands-on game, and the reasoning is within reach.

best_moment: Realising that whichever deck your partner picks, you can always pick one that beats it.
biggest_problem: The K-1 pages front-load three tables of rote comparisons before any play, so the youngest kids may tire before the surprise.
one_change: Start every band with the 'you choose first, I'll choose second and beat you' game, and have kids count pairs only after they suspect something odd.

title: Row and column shadows

k1.why: Putting counters on a small grid to match row and column counts is concrete and nonogram-like, and finding a second picture is a nice challenge. Matching rows and columns at once strains some 5-year-olds, and drawing the full six-picture catalog is long for them.

g23.why: The switch move and 'make a picture your partner can't copy differently' are good puzzles. Several pages are find-every-picture or find-every-switch catalogs that become recording work.

g45.why: Counting pictures and shortest switch routes leads to a real general rule for two rows. But the tasks are dry catalog-and-distance work on 2-row grids with little surprise, and the payoff is a formula rather than an aha.

best_moment: Two children build different pictures that cast exactly the same shadows.
biggest_problem: After the first ambiguity surprise, most pages are catalogs of near-identical small grids, so recording takes over from discovery.
one_change: Make the partner challenge, 'hide a picture, give only its shadows, can I find a different one?', the spine for all bands, with catalogs as optional proof work.

title: Same area, different boundaries

k1.why: Building the five four-tile shapes and making long or short shapes with tiles is concrete and fun. Counting 10-14 exposed sides with edge markers is doable but slow, and Problem 5 (explain why some lengths are impossible) is beyond most K-1 children.

g23.why: Kids build with tiles, discover that every perimeter is even, and find the 4n-2e rule by counting shared sides. Explaining why a straight row is longest gives them an aha earned by building.

g45.why: The early optimisation problems are good, and the row/column bound is real reasoning. Later pages (37, 50 and 73 tiles, a general area-perimeter rule) move to paper-and-formula work far from the tiles, so it gets abstract and dry.

best_moment: Noticing that no matter how you arrange the tiles, the boundary count is always even.
biggest_problem: Counting boundary sides one by one is slow and error-prone, and it dominates the younger tables' time.
one_change: Give K-1 a 'snake versus blob' race (longest and shortest boundary with the same tiles) using a string or edge-marker loop instead of a full catalog, and keep the large-n formula pages as optional 4-5 extensions.

title: Stable pairings

k1.why: A 5-year-old has to read preference strips, remember who is currently paired, and check two different preferences at once for each possible blocking pair. The adult reads and checks while the child points at tokens, so the child isn't making the mathematical move.

g23.why: Finding every stable pairing among six (or 24) pairings means checking many cross pairs against two strips each. That is a long, error-prone bookkeeping task with little joy, and the four-pair problem is especially heavy.

g45.why: Running the asking algorithm and proving it ends and is stable is a classic upper-elementary investigation, and the 'make the greedy rule fail' task is a good construction. But tracking holds and requests by hand is a long simulation, and kids may lose track before the proof.

best_moment: Running the asking rules with the other side asking and getting a different stable pairing.
biggest_problem: The core action is cross-checking abstract preference lists, which overloads working memory and reading at the lower bands and turns into bookkeeping at the upper one.
one_change: Run it as role-play with characters such as animals choosing houses: each child holds one character's card and acts out the asking rules, and only grades 4-5 try to prove stability.

title: Flat folds at one vertex

k1.why: Folding a precreased disk flat is a nice hands-on move. But labelling mountain and valley from a fixed front after unfolding is confusing, small tabs are fiddly, and finding all eight labelings needs systematic bookkeeping a 5-year-old won't sustain.

g23.why: Fitting loose angle wedges into half-turns is a pleasant physical puzzle, and 'which disks can't fold, and why' gives a real obstruction. Folding precreased paper reliably and reading M/V labels will need adult rescue.

g45.why: The alternating-angle condition is a satisfying discovery from paper, and classifying the eight right-angle labelings is solid reasoning. Paper models of the odd angles may not cooperate, and the angle-arithmetic pages are fairly dry.

best_moment: A disk that looks fine refuses to fold flat, and the wedges show why: the alternating angles don't add to a half-turn.
biggest_problem: The kit takes about two and a quarter hours of cutting and precreasing, far beyond a busy parent's 30 minutes, and none of it has been physically folded yet.
one_change: Cut the kit to one or two precreased squares per child, folded from plain paper at the table, plus one wedge set per table, and drop the K-1 tab and route-card materials.

title: Two-length rod builders

k1.why: Building lengths from 3-rods and 4-rods and noticing that 5 can't be made is concrete and a 5-year-old can do it. The 1 cm card-stock rods are small and fiddly to line up for little hands, and 'could you keep going forever?' needs adult framing.

g23.why: Hunting for the last impossible length is a gripping puzzle. Discovering that three consecutive builds plus one more 3-rod cover everything after gives a real aha, and 2-rods and 4-rods are a nice counterexample.

g45.why: Comparing last gaps across pairs and conjecturing ab-a-b is a genuine pattern discovery. The 'finite certificate covers infinitely many' argument is accessible and satisfying.

best_moment: Realising that once you can build three lengths in a row with 3-rods and 4-rods, you can build every length forever.
biggest_problem: At K-1 the 1 cm paper rods are small and fiddly, so building sometimes becomes alignment work instead of thinking.
one_change: Use larger rods (2 cm per unit, or Cuisenaire rods or linking cubes) for K-1 and frame it as a 'which numbers can the shop sell?' story with a hunt for the last impossible one.

title: Two-pan weight kits

k1.why: Laying cube sticks end to end and matching row lengths is a real hands-on move a 5- or 6-year-old can do, and finding that 3 beside the 2 balances 1 is a nice small surprise. But 'beside the target' takes careful adult modelling, and checking every target from 1 to 6 for three kits, then up to 13, becomes adult-tracked checking well before minute 25.

g23.why: Choosing 8, 9 or 10 and finding that only 9 fills 1 to 13 is a satisfying puzzle with sticks in hand. P3 asks for about 40 balance checks, and the counting bound (P5) and the fourth weight (P6) turn into adult explanation for most children this age.

g45.why: It is a classic puzzle with a real 'aha': powers of three, and placing weights on the target's side. Kids can build, guess and check the next weight themselves, and the proofs that it's unique and best possible stretch strong 4-5 children without asking them to know algebra.

best_moment: Realising a weight can go on the same pan as the target, so 1 and 3 suddenly make 2.
biggest_problem: The younger bands drift from moving sticks into systematic checking of long target lists, which is bookkeeping rather than discovery.
one_change: For K-1 and 2-3, make it a partner challenge game: one child names a target, the other races to balance it with the kit, and the 1-3-9 kit is revealed as 'the kit that never loses'.

title: Hidden orchard

k1.why: Stretching a taped thread to a dot and seeing that another dot sits right on it is concrete and easy to show. But keeping the thread exactly through small dots is a fine-motor strain for 5-year-olds, and circling every visible dot on 24 to 48 dots, plus P3's systematic blocker counts, becomes long checking.

g23.why: Thread testing gives way to pattern hunting: 'both even means hidden' fails on (4,4) and (6,6), which is a good surprise. Children can make the divisibility guess themselves, but there's a lot of coordinate listing and near-miss arguing about whether the thread really touches a dot.

g45.why: Kids can discover the common-factor rule from the thread, and (13,8), where the thread seems to hit dots that the rule says it misses, is a genuine 'the math beats the string' moment. The both-directions proof and the target with 99 blockers give real depth.

best_moment: Finding that (1,1) hides the whole diagonal, and later that (13,8) is visible even though the thread looks blocked.
biggest_problem: Thread precision on small dots causes disputes and fine-motor frustration, especially for the youngest, and P1-P3 ask for full-grid sweeps.
one_change: Use a large floor or table grid with pegs or coins as trees and a long string held by two children, so 'can you see it?' becomes a physical game before any recording.

title: Squares inside rectangles

k1.why: Placing card squares onto rectangles is a fine fitting task, but the 1 cm grid and 1 cm cut squares are tiny for 5-year-olds, and each problem's payoff ('which square comes last?', 'do they match?') is an outcome nobody that age cares about. An adult will run the rule while kids place pieces.

g23.why: Drawing the biggest square, then the next, is a clear procedure children can do, and linking the last square to equal tilings is a real pattern to find. Minute to minute, though, it's repeated drawing and recording of side lists, with the 'aha' resting on comparisons an adult has to steer.

g45.why: Predicting the last square (the greatest common divisor) and proving the invariant are substantial, and the 49-rectangle search crowning 13x8 (Fibonacci) is a nice reveal if the search is shared. Kids who already know common factors may find the rule unsurprising, and the search is largely bookkeeping.

best_moment: The pooled search revealing that 13 by 8 alone gives five different square sizes.
biggest_problem: The core activity is a repeated draw-a-square-and-record procedure with a quiet payoff, and the K-1 materials are too small to handle comfortably.
one_change: Make it a race or prediction game on big grids (2 cm or larger, with large cut squares): predict the last square before cutting, and score correct predictions, so the procedure serves a guess children care about.

title: Prime-length necklaces

k1.why: Putting counters on a ring is easy, but the work is reading letter strings from a moved start arrow and judging whether two readouts are the same ring by rotation. That's too many things to hold in mind for most 5- to 6-year-olds, and counting 'readouts' is an abstraction that an adult will end up tracking.

g23.why: Sorting the eight and then the 32 printed cards into rotation families is a real, checkable group task, and finding that every mixed five-bead family has exactly five cards, so 32/5 'doesn't work', is a nice puzzle. But reading and rotating 5-letter strings is dry, and cutting and sorting 32 cards takes much of the hour.

g45.why: The contrast between 4 and 6 beads (early repeats) and 5 and 7 beads (never) is a genuine surprise, and it leads to a real proof and Fermat-style divisibility. The path there is a long letter-card sort, and P6-P7 are abstract enough that only stronger 4-5 children will own them.

best_moment: Discovering that six-bead rings can repeat after 2 or 3 steps but seven-bead rings never do.
biggest_problem: Using letters instead of beads turns a physical, colourful idea into string reading and card sorting.
one_change: Use real coloured beads on pipe-cleaner loops or coloured counters only (no A/B letter cards), and let children physically spin rings to compare, keeping cards as an optional record for older kids.

title: Hidden turns

k1.why: Making a counter pattern 'your partner can't match' is a lovely challenge, but testing each pattern means tracing and colouring every circle onto tracing paper, then turning and flipping it accurately. 5-year-olds can't do that reliably, so the adult traces and the kids watch.

g23.why: The 'can you beat the tester?' framing works, and finding that two colours fail on small rings but work on six is a real surprise. However, each candidate needs a fresh coloured tracing and up to 11 move checks, so much of the time goes to copying rather than thinking.

g45.why: Minimum-colour questions, the unequal-gaps construction and the minority-of-three bound give 4-5 children real reasoning to defend. Tracing-paper overhead still slows the exploration, and kids who can mentally rotate may find the physical testing tedious.

best_moment: Finding that two colours are hopeless on five spots but suddenly enough on six.
biggest_problem: The tracing-copy workflow (trace, colour, lift, flip, for every candidate) dominates the session and sidelines the youngest.
one_change: Put patterns on a rigid clear disc or paper plate with stickers, so a child can simply pick it up, turn or flip it, and drop it on the printed ring, with no tracing.

title: Footprint borders

k1.why: Laying footprint cards into a repeating border is fun, but the tasks then require tracing-strip copies (the adult traces), measured 'shortest slides', glides and half-turns about chosen points. That's far beyond a 5-year-old's grip on the rules, so the adult operates the testing.

g23.why: Building borders that meet a challenge (matches after a glide but not a flip) is a genuine construction puzzle with cards in hand. But the vocabulary, the tracing strips and the 'shortest matching slide' comparisons pile up rules, and few 7- to 8-year-olds will keep them all straight.

g45.why: Glide-squared-is-a-slide and forced half-turns are real discoveries 4-5 children can test with cards and a copy. P6, 'every symmetry and why no other', is a proof-heavy finish, and handling 24 small cards plus tracing strips is fiddly.

best_moment: Seeing that a walking line of left-right footprints matches itself only by a flip-and-slide, not by either move alone.
biggest_problem: Too many moves and rules (slide, flip, glide, half-turn, shortest lengths) for a tracing-paper workflow, so younger children lose the thread.
one_change: Start with children actually walking in paint or chalk, or stamping footprints, then use a single clear acetate strip for testing, and limit the K-1 and 2-3 pages to slides and glides.

title: Making threes

k1.why: Big shape-and-fill tiles and 'find the third' is SET-like play that some 6-year-olds love. But applying two all-same-or-all-different tests at once is hard for many 5-year-olds (the guide itself gates it), and the largest no-three collection needs checking every triple, which an adult will do.

g23.why: Completing pairs, trading puzzles, and the turn-taking game are quick, tactile and replayable, and finding that every game lasts exactly four moves (so the second player always wins) is a lovely surprise children can test many times.

g45.why: Kids can discover and then prove unique completion, the four-tile maximum (with the pair-markers-in-dishes proof), and the forced game length themselves with tiles in hand. It's a compact, complete world with real proofs.

best_moment: Playing the adding game repeatedly and realising it always ends on move four, whatever anyone does.
biggest_problem: For the youngest, juggling two attributes at once is the bottleneck, and failing it makes every later task adult-checked.
one_change: Give K-1 a one-attribute (shapes only, or colours only) version of the game and pair puzzles first, adding the second attribute only for children who are breezing through.

title: Mirror twins

k1.why: Turning a model to match a partner's is fun, but matching four corners of a 3D tetrahedron in your head and hands is hard at 5 or 6. Repeatedly failing on the mirror pair gives no sense of 'impossible' at this age, and the caps held by sticky tack will fall off small hands.

g23.why: Mirror twins that just won't match is a genuine 'wait, why?' moment (like left and right hands), and the twist that making two letters the same makes them match is a second surprise. Building and relabelling models is fiddly, and P3 and P6 need careful bookkeeping of which caps changed.

g45.why: Children can own the viewing-order certificate, the any-merge-works argument and the count of 12 rotations and 2 classes, which is strong mathematics. But about 1.5 to 2 hours of folding models and caps far exceeds the 30-minute prep limit, and the model has never been pretested.

best_moment: Trying every turn and discovering the mirror-image pair can never be made to match.
biggest_problem: Material prep (13 folded card tetrahedra plus sticky-tack letter caps) is far beyond a busy parent's 30 minutes, and the models are untested.
one_change: Use cheap ready-made objects, such as four coloured gumdrops or clay balls on toothpick tetrahedra or a pack of plastic tetrahedra, with coloured stickers instead of letter caps.

title: Seams and cuts (Möbius bands)

k1.why: Running a marker along a Möbius band and colouring 'both edges' with one colour, then watching an adult cut it into one big loop, gives real gasps even at 5. The four-dot partition pictures and the yes/no grids are too abstract for this age and should be skipped.

g23.why: The middle cut and especially the one-third cut (two linked loops) are guaranteed delight. U/L seam tracking gives children a real way to predict and explain. The four-dot yes/no grids are a dull middle, but the cutting surprises carry the session.

g45.why: Predicting pieces versus edges, explaining them from the seam recipe, and the arrow that comes back reversed give older children deep, checkable reasoning tied to a famous surprise.

best_moment: Cutting the Möbius band down the middle and getting one long loop instead of two, and then the one-third cut giving two linked loops.
biggest_problem: The abstract four-dot partition pictures with yes/no grids sit between the magical cuts and the children, and keeping all cutting adult-only removes much of the hands-on joy for 7- to 10-year-olds.
one_change: Let grades 2-5 do their own cuts with safety scissors and replace the four-dot grids with a simple predict, cut and count table (pieces, edges, twists), keeping the partition question as an optional extension.

title: Road detours

k1.why: Moving a pawn on a road map is fine, but the task is writing ordered step cards with endpoint labels and arrows and deleting out-and-back pairs. Adults must prepare and record every card, so the 5-year-old watches a letter-string procedure, with no surprise at the end.

g23.why: Children build long routes as card rows and cancel reversals, which quickly becomes symbol manipulation. The tree results are predictable, and the one surprise, that order matters on two rings, comes late, after a lot of transcription.

g45.why: Kids can reach the uniqueness question, the 'zero net loops but it won't disappear' commutator and the 16-versus-8 count themselves, which is real reasoning for strong 4-5 children. The minute-to-minute activity is still writing and reducing route strings.

best_moment: Finding that going around left, right, left backwards, right backwards cannot be undone, even though every loop is cancelled out on net.
biggest_problem: The concrete pawn quickly gives way to recording and cancelling ordered letter strings, which is bookkeeping without much payoff for the younger bands.
one_change: Make it a physical string or yarn game: children walk a yarn trail around posts (trees versus rings) and pull it tight to see what survives, saving the step-card reduction for 4-5.

title: Loop color certificates (knot tricoloring)

k1.why: The cords are fun to handle, and the 3-by-3 crossing completion (P2) is a good marker puzzle. But counting arcs on a tangled figure-eight, reading the arc/underpass rule, coloring a thin channel and the end-dot move check (P6) are beyond most 5–6-year-olds, so the adult ends up doing the reading and checking.

g23.why: Untangling cords A–D and then finding all nine trefoil colorings are real puzzles a 7–8-year-old can do with tracing paper and a partner referee. The two-crossing end-dot table (P5–6) is abstract bookkeeping with no clear reason to care at that age.

g45.why: The arc is great: cord C refuses to come undone, and the coloring count (9 vs 3) proves it can never be done. It depends on a supplied theorem and a 27-case slide check that feels like a chore, and the cords need careful adult preparation (trefoil handedness, taped joins).

best_moment: Three cords fall open into a plain loop but cord C will not, and then the coloring count shows it never can.
biggest_problem: Most of the session is a rule-checking exercise on thin printed channels and end-dot tables, while the one exciting physical contrast (cords) is a single short problem.
one_change: Build the session around the cord race and a large trefoil to color with fat markers or colored string pieces, and keep the Reidemeister end-dot checks as a 4–5 return visit only.

title: Torus portals and lifts

k1.why: Moving a pawn off the right edge and popping out on the left is a Pac-Man-like thrill, and 'reach every square in two steps' and 'can two pawns swap?' are concrete. On a tiny 3-by-3 map nearly every move wraps, so a 5-year-old will often lose the row or column and need the adult to say where the pawn goes.

g23.why: Finding trips home in 3 and 6 steps is a good open search. Replaying trips on copy arrays and marking which copy you finish in, on 25 mm copies, is fiddly tracking that will feel like a chore for many 7–8-year-olds.

g45.why: Winding pairs (which copy you end in) are an accessible and surprising invariant. Converting RRRUUU to UUURRR by nine square slides on tracing paper is rote, and the classification question (P6) is a very abstract finish that only a few children will own.

best_moment: Two pawns given the same arrows can never trade places: the gap between them travels with them through every portal.
biggest_problem: The good idea (winding = finishing copy) is buried under small-map wraparound confusion and long copy-tracking and slide sequences on paper.
one_change: Use a larger portal map (or a floor grid) with a target-chasing game, and let the repeated tiled map be built physically for every band before asking about copies or slides.

title: Fair results from a lopsided bag

k1.why: Drawing counters and making color pairs is fun, but 'equal chances when a shape comes out', weighing 9/3/3/1 marked pictures and finding every fair rule are conditional-probability ideas a 5–6-year-old cannot hold. The adult would be doing the thinking.

g23.why: Inventing a fair rule for a 3-red-1-blue bag is a real puzzle, and the 4-by-4 labeled grid makes the RB/BR symmetry checkable. Later questions (changing bags, six-pair promises) are wordy, and the random draws are explicitly set aside as only exploration, so hands-on time is short.

g45.why: Discovering that a lopsided bag can still make a perfectly fair coin is a genuine aha, and the optimality and no-replacement questions give depth. The work quickly becomes reading and grid counting rather than drawing, so some children will drift.

best_moment: Realizing that BR and RB are always equally likely, so even a 3-to-1 bag can produce a fair coin flip.
biggest_problem: The concrete drawing gives way almost at once to reading-heavy exact-probability arguments on labeled grids, and K–1 cannot reach the core idea.
one_change: Make it a two-player game first: each child bets on square or circle under their invented rule and plays 20 rounds, so unfair rules lose visibly before the labeled grid is introduced to explain why.

title: Shuffling picture cards (fair shuffles)

k1.why: Making all six rows of A, B, C with real cards is ideal K–1 work, and drawing from a cup is fun. The ticket-and-swap procedure with two ticket sets and resets is an adult-paced routine for 5–6-year-olds, so the later problems become follow-the-steps.

g23.why: Matching the six ticket stories to the six rows is satisfying, and finding several stories that make the same row under the 'wrong' rule is a nice discovery. Juggling ticket sets and swap rules is a lot of procedure, and the 27-story fairness question needs adult help.

g45.why: The natural-looking shuffle has 27 equally likely stories, which can't split evenly among 6 orders, so it must be unfair. That is a crisp, surprising proof that 10-year-olds can own, and designing a 4- and 5-card fair shuffle is a satisfying build.

best_moment: Seeing that the obvious 'swap each slot with any slot' shuffle has 27 stories, and 27 can't be shared fairly among 6 orders.
biggest_problem: Swap procedures with ticket-set resets are easy to misexecute and dominate the younger tables' time.
one_change: Give K–1 and 2–3 more time with direct card choosing and building all rows, and introduce the swap procedure only through an adult-led demonstration with children acting as slots.

title: The bag that copies (Pólya urn)

k1.why: Draw, put back, add a copy is a simple physical action, and 'which bags can you make?' and 'can blue ever disappear?' are answerable by doing. Listing every four-draw color story (P3–4) is recording work an adult will carry, with little surprise for this age.

g23.why: Seeing that color stories and marked histories count differently is real thinking, but tracking marked counters (R1, R2, B1…) through two draws and comparing chances exactly is heavy for 7–8-year-olds. The copy versus no-copy contrast is a good hook if an adult keeps the records.

g45.why: The surprise that 0, 1, 2 or 3 red draws are all equally likely is striking, and predicting the pattern for 4 and 5 draws is a good conjecture task. Getting there requires enumerating 24 marked histories, which is bookkeeping-heavy.

best_moment: After counting histories, every possible number of red draws comes out exactly equally likely, which nobody expects from a bag that 'favors' what it already has.
biggest_problem: Most of the time goes into enumerating and labeling histories rather than playing with the bag, so the delightful uniformity result arrives late.
one_change: Open with a whole-group experiment: everyone runs 3 copying draws many times and stacks a class bar chart of red counts, so the flat result is seen first and the marked histories then explain it.

title: The visible side (Bertrand's box)

k1.why: The behind-the-screen guessing round is fun, but the ticket-to-face mapping, filtering to 'red showing' and then comparing hidden colors, plus ticket-removal ties, needs more abstraction and working memory than most 5–6-year-olds have. The adult would run the sorting.

g23.why: Sorting the six tickets and seeing that red showing hides red two ways out of three is a good surprise for 7–8-year-olds. The card, ticket, screen and cover setup is fiddly, and the later chooser comparisons are wordy.

g45.why: Refuting the friend's 'only two cards remain so 50-50' argument is a classic paradox that 10-year-olds enjoy, and the extra-clue and fair-subset questions add depth. The game is barely played (no tally), so the surprise rests on argument rather than on experience.

best_moment: Realizing the friend's 'two cards, so fifty-fifty' is wrong because the red-red card has two ways to show red.
biggest_problem: The paradox is delivered through ticket bookkeeping with a fiddly screen-and-cover protocol instead of through a game where children feel the 2-to-1 odds.
one_change: Play a betting game: one child always bets the hidden side matches, another bets it differs, over 20–30 rounds. Let the lopsided score raise the question, then use the tickets to explain it.

title: Two boards forget their starts

k1.why: Two three-counter boards and 'set this slot to blue on both' is easy to do and check, and drawing instruction cards from a cup adds a game feel. Once a child sees 'fix each different slot' there is little left to find, so engagement may fade.

g23.why: Which stories guarantee a match, and the contrast that shared toggles can never merge two boards, are nice ideas. The minute-to-minute work is applying instructions to two boards and comparing, with modest surprise.

g45.why: The mixed-story criterion and the 'last visit decides' argument for uniform final boards are real reasoning. The probability problem over 16 color stories is abstract, and much of the activity is applying instruction lists.

best_moment: Toggles can never make two different boards match, however many you use, while one 'set' instruction per slot always can.
biggest_problem: The core idea (matching takes one instruction per differing slot) is nearly obvious, so the activity offers little surprise or struggle before it turns abstract.
one_change: Turn it into a challenge game: one player secretly sets up two boards and the other must write the shortest blind instruction list guaranteed to make any pair match, with toggles added as a 'trap' card.

title: Gentle-step landscapes

k1.why: Placing counters as mountain heights with the 'no big jumps' rule is concrete, quick to check, and full of small puzzles (highest and lowest star, impossible clues). Making a two-clue puzzle for a friend is very appealing at this age, though an adult must read the prompts.

g23.why: Constraint puzzles with counters, impossible clue sets, smallest and largest total heights, and designing puzzles with one or many solutions for a partner give lots of independent play and real 'why it can't work' reasoning.

g45.why: The first four pages repeat the easier 2–3 tasks. The later envelope and fillability questions (P5–7) are meaty but are pure reasoning with no game, so some 10-year-olds will find the start too easy and the end too abstract.

best_moment: Discovering that clues 0 and 3 only two steps apart can never be joined, and then stumping a partner with your own forced-landscape puzzle.
biggest_problem: For grades 4–5 the shared opening is too easy and the general question arrives without a playful hook.
one_change: Give grades 4–5 a puzzle-design challenge (clues that force exactly one landscape on the seven-site board with the fewest clues) as the bridge into the envelope argument.

title: Inside and outside covers (area bounds)

k1.why: Marking whole squares and laying tiles over the triangle is fine. But choosing refinements to remove the most tiles, redrawing the diamond so small cells become 'partly gray' while keeping big-cell status, and drawing shapes with set areas are precise, abstract tasks beyond most 5–6-year-olds.

g23.why: Trapping an area between inside and cover counts is understandable, and the 'same markings, very different areas' question is a good twist. Most of the time is counting cells and converting small squares to big-square units, with little surprise.

g45.why: Optimizing which three squares to split and explaining why refining never worsens the bounds are real thinking, and finding the exact area is a satisfying close. The activity is still count-heavy, and cutting 64 tiles per pair is a big preparation load.

best_moment: Finding that refining the trapezoid shrinks its uncertainty from 12 to 3, not just in half, so it pays to split the right squares.
biggest_problem: It is mostly careful cell counting and recording, with the interesting estimation ideas left implicit, and the tile prep is heavy.
one_change: Frame it as a contest: each team gets a budget of splits to make the tightest trap around a blob, then compare. Drop pre-cut tiles in favor of shading on large printed grids.

title: Four towers and differences (Ducci)

k1.why: Finding the gap between two cube towers by matching is a lovely concrete move, and 'make a start that lasts long' is a clear goal. Rebuilding four towers on a second mat each round with up to 40 cubes is slow and error-prone for 5–6-year-olds, so the adult will manage the simultaneous update.

g23.why: Diffy-square rings are a proven favorite: quick subtraction, a clear race to make the longest-lasting start, and the shock that three stations can cycle forever while four always die. Predecessor puzzles add a good 'impossible' twist.

g45.why: Hunting for a 7-move start, then explaining through parity and doubling why every four-station ring must end, gives a full arc from play to proof that 10-year-olds can follow.

best_moment: The three-station ring 1,0,0 never reaches zero and cycles forever, unlike every four-station ring.
biggest_problem: For the youngest children, the two-mat cube rebuild each round is a slow simulation that an adult has to police.
one_change: Let K–1 work with heights 0–3 and number cards or one-row cube records, and let older children switch from cubes to written numbers as soon as the rule is clear.

title: Staircases and lengths

k1.why: A 5-year-old has to bend string along every corner of a ruled staircase on a blank page and tape it there, then compare two strings. It is fiddly, and 'the straight diagonal is 200 mm' and 'fewest turns' mean little to them, so the adult ends up doing the string work while the child watches.

g23.why: Adding 160+120 and seeing that a zig-zag hugging the diagonal is still 280 mm is a real surprise. But ruling staircases inside a 30 mm strip on an ungridded page is slow, and explaining why 8 turns is the minimum is beyond most of them.

g45.why: The paradox (it looks like the diagonal yet stays 280, never 200) is a good 'wait, what?' and the leftward-path variant is nice. Much of the hour is careful ruler drawing in narrow strips, and the turn-minimum proof needs an adult to steer.

best_moment: Measuring a tiny-step staircase that almost sits on the diagonal and finding its string is still exactly as long as the big L-shaped route.
biggest_problem: The core action is precise pencil-and-ruler drawing on blank paper, plus string taped along small corners, so effort goes into drafting rather than into the idea.
one_change: Print a fine square grid inside the rectangle, or use pipe cleaners or snap-cube trains, so children can build ever-finer staircases quickly and spend their time on the surprise that the length never shrinks.

title: Honest measurement ranges

k1.why: 'A hidden end can be anywhere in its gray band' is an abstract, adult-language idea. Juggling two range cards, a strip set and a target with guarantee words is more than a 5-year-old can hold, so the parent reads everything and in practice runs it.

g23.why: Picking strips and adding them is doable, and 'break my promise' gives a little adversarial fun. But the tightest guaranteed range and the shared-versus-separate A are interval arithmetic dressed up in strips, with no moment an 8-year-old would gasp at.

g45.why: Older children can run the beat-the-claim game and the widest-safe-card design, and the 'remove the very same A' cancellation is a real insight. It is dry, mostly verbal reasoning about bounds, with lots of reading per page.

best_moment: A partner picks the most awkward allowed strips and breaks the other child's 'it always ends between 8 and 9' promise.
biggest_problem: Guaranteed ranges and dependency are abstract ideas with no natural surprise, and the strips only illustrate addition, so it feels like careful worksheet logic rather than play.
one_change: Rebuild it as a two-player bluffing game, with a hidden length in a bag that you must promise a range for and the opponent tries to beat, and drop the formal tight-bound wording for younger bands.

title: Hinged frames and braces

k1.why: Pushing a wobbly square, then feeling it lock when a diagonal goes in, is immediately satisfying for small hands. But they cannot open and close brass fasteners to move braces, so an adult swaps every bar, and the drawing they are asked to do is a weak record.

g23.why: Testing designs on a 2-by-2 frame and hunting for the fewest braces is a hands-on puzzle with an instant physical check. The surprise that 'a brace in every row' can still wobble is very engaging.

g45.why: The physical 2-by-3 work is great. The jump to row/column dots and connectivity is beautiful but is introduced through an adult-led handoff, and the later problems are paper-only claims about 4-by-5 grids that many children will not own.

best_moment: A frame with a brace in every row and every column still flops sideways when pushed.
biggest_problem: The kit (108 bars, 35 braces, 90 pin fasteners, an estimated 70-90 minutes of cutting and punching, unrehearsed) is far beyond a busy parent's 30 minutes, and every brace change needs fiddly pin work.
one_change: Use a ready-made kit or a quick build (craft sticks or straws with pipe cleaners, braces that clip on without unpinning) so children can move braces themselves and prep fits in 30 minutes.

title: Connecting networks

k1.why: Buying roads with counters and checking a pawn can reach every town is a playful frame, and the three-town maps are small enough. 'Find every cheapest purchase' is beyond them, so the adult reads and steers, and the fun is mostly in paying and tracing.

g23.why: Spending counters to connect towns is a game with a clear goal and a quick check. The trap (buying the three cheapest roads leaves D stranded) gives a real 'oh!' Children can play with 4-5 town maps on their own.

g45.why: Swaps, must-buy and never-buy links, and designing prices for unique optima are genuine puzzles. But pages 6-9 become wordy proof questions (Problem 8 asks three things at once) that will lose some children.

best_moment: Grabbing the three cheapest roads, then realizing the traveler can't get to D.
biggest_problem: Most maps are small, so the younger tables run out of challenge quickly, while the upper pages swing to reading-heavy proofs about every/some/none.
one_change: Add one or two bigger, juicier maps (8-10 towns) for a beat-the-adult's-cost challenge between the small catalogs and the proof pages.

title: Partitions and rebuilding

k1.why: Snapping cubes into strips and hearing 'that's the same as before' is approachable, and joining nine 1s down to an 8 and a 1 is satisfying. But deciding whether two collections are the same takes more than they can hold, the parent records everything, and there is no packet of their own.

g23.why: Building all the collections of 4, 5 or 6 cubes is concrete. Finding that the odd-only and all-different lists come out the same length is a nice coincidence. Complete catalogs are bookkeeping, and an unsystematic 8-year-old will miss and repeat cases.

g45.why: Join-pairs and halve-evens as a reversible machine that matches the two lists is a gorgeous, physical aha. The row/column flip on drawings gives a second surprise they can check themselves.

best_moment: Splitting all the evens to odds, then joining equal pairs back, and watching exactly the starting collection reappear.
biggest_problem: Complete enumeration of partitions carries the early pages, and it leans on systematic listing that younger children find tedious and error-prone.
one_change: Let a table pool their collections on movable cards (one partition per card) so the count comparison emerges from sorting rather than each child listing everything.

title: Few sums and equal spacing

k1.why: Every move is an addition fact up to 18, and the parent supplies sums when counting is slow. The question 'how many different places?' is a counting chore with no visible payoff for a 5-year-old.

g23.why: Third graders can add the pairs and enjoy trying to make as few or as many totals as possible. Minute to minute, though, it is checking all pairs and placing counters, essentially addition practice until the pattern appears.

g45.why: Designing card sets for the fewest totals and predicting m+n-1 is a real conjecture hunt, and the grid route argument is elegant. It is bookkeeping-heavy, and the equality-case proof (Problem 10) is adult-level.

best_moment: Discovering that 0,1,2 with 0,1,2 gives only 5 totals while scattered cards give 9, and that equal spacing is the trick.
biggest_problem: The core action is exhaustively adding every pair and marking repeats, which feels like arithmetic drill before any surprise arrives.
one_change: Open with the design challenge as a two-team contest (fewest totals wins) using a pre-made addition table to read sums, so effort goes to choosing sets rather than computing.

title: Corners of a solid

k1.why: Holding models, closing triangle fans into points versus flat, and seeing eight quarter-circle gaps make two whole circles are lovely concrete moments. But edge counting on a cube is error-prone, cutting gap copies is fiddly, and the parent does most of the recording.

g23.why: Counting faces, edges and corners and making fans is engaging, and both totals coming out the same is a pleasant surprise. Filling the four-row V/E/F tables and the degree arithmetic is bookkeeping, and counting edges reliably is hard.

g45.why: Euler's formula and the total gap of 720 degrees are genuine surprises across different solids, and the cube-subdivision tests are nice. Much of the time goes into tables, and the tree-reduction explanation needs heavy adult help.

best_moment: Gathering the cut-out gaps from every corner of a cube and a tetrahedron and finding both piles make exactly two full circles.
biggest_problem: Prep is enormous: 15 tabbed paper polyhedra (72 closing seams), about 90 polygon pieces and 36 gap circles. Children then spend much of the hour filling count tables.
one_change: Use magnetic tiles or Polydron (already suggested as an option) as the default, and cut the tables down to a few solids so the gap-circle surprise comes sooner.

title: Area from dots (Pick's theorem)

k1.why: The side route is building four-square shapes and counting outline dots while the parent traces outlines. The 'always 10 dots except the square' pattern is fine, but it is mostly counting dots with no real hook for a 5-year-old.

g23.why: Finding the area of slanted shapes with squares, halves and cut-and-move tricks is a good puzzle for third graders. Keeping I, B and area records gets tedious, and the rule hunt will need support.

g45.why: Pick's rule is a classic discovery, and building area-6 shapes with different dot counts is satisfying. But a three-variable formula from scattered records is hard to spot unaided, and Problems 7-10 are proof and holes work for a return visit.

best_moment: Two very different-looking shapes with the same inside and boundary dot counts turn out to have exactly the same area.
biggest_problem: The discovery depends on many accurate I/B/area records, so the aha arrives late and only for children who keep careful tallies.
one_change: Hold one variable fixed (all shapes with I=0, then I=1) and pool records on a shared board, so the pattern pops out within 15 minutes.

title: Fair division

k1.why: Children must value trays using someone else's assigned dot card ('A values red at 3') rather than their own wants, which 5-year-olds will not hold. The parent reads the cards, and 'nobody wants to trade' is judged by counting dots.

g23.why: 'I divide, you choose' is instantly understood and fun. Role-playing fixed preference cards, completing the Problem 2 catalog and measuring cuts in mm make it feel more like an exercise than a game.

g45.why: Envy-free versus proportional, and the three-person case where everyone is 'fair' yet everyone envies someone, are genuinely interesting. The definitions take careful reading, and Problems 4 and 7 are verbal proofs.

best_moment: With whole cards someone always wants to trade, but cutting the third square in half suddenly makes everyone happy.
biggest_problem: Fairness is judged from artificial preference cards instead of children's real tastes, which drains the natural emotional pull of 'that's not fair!'
one_change: Use real treats or stickers the children actually prefer differently (or let each child write their own preference card) for the cut-and-choose and envy checks.

title: Constant width

k1.why: Spinning shapes between taped rails and sorting them into stuck, wobbly and snug is hands-on, and the curved triangle spinning snug like a circle is a real surprise. Keeping rails parallel and card pieces from riding over them needs adult help.

g23.why: The rail-spin test in Problem 2 is great. Problem 1 asks for millimetre width measurements with two parallel edges held perpendicular, which is fiddly for 8-year-olds and slow before the surprise.

g45.why: Finding a non-circle that rolls like a circle, building one with a compass, and discovering its center bobs while its width stays fixed are memorable and hands-on. The Problem 4 proof can wait.

best_moment: The curved triangle turns all the way round between the rails, touching both sides the whole time, just like the disk.
biggest_problem: The opening problem is precise width measurement with improvised parallel guides, so younger children may tire before the spin surprise. Prep is an estimated 60-90 minutes for stiff-card pieces.
one_change: Lead with the rail-spin test (and a book rolling on Reuleaux rollers) and make measurement a later check, with pieces cut from thick foam board so they cannot slip under the rulers.

title: Take it or pass

k1.why: Rolling the die and saying take or pass is fun for a few rounds, but inventing a fixed rule and the forced last take are beyond them. The tower comparison of card rows is an adult procedure that children carry out.

g23.why: Playing rounds with the die and counters is a real game, and comparing take and pass on the nine two-offer cards is within reach. The opening rules paragraph is dense, though, and scoring 27 cards twice each is a chore.

g45.why: The core surprise is that you take a 4 with two offers left but pass it with three. Getting there means scoring 54 card lines and comparing averages like 134/27, so the aha comes late and through bookkeeping.

best_moment: Finding that the same 4 should be taken with two offers left but passed with three.
biggest_problem: After a few minutes of genuine game play, the activity turns into scoring long printed card lists, and the averages behind the insight are fractional.
one_change: Keep it a game. Pit two rules against each other in a class tournament of many quick rolled rounds tallied with cubes, and keep the exhaustive card scoring as a short pooled check at the end.

title: Triangles on a ball

k1.why: Holding strings taut on a ball while a partner pins the endpoints is hard for 5-year-olds, and checking right angles on a curved surface with a paper tab is fiddly. The three-square-corner triangle is a real wow, but the adult will end up making it.

g23.why: Problems 1–3 are hands-on, and the three-right-angle triangle is a genuine surprise. String handling and drawing back-side arcs on paper will need a lot of adult steadying.

g45.why: Lune fractions (Problem 4) are accessible. The Girard route through lune pairs and an eight-region count table (Problems 5–7) is a long abstract bookkeeping exercise done on paper views rather than on the ball.

best_moment: Building a triangle with three right-angle corners on the ball, after seeing it is impossible with straws on the table.
biggest_problem: Prep is far beyond a busy parent: globes with meridians, calibrated references and an untested 60–90 minute setup. The string-on-ball handling is fiddly too.
one_change: Use cheap balls and rubber bands, or a marked globe, for one big Problem 2–3 investigation (three right angles, growing the N corner). Drop the lune-pair counting to an optional return visit.

title: Conflict networks (graph coloring)

k1.why: Putting coloured counters on circles so that no line joins two of the same colour is a simple, checkable puzzle that young children can do. The slot-header-and-card layer and the reading need an adult.

g23.why: Small colouring puzzles with a clear goal, a partner checker and a 'why can't fewer work?' question are absorbing at this age. Problems 1–3 and the tree on page 6 give good variety.
