g45.why: Finding the odd-cycle rule and making the greedy first-slot rule waste slots with a bad order are satisfying discoveries with puzzle feel. Problem 9's counting is heavier but optional.

best_moment: Finding an order that makes the first-slot rule use four slots on a network that needs only two.
biggest_problem: The card-under-header plus counter-on-circle double representation adds handling and setup overhead to what is really a colouring puzzle.
one_change: Drop the activity cards and slot headers and just colour circles with counters or crayons, keeping 'slots' as story language.

title: Cards away from home (derangements)

k1.why: Placing A, B, C picture cards so that none sits on its own home, and seeing that exactly two at home is impossible, is doable and has a small aha. The nine-row A–D catalog depends on the adult writing everything.

g23.why: Problems 1 and 3 are a reasonable systematic-listing challenge. The 'repair this student's count' overlap tasks are abstract and lean on the adult.

g45.why: Inclusion–exclusion and the two-family recurrence are real mathematics. The minute-to-minute work is listing and pooling up to 44 five-letter rows and correcting other people's subtractions, which is mostly bookkeeping with little play.

best_moment: Realising that with three or four cards you can never have exactly one card out of place.
biggest_problem: There is no story or game to make 'nobody gets their own' matter, so the work is cataloguing permutations and fixing arithmetic.
one_change: Frame it as a gift swap or hat mix-up. Have children actually shuffle and deal many times and guess how often nobody gets their own before cataloguing.

title: Straight paths on an octagon surface

k1.why: Ruled parallel lines across slanted glued edges with tick matching are far beyond K–1 motor and reading skills. The guide itself points to another week's packet as the real fallback.

g23.why: The packet is labelled grades 3–5. Third graders can enjoy the Pac-Man wrap idea, but keeping a constant heading with a ruler across slanted edges and matching fractional tick positions will need constant adult rescue.

g45.why: Older children can trace trips and compare lengths, and cutting out corner sectors to find three full turns is a lovely concrete surprise. Precise drawing and the dense rules paragraph slow everything down.

best_moment: Fitting the eight cut-out octagon corners around one point and finding they make three full turns.
biggest_problem: Most of the activity is precise ruler drawing and transfer across slanted edges, so accuracy and fine motor control rather than ideas decide success.
one_change: Start with the L-shaped square model, or a square torus on grid paper where paths follow grid lines, and bring in the octagon only for the corner-sector surprise.

title: Hyperbolic octagon streets

k1.why: Moving a 10 mm arrow and choosing turns on the square grid is doable with an adult. The octagon and bending roads only make sense if you accept 'these are straight', which a 5-year-old can't use.

g23.why: The robot walking is accessible, but the key facts (rooms the same size, curved streets are straight) are only asserted. Walking around an octagon taking eight left turns to get home is unsurprising, since it has eight corners.

g45.why: The two parallels through P and the turn-count comparison (two octagons vs two squares) give older children something to reason about. It still rests on trusting the map rather than experiencing the curvature.

best_moment: Finding two straight streets through P that both miss street R, which is impossible on flat paper.
biggest_problem: The hyperbolic geometry is told rather than felt: children walk on a picture whose strangeness they must take on faith.
one_change: Have children tape paper right-angled octagons four to a corner and watch the surface ruffle and refuse to lie flat, then walk the streets on that model.

title: Lamplighter streets

k1.why: Children can build the lamp pictures with counters, but writing move words and comparing fewest moves would be done by the adult. Signed positions and the two-part state are too much.

g23.why: A clear fewest-moves puzzle with a walker and lamps suits third graders, and the partner roles help. Negative positions and small counters on 19 mm spacing need care.

g45.why: Shortest-route puzzles with a convincing lower-bound argument are engaging. The dead-end twist, where every possible move makes the target easier to reach, is a genuine surprise.

best_moment: Discovering that from the seven-move target, every single move L, R or F lands somewhere reachable in six.
biggest_problem: Small counters on a printed strip plus written move words make the state easy to disturb and the work feel like transcription.
one_change: Play it on the floor: a taped number line, cups or cards as lamps, and a child as the walker, with the partner calling and counting moves.

title: Meeting on shortest roads

k1.why: Checking whether a dot is on some shortest route for each of three pairs is too much to hold at once. The adult draws every route while children move counters.

g23.why: Third graders can count steps and find the meeting dot on a grid with an adult. Testing one candidate against three pair conditions taxes working memory, and the payoff ('always exactly one') is quiet.

g45.why: Finding the middle-row, middle-column rule, the triangle with no meeting point and the cube majority rule are good reasoning tasks. The checking routine is heavy and the activity lacks game energy.

best_moment: Trying to place three homes so that no meeting dot works on the grid and failing every time, then finding the triangle map where none works.
biggest_problem: Each candidate needs three simultaneous shortest-route checks drawn in three colours, so the effort goes into verification rather than discovery.
one_change: Make it a 'where should three friends meet so nobody walks out of their way' game on a big floor or table grid with walking tokens, and let the coordinate pattern emerge from several trials.

title: How many ways out (ends of graphs)

k1.why: Placing blockers and tracing with a finger is doable. Closed roads, components and 'forever beyond the page' are subtle, and 6–8 mm blockers on 12 mm spacing are fiddly for small hands.

g23.why: The line problems are almost too easy, but the ladder split (the diagonal pair works) and the tree doubling 3, 6, 12 give real puzzles. An adult helps keep the 'forever' idea straight.

g45.why: Trying and failing to split the endless grid, then seeing why, and watching the tree's forever pieces double are satisfying puzzle-and-argument moments with a nice infinity flavour.

best_moment: Discovering that no finite wall can cut the endless grid into two forever pieces, while a two-dot diagonal cuts the ladder.
biggest_problem: The opening line problems have a trivial answer (always two), and the tiny blockers on dense dot maps are fiddly.
one_change: Open with the ladder challenge on a large board with big blockers, and save the line as a quick warm-up comparison.

title: Thin and fat road triangles

k1.why: Gap distances between colored sides are far beyond K–1. The suggested strip-laying route is adult-run and has no payoff for them.

g23.why: Drawing three shortest routes on trees is fine, but the gap definition (distance to the nearer of two other sides using any road) is a hard multi-part idea to check.

g45.why: The tree fact (every road used by exactly two routes) and building ever-fatter grid triangles to beat a partner's number are nice. Measuring gaps correctly is effortful and error-prone.

best_moment: Beating any number your partner names with a bigger grid triangle.
biggest_problem: Measuring gaps is a slow, abstract definition to apply, so the work is careful distance checking rather than play.
one_change: Make Problem 4 a 'name a number, I'll beat it' duel from the start, using the corner construction on big grid paper, and keep gap measurement to one or two examples.

title: Shields in a portal room

k1.why: There are no K-1 pages and no K-1 route. Wraparound edges, exact-point shields and unfolded room maps are far beyond a 5-year-old.

g23.why: The guide's untested 15-20 minute route needs an adult to trace the drawn portal shots through their edges and then lay a ruler to far target copies. The children mostly watch and mark crosses.

g45.why: Problem 1 (the fewest crosses to block six drawn shots) is a genuine small puzzle. After that, the core move is drawing long ruler lines to target copies and judging whether a pencil line passes exactly through a pencil cross, then carrying shields between copies with tracing paper. That is a precision-drawing chore where measuring error decides the outcome. The midpoint 'aha' needs coordinates and odd/even halving that most kids will only hear from the adult.

best_moment: In Problem 1, seeing that the four corner-to-centre diagonals can't share a shield, so at least four are needed, and then fitting in the two forced shields.
biggest_problem: Whether a shot gets through depends on exact point-on-line judgments across unfolded copies, so the game turns into careful ruler work and tracing-paper transfers instead of reasoning.
one_change: Use only lattice-point shields and shots drawn on a coarse grid (or string on a pegboard), so a hit is obvious at a glance. Turn Problem 3 into a quick blocker-versus-shooter game.

title: Can you hear the room? (billiard bounce words)

k1.why: There is no K-1 material, and reflected-copy unfolding plus wall-letter words is far beyond this age.

g23.why: The packet is Grades 4-5 only with no younger route. Holding ruler lines through reflected copies while reading letters in order is too much for most 7-year-olds.

g45.why: Drawing straight shots through the printed grid of copies and reading off three-letter words is something a 10-year-old can do alone. ABA being impossible in the square but possible in the rhombus is a real surprise. The rhombus unfolding and mirror checks are fiddly, though, and the secret-room game needs impossibility arguments that kids will replace with 'I couldn't find one' unless the organizer steers. The all-words stretch proof is adult-led.

best_moment: Discovering that a shot can go A, B, A in the pointy rhombus (it bounces straight back off B) when that seemed impossible in the square.
biggest_problem: Past Problem 1, progress depends on precise rhombus constructions, mirror alignment and proofs of impossibility. These stall children and push the adult into constructing shots.
one_change: Supply pre-drawn rhombus unfoldings with a few candidate shots to check, and play the secret-room guessing game only with already-checked words, so the game runs without new constructions.

title: A robot that remembers (signed area)

k1.why: There is no K-1 route, and adding column numbers to a separate memory strip is beyond this age.

g23.why: The packet is Grades 4-5 only. From Problem 2 on it needs adding and subtracting negative column numbers on a signed strip, which most 7-year-olds can't do yet.

g45.why: The card routes in Problem 1 are concrete and finishable, and 'same place, different memory' is a nice surprise that links to counting squares left of the route. Kids juggle a robot counter, a move-card sequence and a memory marker with signed arithmetic, so one partner is mostly doing bookkeeping. Negative columns will need repeated adult help.

best_moment: Realising that a route's memory is just the number of squares on one side of it, so a loop remembers its area.
biggest_problem: Running three parallel records (position, card order, signed memory) makes the minute-to-minute activity bookkeeping, and the signed steps invite errors that hide the pattern.
one_change: Let children shade the squares left of the route as their 'memory' from the start, and bring in the strip and negative columns only after the area idea lands.

title: The gentlest stretch (rectangle to square)

k1.why: There is nothing for K-1. Ratios of distances and whole-sheet maps don't fit this age.

g23.why: The guide says there is no Grades 2-3 route. Stretch ratios and homeomorphism-style rules are out of reach.

g45.why: The concrete part is ruler-and-paper-strip measuring of many dot pairs, where the key differences are below a millimetre (the guide admits this). The intended discoveries (every placement ties, the midpoint tests single out the centre, any legal map stretches some pair by 2) come from adult arguments, not from anything children can see. Inventing a 'rule for every point' is very abstract for a 10-year-old.

best_moment: Noticing that the pair A-D always doubles no matter where O goes, so the score can never beat 2.
biggest_problem: The hands-on activity is tedious measuring that can't reveal the intended distinctions, so the real mathematics stays with the adult.
one_change: Rebuild it around physically stretching a gridded rubber sheet or elastic onto the square and comparing a few dramatic pairs, and drop the near-centre midpoint precision task.

title: Doubling elevators

k1.why: The adult-led route has a 5-year-old move a marker along tiny 5.8 mm dot spacings while the adult tallies, and the payoff is one-move savings (6 versus 5). There is a seed of 'going up is faster', but the adult carries the counting.

g23.why: Problem 1 and target 8 need only adding 1, 2 and 4, and finding a shorter route than a partner is motivating. The small dots and the stride-strip procedure need adult steadying, but children make the real choices.

g45.why: It's a clear game with a goal (fewest moves) and a challenge-your-partner structure, and the elevator shortcut and stepping past 23 and back are genuine surprises. Problems 3-4 turn naturally into 'can anyone beat 8?' arguments. The strip handling and small dot spacing are the main friction.

best_moment: Finding that the fastest way to 23 is to go to 24 and step back left, beating every route that only moves right.
biggest_problem: Dots 5.8 mm apart and a ruler-like stride strip make each move fiddly, which slows the game and invites miscounts.
one_change: Print a larger board where the higher levels have marked landing spots (or use a floor or number-line version with tape), so moves are instant and kids can focus on route choices.

title: Twists on a cylinder (winding)

k1.why: There is no K-1 route. Signed seam crossings and fixed-endpoint yarn routes on a tube are beyond this age.

g23.why: The packet is Grades 4-5 only, with signed counting, repeated-strip lifts and twist words, and there is no younger entry.

g45.why: Wrapping yarn around a taped paper tube and counting signed seam crossings is tactile, and a 10-year-old can do it. The crossing puzzle in Problem 6 has a satisfying hidden rule. The guide admits the yarn slides toward a helix and won't hold a route, and the twist operation (shifting points by fractional turns per height) is a drawing chore. Twist words reduce to counting plus and minus signs, which is too easy.

best_moment: Finding that two yarns with windings 0 and 3 can't avoid crossing twice, however you lay them, and then guessing the rule for 2 and 7.
biggest_problem: The physical yarn routes are hard to hold in place on a paper tube, so the concrete model may fight the children exactly when they need it.
one_change: Use a cardboard tube with pegs or pins at A and B and a few anchor pins up the sides so yarn routes stay put, and cut Problems 4-5 down to a quick oral question.

title: Substitution strips (Thue-Morse)

k1.why: With a parent reading, a 5-year-old can place AB under A and BA under B with big tiles and watch the row double. 'Can three of the same sit together?' is a question they can check by looking. The proofs and crops are beyond them, and the adult paces it.

g23.why: Growing to 16 tiles, finding triples and spotting forged whole rows by undoing pairs suit third graders (the packet says 3-5). Second graders may find the 16-tile build and the reading load tiring. Crops and Problems 5-7 are beyond most.

g45.why: Tiles keep it hands-on, and the forgery-detection framing (which rows were really grown? find the hidden seam) is a detective game with clear verdicts. The equal-neighbour seam trick is an aha kids can find themselves. Problem 7's proof needs adult support, but the first four problems carry a session.

best_moment: Unmasking a fake row because undoing it leaves a pair like BB or AA, which no tile could have made.
biggest_problem: Building and rebuilding long tile rows takes table space and time, and the crop and pairing rules in Problems 4-6 add enough conventions that some children lose the thread.
one_change: Supply pre-built 8- and 16-tile 'suspect' strips on card so children spend their time detecting and arguing, not re-laying tiles.

title: Persistent holes

k1.why: In the adult-led route, the child lays strips and covers triangles while the adult reads and records. 'Is every triangle inside covered?' is easy, but there's nothing to puzzle over, and the saved-loop idea is invisible at this age.

g23.why: The same adult-led route plus the DA-versus-AC ordering question. Children place pieces, but keeping a saved loop separate from the growing board and following stage schedules is adult-run.

g45.why: The pieces are concrete, but the minute-to-minute work is copying edge tokens, cancelling pairs and replaying four-stage schedules under many rules (saved lists unchanged, batches, legal fillings). The interesting contrast (hole counts identical, loop lifetimes differ) arrives late and needs adult interpretation. Few 10-year-olds would ask to play again.

best_moment: Seeing that one tile kills the triangle loop but the outer square loop survives either single tile and needs both.
biggest_problem: Rules and token bookkeeping dominate, so children spend their time running a procedure the adult has to police instead of exploring holes.
one_change: Cut to the square and joined boards with a physical 'pour water in the loop' framing (does the filled region seal the rim?), and drop the token cancellation and stage cards.

title: Three-armed lines (tropical geometry)

k1.why: The adult-led route has children slide a traced shape without turning it to touch dots. That's a small physical game, but with little to discover at 5, and keeping the shape unrotated is uncertain.

g23.why: The same adult-led slide-the-shape route on two boards. Children can find 'one place' versus 'lots of places', but the adult reads everything and the session is short and thin.

g45.why: Drawing three-armed lines from chosen junctions with a traced template is concrete, and 'these lines always meet, sometimes along a whole ray' is a real surprise against ordinary parallel lines. Problems 1-2 and 4 work independently. The 'least number is tied' definition and the general rules in 3, 6 and 7 lean on the adult's rectangle proof.

best_moment: Trying hard to make two three-armed lines miss each other and discovering they never can.
biggest_problem: The min-of-three definition up front is abstract and adds reading, and the general-rule problems turn into adult proof talk.
one_change: Launch purely with the tracing-paper shape as the definition and frame Problem 6 as a challenge: 'make two lines that never meet; your partner wins if they cross'.

title: Numbered-ball detectives (Ross-Littlewood)

k1.why: There are no K-1 pages. In the adult-run route the child finds and moves the smallest card, which is doable, but it's a repetitive simulation with no surprise at this age.

g23.why: Cards in bowls are concrete, and predicting card 20's days without running 20 days is a satisfying pattern find. Problem 4's choose-the-moves puzzle with an impossible row is a real challenge. The first problems are a repetitive enactment that can drag.

g45.why: The simulations go quickly for 10-year-olds. Problem 5's paradox (every card eventually leaves A, yet A keeps growing) can produce a real 'whoa', but it's phrased abstractly and needs a skilled adult to land. Problem 4's stuck day is a good proof-of-impossibility moment.

best_moment: Realising that every card eventually moves to B, yet bowl A holds more cards every day, and that under the other rule half the cards stay in A forever.
biggest_problem: Problems 1-3 are rote day-by-day card moving before the interesting questions arrive, so some children tire before the paradox.
one_change: Shorten the enactment to three or four days, jump to the 'predict card 20' and 'when is A empty?' questions, and stage the paradox as a debate.

title: Midnight laboratory (lamp paradox)

k1.why: The adult folds the strip and tells the story; the child only flips a card four times and says ON or OFF. 'Will there ever be a last fold?' is a nice question, but it gets a one-word answer and then the activity is over.

g23.why: The hands-on part is four folds and four card flips, which takes about five minutes. After that it is talk about something nobody can do, and Problem 3 ('make up a rule that settles') needs abstract rule-writing, which these children will need an adult to scribe and steer.

g45.why: Ten-year-olds can enjoy arguing about whether the light is on or off at midnight, and the halfway counter against the flipping card is a good contrast. But Problems 4-6 are worded as philosophy ('What, if anything, does the switching rule alone tell you'), and the discussion lives or dies on how well the adult runs it.

best_moment: Children who were sure the light ends ON or ends OFF realize there is no last switch to decide it.
biggest_problem: There is almost no concrete action: after a few folds and flips, the session is an abstract endpoint debate.
one_change: Make it a commit-and-defend debate game: each child bets ON or OFF at midnight and tries to convince the others, and pair it with a physical Zeno walk toward a wall to set up the contrast with the counter that converges.

title: Buckets of Fish

k1.why: Five-year-olds can move counters in the simplified two-bucket game, but sorting nine cards by who can force a win is game-tree analysis. In practice the adult works out the answers while the children play aimless short games.

g23.why: The capped game is quick to play with real counters, and partners can check each other's moves. The 'strictly left, at most one per bucket' rule takes practice, and deciding forced wins across 16 cards is heavy, so most pairs will play rather than analyse. Parity is unlikely to be found without hints.

g45.why: 'Make the game last 10, then 30, then 100 moves' and 'can you make it go forever?' are hooks children push hard on. Realizing that one big refill makes the game as long as you like, yet it still always ends, is a real surprise, and the argument from the rightmost bucket is within reach with counters.

best_moment: Finding that one huge refill makes the game as long as you want, then failing every attempt to make it last forever.
biggest_problem: The capped game the younger bands get is the less surprising half; the delightful 'arbitrarily long but always finite' twist is reserved for 4-5.
one_change: Give grades 2-3 a small-number version of the 'make it last as long as you can / can it go forever?' challenge, instead of the 16-card forced-win sort.

title: Endless class lines (ordinals)

k1.why: The adult-led route matches three red cards to three blue cards with yarn and finds six ways, which is fine finite matching. It has nothing to do with the endless lines, and 'which way has no crossing' runs out quickly.

g23.why: The packet is labelled grades 3-5 and is reading-heavy. Children have to accept 'numbers continue forever' arrows and the 'after EVERY kid' panels as rules, and grasp the definition of 'keeps order'. Most 7-8-year-olds will hand the thinking to the adult once the lines become endless.

g45.why: The star in front getting absorbed by everyone shifting one place is a Hilbert-hotel surprise that 10-year-olds enjoy, and contrasting it with a star at the very end is a real 'aha'. But the cards are only a schematic of infinite lines, Problem 3 and especially the open Problem 4 arrangements are abstract, and a strong adult is needed.

best_moment: Everyone shuffles over one place and the extra star kid gets a partner after all; then the star at the end can't be fitted in that way.
biggest_problem: After the finite warm-up there is no real concrete action: matching endless lines is reasoning about a drawing with an arrow, and the distinction between size and order is subtle.
one_change: Act it out with the children as a 'class line' that can't really end (an adult's 'and so on' card at the end), and cut Problem 4 to one guided pair of arrangements.

title: Hackenbush balances

k1.why: Pulling cubes off snap-cube towers, so that everything above comes away, is satisfying and needs no reading. One-colour towers make the rule 'more cubes wins' findable. Keeping turns and starters straight needs an adult, but the children make every move.

g23.why: The cube towers make the cut rule self-enforcing and the games are short and fun. Judging whether a board 'balances' needs best play from both starters, which 7-8-year-olds will often get wrong, so their conclusions may rest on lucky games unless an adult challenges them.

g45.why: Playing to beat a partner, then discovering that two blue-red stalks exactly cancel one red cube (a stalk 'worth a half') and that two BR do not balance RB, is a genuine surprise. Building their own balanced boards is a creative follow-up. The surreal 'nursery' is optional and rightly deferred.

best_moment: Realizing that two little blue-red towers exactly balance one red cube: a tower can be worth half.
biggest_problem: Finding a balance needs near-optimal play from both starters, and younger children will judge from lucky games.
one_change: Give each board a referee child whose job is to find a better reply for the losing side, so that 'balances' is tested rather than inferred from one game.

title: Public knowledge (logic cafe and headbands)

k1.why: Five-year-olds can say NO or NOT YET from their own card, but the point is reasoning about what others' answers reveal. That second-order inference is beyond most of them, so the adult does the reasoning.

g23.why: This means keeping eight deal cards for possible worlds, tracking what each person privately knows, and following simultaneous-reveal rules about what may be removed when. That is too many rules and too much perspective-taking; the adult will end up making each elimination.

g45.why: The cafe joke (the 'NOT YET' that proves YES) is a real click for 10-year-olds, and seeing the two blue dolls both prove blue in round 2 is a striking moment. The headband induction is fragile even for adults, though, and the card-elimination protocol is fussy, so only the quickest groups with a skilled adult will get there themselves.

best_moment: The cafe: person 1's 'not yet' suddenly tells everyone that person 1 wants a cup.
biggest_problem: The possible-worlds card protocol and the private-versus-public bookkeeping are so heavy that the adult, not the child, will usually be doing the inference.
one_change: Build the session around acting out the three-person cafe with real children holding hidden cards, and keep the headband induction as a short adult-led finale for 4-5.

title: Drawing machines (pantograph)

k1.why: This is a one-child-at-a-time station with an adult steadying the machine, so the others wait. Steering T while watching P is hard fine-motor and attention work for 5-year-olds; they will enjoy seeing a big copy appear, but briefly.

g23.why: If the machine works, tracing a shape and watching the other pencil draw it twice as big is genuinely magical, and steering P to the dots is a good puzzle. But the foam-board linkage has never been built. Prep is well over 30 minutes (craft-knife cutting, rehearsal), and wobbly joints can ruin the copies.

g45.why: The doubled-length, four-times-area surprise with unit squares is a good aha, and reversing the machine or moving the anchor gives real questions. All of it depends on hardware that is fiddly and untested, and the bar-vector explanation in Upper Problem 1 is abstract.

best_moment: Tracing a small house with one pencil and watching the other pencil draw a big house by itself.
biggest_problem: It depends on a homemade linkage that has never been built, needs an hour or more of adult prep and rehearsal, and may wobble too much to give clean copies.
one_change: Buy one or two inexpensive commercial drawing pantographs and write the problems for those, rather than relying on an untested foam-board build.

title: Pursuit and escape (cops and robbers on graphs)

k1.why: A chase game where you move one dot or stay is simple and appealing, and the triangle versus square contrast is visible. 5-year-olds may lose track of turns and stays, so the adult must manage the turn tile, but the children make the moves.

g23.why: Chase games are instantly engaging, and the rules are tiny. Discovering that the cop always wins on paths and trees but the robber can run around a square forever is a real 'aha' they can find and demonstrate to a partner.

g45.why: Beyond the chase, adding the fewest roads to trap the robber, designing a cop-win and a robber-win map, and coordinating two cops are puzzles 10-year-olds will want to keep testing against each other. Folding is a harder optional step.

best_moment: The robber discovers it can circle the square forever, always staying opposite the cop.
biggest_problem: Children will be tempted to take a long game as proof of escape; the 'works against every reply' standard needs adult questioning.
one_change: Start with a big floor-sized version (a path and a square of paper dots) where children are the cop and robber, before moving to tabletop boards.

title: Voting and agendas

k1.why: The adult reads every ranking card aloud and the children place tokens and count to three. The voters are imaginary and the cycle is abstract, so the children are mostly operating an adult's procedure.

g23.why: 'Make A win, now make B win, now C' is a good rigging challenge with a nice surprise: whoever waits wins. But voting on behalf of three imaginary cards, one pair at a time, is procedural, and the line packet's distance comparisons are beyond many of them.

g45.why: Rigging the agenda and designing profiles where the order matters is a creative puzzle with a real twist. The line packet (five voters, comparing distances for many proposals) turns into tally bookkeeping before the median insight arrives. Upper Problem 2's impossibility argument is good but needs adult guidance.

best_moment: Finding that whichever letter is made to wait wins the knockout, with the same voters and no one changing their mind.
biggest_problem: The voters are imaginary cards, which drains the fun out of rigging an election and makes each vote a lookup chore.
one_change: Use the children's own real three-way preferences (snacks or games) for the cycle, and let one child secretly choose the agenda to 'rig' the outcome.

title: Packing and kissing circles

k1.why: 'How many disks can touch this one?' is a perfect kindergarten question: they build it, count six, and can try a bigger middle disk. Sliding disks into a snug ring takes some motor care, and the later problems are well beyond them.

g23.why: There is lots of hands-on building with a clear goal: it is always six around an equal disk, nine around a bigger one, only four big ones around a small one. Squeezing an extra disk into the tray by staggering rows is a tangible 'aha'.

g45.why: Moving from building to proving (equilateral wedges show why a seventh can't fit, and why the neighbours must all touch) is a satisfying, concrete proof. The mixed-size rings and the general rule give real depth for return visits.

best_moment: The staggered rows let eleven disks into a tray that held only eight in a square grid.
biggest_problem: Preparation: about 95 card disks to cut (roughly 1.5 hours), and cutting errors of under a millimetre can make the tight tray problems give the wrong answer.
one_change: Use bought equal-size disks or coins (pennies and quarters, say) and resize the trays to match, so prep is minutes and the fits are exact.

title: Growing shapes and totals (differences and accumulators)

k1.why: Growing squares and stairs with tiles and counting the new tiles suits 5-year-olds with an adult counting along. The tray and counter machines are mostly adult-operated, but the cube growth is fun.

g23.why: The tile problems are strong: two staircases click into a rectangle, and a square peels into odd layers. The one-tray input problems are fine. The two-stage cascade is a step-by-step simulation where copying totals between trays becomes the main demand.

g45.why: Maximizing the second tray by ordering inputs is an interesting puzzle, and the cube shells and corner piles are good hands-on encores. But much of the minute-to-minute work is running cascaded totals, and the 20-problem, 11-page packet sprawls.

best_moment: Two copies of a staircase fit together into a perfect rectangle.
biggest_problem: The accumulator machines turn into simulation and bookkeeping (keep, copy, add, repeat) that crowds out the delightful shape work.
one_change: Split it: make the tile and cube growing shapes the main week, and replace the cascade machines with a single puzzle such as 'order these cards for the biggest final total'.

title: Sliding number arrays (jeu de taquin)

k1.why: No K-1 packet; the adult-read A-board route asks five-year-olds to track gray, dark and ring pieces plus a smaller-neighbor rule, and the only payoff is sorting finished shapes into two piles.

g23.why: The single slide move (compare two neighbors, slide the smaller) is doable, but children juggle three mask types, a ring, reset cards and saved sketches, and the headline discovery is that nothing changes when you switch corners, which feels like a non-event at this age.

g45.why: Upper children can run slides, design starts for target outlines (Problem 4 is the liveliest task) and argue order is preserved, but the 16-card catalog with two runs each is a long pooled simulation, and the order-independence theorem only lands if an adult frames it as surprising.

best_moment: Problem 4: arranging 1-5 so the slide produces a chosen target outline, then testing it.
biggest_problem: Most of the time goes on executing a multi-piece sliding procedure and resetting from cards, and the payoff is a confirmation that the result is the same both ways rather than a surprise children can feel.
one_change: Cut to one-hole A and D boards plus the design-a-start challenge, drop the dark/gray distinction where possible, and make the 'does the choice matter?' question a bet children commit to before running both orders.

title: Rotor-router machines

k1.why: Pushing a counter along arrows and flipping cards is a hands-on, marble-run-like action five-year-olds can do, and 'does every exit get one?' is answerable by looking; an adult must read and keep the flip discipline, and 12 counters on one switch gets repetitive.

g23.why: Operating the four-exit tree and programming it to hit target orders (and finding ones it can't make) is a real puzzle with a mild aha, but Problem 1's twelve-counter XYXY run is dull and writing arrival strings adds bookkeeping.

g45.why: Programming the eight-exit tree, discovering bit-reversal order, spotting impossible orders and counting 128 programs gives upper children a machine they can both play with and reason about; 'every exit gets one before any gets two, whatever the start' is a satisfying surprise.

best_moment: Discovering that four (or eight) counters always land on every exit exactly once no matter how the arrows start.
biggest_problem: Preparation (cutting, folding and gluing 33 reversible cards, estimated at an hour) exceeds what a busy parent will do, and a missed flip silently corrupts every later result.
one_change: Replace fold-and-glue cards with something faster to make (coins or two-color counters as switch states) and shorten Problem 1 to four or six counters before moving to the tree.

title: Fold-and-stretch predictions (tent map)

k1.why: Folding the track at 8 to see which numbers touch is a nice concrete moment, but hopping by counting the gap to the nearer end and laying it twice is a demanding procedure for five-year-olds and the adult will be operating it.

g23.why: Point moves are a chain of measure-then-double steps read from a graph, and shading 'all possible positions' of a band is an abstraction most seven- and eight-year-olds won't hold; it becomes procedure-following with little visible payoff.

g45.why: Children who can halve repeatedly can find markers that meet, bands that grow, and the 'how close must you start to stay predictable?' question, which carries real chaos ideas, but the work is pencil shading on number lines with no physical stretching and little play.

best_moment: Folding the track and seeing 3 and 13 land on top of each other, so they go to the same place next move.
biggest_problem: After the fold, the activity is repeated map-reading and shading of intervals; the striking idea (tiny differences blow up) is delivered as interval bookkeeping rather than a race children can watch.
one_change: Turn it into a two-marker race game where partners start close together and bet how many moves until they are far apart, saving band shading for upper return visits.

title: Squaring a rectangle (Babylonian square roots)

k1.why: Only an adult-led side route: making every rectangle from 12 tiles is a decent K-1 task, but it is not what the week is about and the rest has nothing for this age.

g23.why: Tile rectangles of 24 and the cut-and-fit squares work for some third graders, but the reshaping move needs division into fractions (3/2, 24/7) and comparing them, which second graders can't do and most third graders will need an adult to compute.

g45.why: Tiles, cutting rectangles to fit inside a square, and watching the bracket close on the side of a 12-square are satisfying, but Problems 3-5 become fraction arithmetic (336/97) and decimal checking that many ten-year-olds will find a chore.

best_moment: Cutting the 6-by-2 rectangle, fitting it into the 4-by-4 square and seeing exactly one small square left uncovered.
biggest_problem: The engaging physical part ends after Problem 2; the convergence story runs on fraction calculations that slow children down and hide the idea.
one_change: Keep the reshaping on whole-number or tile-countable examples longer and let a calculator do the fraction steps so children focus on watching the bracket shrink.

title: Calibration lab (secret-extra machines)

k1.why: Measuring strips on a ruler that doesn't start at 0 and playing a hidden 'adds 1, 2 or 3 cubes' tower machine behind a folder are concrete and game-like; Problems 5-6 (every pair that could have gone in) will need an adult to steer.

g23.why: Being the secret machine is fun, but one known strip gives the extra away by subtraction, so the guessing game is over in one request; the 'could P be longer than Q?' and repair-the-box puzzles have some bite.

g45.why: The copies-plus-extra game makes 'how few requests?' a real strategy puzzle, but the later stretch-and-shift and error-range pages (Problems 3-7) are linear-function word problems with fractions that feel like schoolwork.

best_moment: Lifting the folder to check whether the partner guessed the machine's secret extra.
biggest_problem: For the middle band the game is trivially solved by one subtraction, and the upper band's interesting game quickly gives way to abstract slope-and-error problems.
one_change: Give the middle band machines where one request is not enough (e.g. the copies-and-extra machine with small numbers) so the guessing game stays a strategy puzzle.

title: Count the unseen (capture-recapture)

k1.why: No packet; the 15-minute adult-led route is a one-question demonstration, not a session.

g23.why: Catching, marking and recatching counters to guess a hidden total has a game feel and kids will enjoy the reveal, but overlaps with catches of 4 are noisy, so guesses feel like luck, and the 'smallest possible bag' puzzles are dry next to it.

g45.why: The proportion rule gives older children a real estimation method and the 'no matching total when overlap is 0' surprise is good, but Problems 6-8 on expected overlap and budgets are formula-driven and the erasable-mark materials are fiddly.

best_moment: The keeper revealing the hidden total right after children commit to a guess from their overlap.
biggest_problem: With small catches the overlap jumps around, so children may conclude the method is just guessing before they ever see why it works.
one_change: Pool every pair's rounds on one shared board so children see the guesses cluster around the true total before tackling the exact-bound puzzles.

title: Prime bags (factorization and divisors)

k1.why: Only an adult-led route: building counter rectangles for 2 to 20 and sorting 'only one row' numbers is a reasonable activity for older first graders, but long for five-year-olds and not the week's material.

g23.why: Third graders who know multiplication facts can split cards into prime tokens and list sub-bag values, and Problem 4's build-a-bag puzzle is a nice design task; second graders without fluent multiplication will depend on an adult or a times table.

g45.why: Divisor counting, token patterns and 'least number with 12 divisors' are a solid puzzle sequence, but it reads close to accelerated school number theory and the moment-to-moment work is listing and multiplying.

best_moment: Finding that 60 has more divisors than 64, or hunting for the smallest number with exactly 12 divisors.
biggest_problem: The activity is mostly listing factors and products on paper, so it can feel like a worksheet rather than an investigation.
one_change: Frame the upper band as a contest to find the smallest number with N divisors, with a class record board, and open with that challenge rather than with routine factor trees.

title: Square remainders (quadratic residues)

k1.why: The adult-led route is building squares and grouping by 3s or 4s to see leftovers; there is little for five-year-olds to decide and nothing for them to discover.

g23.why: Only third graders are in range, and after the first few squares the work becomes dividing 36, 49, 64 by 7, 8, 9 to find remainders, which is arithmetic drill with an adult helping.

g45.why: The secret-input partner game gives a little play and the pairing pattern for prime bundle sizes is a real discovery, but most of the time is computing remainders of printed squares and filling collections.

best_moment: In the partner game, realizing an output always hides exactly two inputs with bundles of 7, except 0.
biggest_problem: The concrete counter-square stage is short; the rest is remainder computation that crowds out the pattern-spotting.
one_change: Supply a remainder strip or wheel so children read outputs instantly and spend their time on the hiding game and on comparing prime versus composite bundle sizes.

title: Growing from a few seeds (bootstrap percolation)

k1.why: Put counters down and add one wherever two neighbors are filled is a single rule five-year-olds can follow with a partner pointing, and 'did it fill or get stuck?' is visible; holding 'side not corner' and searching for fewer seeds will need adult help.

g23.why: Designing a few seeds that fill the board, watching it spread, and chasing the fewest seeds is a self-checking puzzle children replay; the different-order question gives a gentle surprise.

g45.why: The search for fewest seeds on 4x4, 5x5 and 10x10, then the perimeter-never-grows argument, is a classic aha that ten-year-olds can actually see with counters and edge counts.

best_moment: Realizing the outline of the filled region never gets longer, which is why you can never fill an n-by-n board with fewer than n seeds.
biggest_problem: Marking seeds and additions on small paper boards and redrawing for each attempt can slow the search, especially on 10x10.
one_change: Provide a big reusable grid and two colors of counters for all the searching, keeping drawing only for a final record of a best start.

title: Moving piles (least work / earth mover's distance)

k1.why: Adult-led route only: moving two or three counters along bins and counting steps is doable, but the adult sets every start and target and counts aloud, and there is little decision-making for the child.

g23.why: Matching a target with fewest moves is a clear puzzle and finding that 'shortest delivery first' can lose is a good surprise, but small cases are fairly obvious and writing each move adds recording.

g45.why: The 'what must cross this gap?' lower-bound idea, the star-road version and the triangle-inequality question give real reasoning, though the activity is quieter and less playful than a game.

best_moment: Showing that the greedy shortest-delivery-first plan costs 6 when a smarter plan costs 4.
biggest_problem: For small piles the best plan is often obvious, so much of the time is counting and writing moves rather than puzzling.
one_change: Lead with the greedy-fails challenge and the partner game of building a start exactly N moves away, and drop the requirement to write each move.

title: Distance in nested worlds (ultrametric / 2-adic)

k1.why: No packet; the 15-minute close/far loop route is a brief adult-led aside, not a session for this age.

g23.why: Only third graders are in range, and the definition (smallest common group's label, labels increasing outward) is a dense paragraph to retain before any building; most will need an adult to decide each distance.

g45.why: Building loop worlds with cord and testing which distance triples are possible is concrete, and the hidden-world guessing game (Problem 10) is genuinely game-like, but the reading load is high and the ball and 2-adic pages are abstract.

best_moment: Problem 10: reconstructing a partner's secret world from as few distance questions as possible.
biggest_problem: Children must absorb an unfamiliar, wordy distance definition before doing anything, and the surprising 'isosceles only' fact comes late.
one_change: Open with the secret-world game on three or four cards and a simple close/far/very-far vocabulary, letting the triangle surprise emerge from play before introducing balls.

title: Bead machines and the odd triangle

k1.why: The same/different colour rule is a two-cell binary choice a 5-year-old can apply, and triangles appearing is a real reveal; but one wrong cell spoils every row below it, so an adult has to check each row, and 36 small hexagon cells take patience. Coin-flip beads with stacking cubes are fine but light.

g23.why: Watching triangles inside triangles grow over 16 rows is genuinely satisfying and counting red cells per row gives a pattern to chase, but 136 cells is a long fill where errors spread, and the pooled 32-bead comparison is mostly waiting and tallying.

g45.why: Matching the colour picture to odd entries and predicting row 13 from binary is a real aha, but filling numbered Pascal to row 15 means adding numbers into the thousands, which turns the first 20 minutes into arithmetic chore.

best_moment: Upside-down white triangles of growing sizes suddenly appearing as the colour rule is applied row after row.
biggest_problem: A single mistake propagates down the whole triangle, so long fills either need constant adult checking or end in a broken picture.
one_change: Give a self-check (pre-coloured cells every few rows, or a reference strip) so children can catch errors themselves, and skip the numbered Pascal fill for 4-5 in favour of the colour triangle plus a few spot numbers.

title: Domino diamonds (Aztec diamond)

k1.why: Placing real dominoes on a small printed diamond and doing a flip is hands-on and easy to grasp, but orders 1 and 2 hold only 2 and 8 tilings, so the activity runs out quickly and 'a tiling no neighbour has' needs adult sorting.

g23.why: Finding all 8 order-2 tilings and sorting by the top squares is a good complete-list puzzle, but the pooled order-3 sort (64 tilings) becomes drawing, duplicate-checking and bookkeeping.

g45.why: Predicting from 2, 8, 64 and seeing the arctic-circle picture are nice, but children cannot check 64 or 1024 themselves, so the count pattern is handed to them, and the large random tiling does not exist yet.

best_moment: Seeing the printed large random tiling with frozen brick-wall corners and a messy round middle.
biggest_problem: The hands-on part (orders 1 and 2) is small, and the interesting growth (64, 1024) is beyond what children can verify, so the middle of the hour is recording tilings.
one_change: Supply printed half-filled order-3 boards with the top fixed so tables can each own a small, checkable sub-case, and generate the arctic-circle print before scheduling.

title: Tower maps and one-switch codes

k1.why: Two-cup Hanoi is solved in three moves, and matching each arrangement to a picture card and joining the right cards on the floor is an abstract state-graph task an adult will mostly run; walking the taped map is fun but the child is following the adult's map.

g23.why: Three-disc Hanoi in 7 moves is a reliably engaging puzzle, and the neighbour-pegs 26-move challenge is long but has a clear goal; building the 27-card class map with its 39 links is slow and logistics-heavy, though the triangle-of-triangles reveal is a payoff.

g45.why: Proving 2^n-1, the self-similar map and matching disc moves to one-switch lamp patterns give real ahas, but many children already know Hanoi and the map build is a big class-wide logistics job.

best_moment: Stepping back from the finished state map and seeing that it is a triangle made of three smaller triangles.
biggest_problem: The new idea (the state map) requires finding and joining many cards, which is bookkeeping an adult ends up coordinating, while the familiar move-count puzzle is the part kids enjoy.
one_change: Give 2-3 and 4-5 a pre-printed map with blank dots to label by playing, instead of building a 27-card floor map, and drop the map for K-1 in favour of just the neighbour-pegs cup challenge.

title: The sixteen-card square

k1.why: Nine coloured shape cards on a 3x3 mat is tactile and attractive, but two simultaneous conditions (colour and shape in every row and column) is a lot for a 5-year-old; many will manage one attribute and need adult help for the second.

g23.why: Real playing cards and a clear goal make this a classic, tempting puzzle, but juggling rank and suit across rows and columns with 16 cards leads many 7-8 year-olds to get stuck without a 'ranks first' hint.

g45.why: The card puzzle, the harder diagonal version, the 5x5 step rule and the 36-officers story with a 1959 surprise and a quantum twist give challenge and narrative children of this age enjoy.

best_moment: Finally placing the sixteenth card so every row and column has one of each rank and each suit.
biggest_problem: For younger bands the double constraint arrives all at once, so trial-and-error can turn to frustration before any pattern is seen.
one_change: Stage it: solve the rank-only (or colour-only) square first with the cards, then add the second attribute on top, for K-1 and 2-3.

title: Knight's tours on small boards

k1.why: The L-shaped knight move is hard for 5-year-olds to execute reliably, and on 3x3 every move is forced, so the child is following the move card or an adult rather than making choices.

g23.why: A 3x4 tour with numbered counters is a good trial-and-error puzzle with easy backtracking, and pooling start squares is a nice class find, but knight moves stay error-prone and 4x4 offers only failure.

g45.why: Hunting a 5x5 tour, discovering that the 'fewest exits' rule usually works, and the colour argument for where tours must start give strategy, failure and explanation at the right level.

best_moment: Trying Warnsdorff's 'go where there are fewest exits' rule on 5x5 and watching it carry the knight all the way round.
biggest_problem: Younger children struggle to make legal knight jumps, so the core move is not theirs, and some boards produce only frustration with a 'computer says no' ending.
one_change: Print each board with the legal knight links drawn as lines (or use a jump template) for K-1 and 2-3, so children choose routes rather than struggle with the L move.

title: Colouring maps

k1.why: Colouring is natural for this age and tracing round cups is easy, but ruler lines right across the page and small regions are hard for 5-year-olds, and the two-colour surprise is subtle for them.

g23.why: Drawing their own maps, discovering two colours always work for line maps, and the open challenge to draw a map needing five colours gives a 'try to beat it' drive kids enjoy.

g45.why: The parity explanation is within reach, the odd-ring obstruction is a clean find, and the four colour theorem's story is compelling; the torus seven-country map is a strong extension once it exists.

best_moment: A child's elaborate 'impossible' map turns out to need only four colours again.
biggest_problem: The torus station depends on a seven-country portal map that has not been made, and K-1 regions may be too small to colour well.
one_change: Provide prepared large-region line and circle maps for K-1 and build and hand-check the torus map before the session.

title: Mazes, walls and random trees

k1.why: Solving and building mazes for a friend is something young children love, and walking a token with a hand on the wall is a concrete rule; consistent hand side and fiddly wall strips need adult help but do not spoil it.

g23.why: Building mazes that defeat the hand rule is an adversarial challenge with a clear payoff (wall islands), and Trémaux marking gives a method that always works.

g45.why: The 2-3 tasks suit them well, but the Wilson's-algorithm die walk wanders and is a long simulation, and the fair-versus-unfair comparison (5/84 vs 1/14) needs far more trials than a class can tally.

best_moment: A partner's hand-on-wall walker circling an island forever while the exit sits just out of reach.
biggest_problem: The 4-5 headline (fair random mazes) is a slow dice simulation whose statistical point cannot be seen in one session.
one_change: Make the 4-5 core 'design a maze that beats Trémaux or the hand rule' and keep Wilson's walk as a short 2-by-3 demonstration rather than a frequency experiment.

title: Hailstone numbers

k1.why: Tripling a pile of counters and adding one quickly yields piles of 40-50 that a 5-year-old cannot count or pair reliably, so the adult ends up running the machine.

g23.why: Racing starts up to 20 and watching numbers shoot up and crash has real drama, but 3n+1 on numbers like 35 or 53 and 20-step chains are an arithmetic chore for many 7-year-olds.

g45.why: The shared run of 27 climbing to 9232 is a genuine gasp, and an unsolved problem they can test with their own arithmetic excites this age; the backward tree adds a proved fact.

best_moment: The class's shared run of 27 climbing past 9000 before finally crashing to 1.
biggest_problem: The whole activity is repeated arithmetic, too heavy for K-1 and borderline for 2-3.
one_change: Give K-1 and 2-3 a prepared hailstone number line or lookup chart so they can move a marker and watch the ups and downs without doing the multiplication.

title: Sharing loaves the Egyptian way

k1.why: Folding and cutting thirds and sixths is beyond most 5-year-olds' motor control, so an adult cuts and the child just hands out pieces.

g23.why: Building each twelfth from one of each strip is a nice puzzle, but 4 loaves for 5 and 9 for 10 need twentieths and fifteenths that the strip set does not contain, so the sharing tasks stall.

g45.why: The 4/n challenge and the greedy-machine surprise are good for strong 10-year-olds, but the work is mostly written-fraction arithmetic and the 'why it stops' argument is abstract.

best_moment: Discovering a share like 'half plus a third' really covers five-sixths of a loaf when the pieces are stacked on a whole.
biggest_problem: The concrete materials do not support the tasks given (cutting accuracy for K-1, missing strip sizes for 2-3), so children drift into paper arithmetic.
one_change: Use pre-scored loaves or a fraction-strip set that actually covers each assigned share, and choose loaf-and-worker problems that fit that set.

title: Fibonacci coins

k1.why: Paying amounts with coins is concrete, but the 'no neighbouring coins' rule is arbitrary to a 5-year-old, the uniqueness discovery needs a systematic search, and the Zeckendorf merging game has too many rules for this age.

g23.why: Fibonacci Nim is a real game with a hidden secret and kids like hunting for an amount with two payments, but tracking the changing 'at most double' limit needs a marker card and steady attention.

g45.why: A two-player game with a learnable winning strategy, a 'try to break it' uniqueness hunt and an argument with coin rows give competition, surprise and explanation.

best_moment: Realising you should refuse to go first when the pile is 8, 13 or 21, and then beating an adult with 'take your smallest coin'.
biggest_problem: The neighbour rule and the doubling limit are two unnatural rules to juggle, and Fibonacci themes have engaged this group poorly before.
one_change: Lead with Fibonacci Nim (with a limit marker card) and let the coin system arrive as the key to winning, dropping the Zeckendorf game for K-1.

title: Staircase numbers

k1.why: Building two- and three-step staircases from cubes and posting them on a chart is concrete and within reach, though K-1 will mostly make two-step staircases and see the 'missing numbers' only with adult framing.

g23.why: Filling a shared 1-30 chart by building, noticing that 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 resist everything, and testing 32 gives a clean conjecture they find themselves.

g45.why: Evening out a staircase into a rectangle is an object proof, and matching staircases to odd divisors gives a satisfying deeper rule.

best_moment: Predicting that 32 has no staircase and nobody at the table being able to build it.
biggest_problem: Bigger targets need many cubes and the chart work can slide into listing sums rather than building.
one_change: Keep the chart shared across tables so each child builds a few numbers in several ways rather than everyone covering 1 to 30.

title: Spreading claps around a circle

k1.why: Placing cups on plates and playing the rhythm as a group is physical, musical and joyful, and judging whether it 'sounds even' is a decision they can make by ear.

g23.why: The cinquillo-is-the-tresillo's-rests surprise is lovely, but counting the different 3-on-8 patterns up to turning (7) is a fiddly necklace-sorting job for 7-year-olds.

g45.why: Finding the most even placement and comparing gap lists is good work, but 'most even' is a subtle condition and x.xxx. versus xx.xx. needs careful adult framing to land.

best_moment: Flipping cups and rests on 5-on-8 and hearing the tresillo come back.
biggest_problem: The mathematical criterion of 'most even' is hard to state for children, so beyond K-1 the music is fun but the mathematical question can feel vague.
one_change: Give 2-3 and 4-5 a concrete test (every clap's next-clap and second-next-clap gaps) on the recording strip so they can check evenness themselves rather than by ear.

title: One magic square

k1.why: Adding three numbers to 15 over and over is too much arithmetic for 5-year-olds, and Pick 15 requires tracking all triples in your hand, so the adult does the sums.

g23.why: Hunting for a magic square with tiles is a classic, achievable puzzle and Pick 15 is fun, but it leans on repeated addition and the 'really different?' question needs adult prompting.

g45.why: Proving there is only one square by counting triples is within reach, and finding out that Pick 15 is tic-tac-toe in disguise is a genuine gasp moment.

best_moment: Laying the Pick-15 cards on the Lo Shu and seeing that every win was a tic-tac-toe line.
biggest_problem: For younger children the activity is mostly addition practice, which the plan itself flags as the risk.
one_change: For K-1 replace the sum-to-15 task with a dot-card or rod version where totals are seen by length, or skip K-1.

title: Sunflower spirals

k1.why: Sticking numbered seed dots like a dot-to-dot is enjoyable and the quarter-turn spokes are clear, but placing seed i on ray i at circle i on a crowded golden sheet is fiddly and pinecone spiral counting is adult-led.

g23.why: Predicting spokes for 2/5 and 3/8 then seeing them appear is a good reveal, but placing 60 stickers per sheet is long, and pinecone spiral counting is unreliable without an adult marking a start.

g45.why: Why p/q gives q spokes and the approaching Fibonacci fractions are good ideas, but the golden sheet's spirals only become visible after many stickers, and the approximation work is abstract.

best_moment: Comparing a finished spoked sheet with the golden sheet and seeing straight spokes on one and crossing spirals on the other.
biggest_problem: The payoff picture appears only after a long sticker-placing session on sheets that do not yet exist.
one_change: Split each sheet's seeds among a table so every sheet is finished in ten minutes, and show a pre-made 300-seed golden picture alongside.

title: Wallpaper patterns

k1.why: Tracing a patch of a busy pattern, pinning it and turning it until it matches again is fine-motor work a 5-year-old can't do alone, so the adult does the turning. Stamping a quarter-turn pattern is the one part their hands can manage, but its result is just a sticker count.

g23.why: Finding every kind of spin point and mirror line on every sample is hard for adults too, and stamping a pattern with a 3-spin but no mirror is hard to get right. The pentagon gap is a real aha, but it comes after a long, tiring hunt.

g45.why: The bead-purse puzzle is a tidy find-all-ways problem, but the prices are arbitrary numbers to a child, so the link to spins is told to them rather than felt. The shortest-slide proof with arrows can land with an adult guiding it.

best_moment: Three paper pentagons around a point leave a 36-degree gap, so no pentagon floor is possible.
biggest_problem: The core action, tracing and spinning a patch of a dense printed pattern to find spin points, is fiddly and slow, and telling kinds of points apart is too subtle for most children.
one_change: Use a few bold, pre-made patterns with pre-cut transparent overlays, and centre the session on building and stamping patterns rather than classifying found ones.

title: Kaleidoscopes

k1.why: Standing a mirror hinge on a wedge and counting copies, or choosing a wedge to make a 6- or 8-petal flower, is instant magic that small hands can do. No reading is needed.

g23.why: Predicting copies from the angle and then checking is a satisfying guess-and-test loop, and the odd-angle seams that look wrong are a real puzzle. Sorting logos into spin-only and mirror sets gives a second task.

g45.why: The mirrors still delight, and why there are 2n copies can be checked with an arrow. Leonardo's theorem argued with tracing paper and flip-tracing card triangles around a corner are fiddly and lean on an adult.

best_moment: Closing the hinge and watching the flower gain petals, then seeing the 72-degree picture come out wrong at the back seam.
biggest_problem: Material fit is unproven: mirrors may slip on the sheet, the odd-angle clash may be hard to see, and a class set of mirrors costs money and needs care.
one_change: Rehearse with real mirrors and pre-cut card triangles; make the triangle-closing test a guided table activity with templates rather than free flip-tracing.

title: Commutator puzzles

k1.why: Bringing five animals home after a two- or three-turn scramble is a nice small puzzle. But sliding every token on a ring by hand is error-prone, and one slip spoils the result, so an adult will hover.

g23.why: Each turn means moving five tokens one by one and writing it down, and finding a three-token move by search is long and error-prone. The can-you-swap-two question has no answer they can reach, so it frustrates rather than surprises.

g45.why: Following each token through do-do-undo-undo, building conjugates and the parity argument are real mathematics with a good wall-you-can't-cross moment. Still, the physical turning is a simulation chore, and long turn words are easy to garble.

best_moment: Doing L R l r on a scrambled-looking board and finding that only three tokens moved, every time.
biggest_problem: On a printed board a turn is five separate token moves, so the activity becomes careful bookkeeping where one slip ruins the experiment.
one_change: Build a real turning device, such as two overlapping paper-plate wheels on brads or a token track in a cup, so that a turn is one hand motion.

title: Card magic

k1.why: Performing the pairs trick and trying hard to break it suits this age, and taking a top card from either pile is easy for small hands. The column trick's pick-up procedure and checking pairs in order will need an adult's hands.

g23.why: Performing a trick, then hunting for why it works (the two top cards always differ) and finding when a plain cut fails is a good puzzle loop. The 3-card warm-up code is a satisfying secret.

g45.why: The 56 hands against 56 messages count, with 9 cards impossible, is a sharp aha, and performing the five-card trick is a strong motivator. Designing the 3-from-8 code may need a partial crib ready.

best_moment: A child riffles the piles any way they like, flips the row in pairs, and every pair has one of each colour.
biggest_problem: Designing the 3-from-8 code is open and may stall 4-5 without a crib, and performance time can crowd out the why questions.
one_change: Have a staged crib for the code design (a worked 3-from-5 example) and protect a fixed block of time for the why questions after each trick.

title: Juggling patterns

k1.why: Laying colour-coded card arcs from every beat of a 20-beat strip is fiddly, and stacked arcs pile up and slide. Counting arcs crossing a pencil is mostly an adult-led procedure with little meaning for them; only the optional beanbag passing gives the juggling joy.

g23.why: Testing patterns like 441 and 432 and noticing that the ball count is the average is a genuine discovery. But each test means laying many arcs, so it is slow, and the 7 two-number patterns turn into a long recording task.

g45.why: The landing-remainder test and the average argument are good, and the 1, 3, 5, 7 table invites a formula guess. It works better if arcs are drawn on a printed ladder instead of placed as card pieces.

best_moment: Laying 4 3 2 and watching two rainbows land on the same beat: a crash.
biggest_problem: There is no actual juggling: the activity is laying many card arcs on a strip, which is fiddly and repetitive, and the throwing that would make it fun is optional.
one_change: Make passing beanbags to a clap for each pattern the core experience, and record patterns by drawing arcs on a printed beat ladder rather than laying cut card arcs.

title: Eight triangle gems

k1.why: Building closed gems from magnetic triangles is absorbing and needs no reading, and a number line of what the table found is a fine shared record. The large gems may collapse, and counting faces on a 3D object needs adult help.

g23.why: Hunting for new triangle counts, failing to make an odd one, and trying for 18 or more than 20 is a real challenge with a clear goal. Checking how many triangles meet at a corner is easy on a model.

g45.why: The even-count and at-most-five-at-a-corner explanations are within reach with models in hand, and the 18 that counting allows but nobody can build is a good puzzle.

best_moment: Trying to build an 18-face gem and finding it won't close, though every simple count says it should.
biggest_problem: It needs many magnetic equilateral triangles (about 20 per pair), which few families own in that number, and the paper fold-and-tape fallback is much slower and fiddlier.
one_change: Secure a class set of Polydron or Magna-Tiles triangles before scheduling, with photo cards of the 12-, 14- and 16-face gems as optional targets.

title: Cube nets

k1.why: Folding six-square shapes around a cube block and sorting them into box and not-a-box is a good hands-on guess-and-check. Cutting and taping paper squares is hard for them; magnetic squares make it work.

g23.why: Predicting whether a shape folds, then testing it, is a satisfying loop, and pooling a class collection of the 11 gives a shared goal. Deciding when two nets are the same is a real reasoning task.

g45.why: The 7-cuts-and-5-hinges question and an organised completeness search have substance, and the open Dürer problem is a nice story. Many children have already met cube nets in school, so the surprise is smaller.

best_moment: The plus shape folding up into a box, and a near-identical shape that won't.
biggest_problem: It is a familiar school topic, and with paper, scissors and tape, testing each candidate is slow for younger children.
one_change: Use magnetic squares for testing so each fold takes seconds, and keep paper only for the final favourite net.

title: Tangram shapes with no dents

k1.why: Filling even a square outline with all seven tans is famously hard without piece lines, and tracing found shapes is fine-motor work. Most 5-year-olds will need an adult to place pieces.

g23.why: Hunting for band-passing shapes and pooling them is a real challenge, but free search with all seven pieces often stalls, and duplicates are hard to recognise. The rubber-band test is a nice concrete check.

g45.why: Corners of only 45, 90 or 135 degrees and at most 8 sides are reachable on the half-square grid, and checking the class list against the number 13 is satisfying. The search is long and may frustrate without silhouette cards held in reserve.

best_moment: Stretching a rubber band around a shape and watching it skip over a dent.
biggest_problem: Finding convex tangram shapes from scratch is hard, so many children spend the time stuck, and K-1 cannot fill the outlines alone.
one_change: Give K-1 outlines with piece lines, and keep a deck of silhouettes of the 13 to hand out one at a time when a table stalls.

title: Guards in a gallery

k1.why: Hide-and-seek in a taped room is physical and fun, and moving the guard to fix a hiding place is something they can do themselves. The paper plans need adult help with sight lines.

g23.why: Finding the fewest guards for each plan and designing rooms that need 2 or 3 guards are open puzzles with clear goals and a nice design-challenge feel.

g45.why: Fisk's triangulate-colour-and-pick method is short and checkable, and seeing why n/3 is always enough is a real aha. Building a comb that needs that many is a satisfying construction.

best_moment: A child finds a hiding spot in the taped room that the guard truly cannot see.
biggest_problem: Sight-line disputes at corners and a 10-corner floor outline need space, prep time and a clear rule.
one_change: Fix a clear rule (string must not cross or touch a wall) and use large printed plans on 11x17 paper so string sight lines are easy to check.

title: One straight cut

k1.why: Fold, cut once, predict and unfold is a natural delight at this age and needs no reading. The square-target trick shown by an adult is a good surprise.

g23.why: One-cut targets like the square, triangle, plus sign and letters are clear challenges with an instant check, and finding the corner-bisector fold is a real discovery.

g45.why: The fewest-folds table for regular shapes and the halving explanation give depth, and the five-point star is a memorable payoff. Accurate folding of 8- and 10-gons will need care.

best_moment: Unfolding a single straight cut to find a perfect square or star dropping out.
biggest_problem: Several layers of printer paper are hard to cut cleanly and fold accurately, especially for younger children and higher-sided shapes.
one_change: Use thin origami paper and pre-printed fold lines for the harder targets, and rehearse the star.

title: One tile that never repeats

k1.why: Hats have 12 orientations and a complex outline; random building quickly leaves gaps that 5-year-olds can't fix, so the adult will end up placing tiles. The flipped-colour noticing is pleasant but thin.

g23.why: The one-colour challenge and slide test are interesting ideas, but children get stuck early with free placement. The key fact, never periodic, cannot be seen in a patch and so must be told.

g45.why: The patch-of-eight build and comparing patches can work as a guided construction, and the einstein story is exciting for this age. The discovery is still mostly told, and the Heesch task is unchosen.

best_moment: Building a patch of hats and noticing that a few must be flipped over.
biggest_problem: The theorem's payoff (no repeating slide) is invisible on any patch children can build, and a 13-sided hat can't be cut with a paper cutter, so preparing 160 of them is a heavy job.
one_change: Provide a printed kite-grid mat on which hats snap into outlines, and frame the session as building a growing floor together rather than discovering aperiodicity.

title: Cut and rearrange

k1.why: Rearranging pre-cut pieces of a square into different shapes is easy and pleasant, but counting grid squares under each shape is tedious and the same-area point is mild.

g23.why: Turning 5x8 into 4x10 and 3x3 plus 4x4 into 5x5 are good puzzles, but the staircase cut is hard to discover, and cutting on grid lines takes time.

g45.why: The 3-4-5 squares challenge, chasing fewest pieces, and the triangle-to-rectangle-to-square recipe give a real sense of a general method, with a nice 3D contrast at the end.

best_moment: Fitting a cut-up 3x3 square around a 4x4 to make a perfect 5x5.
biggest_problem: The key moves, such as the staircase cut, are hard to find unaided, so younger children may just follow a shown cut.
one_change: Give 2-3 a hint card that shows a staircase on a smaller rectangle, and let them find the staircase for the 5x8 themselves.

title: How long is a coastline?

k1.why: Comparing a straightened string from a wiggly edge with one from a straight edge is a quick, mild surprise. Walking strips and counting steps along a printed coast with stickers is slow and imprecise.

g23.why: Walking a 1 cm strip around a coast or a stage-3 Koch curve means 64 or more careful steps, and then multiplying steps by strip length. The trend will be noisy, and counting dominates.

g45.why: Why the Koch length grows by 4/3 each stage is a real aha, and box counting has a clear idea. But counting hundreds of touched boxes on a 1 cm grid is tedious, and coast results will wobble.

best_moment: Realising the coast keeps getting longer every time you use a shorter ruler.
biggest_problem: The minute-to-minute activity is counting many tiny steps or boxes, and the imprecision can hide the pattern the session depends on.
one_change: Have children draw Koch curves themselves (stages 0 to 3) and compute the lengths, and keep coast-walking to a single short demo comparison.

title: Splitting necklaces

k1.why: Cutting a short paper strip and sharing pieces into two cups until they match is doable, but with 4 beads it is close to trivial, and matching two colours at once is the real demand.

g23.why: Sorting strings into one cut and two cuts and trying to stump a partner works, but the never-needs-three result means the stump game always fails, and cutting uses up strips.

g45.why: Three-colour splits, finding a string that needs all three cuts, and the sliding half-window argument give a real explanation they can hold in their hands.

best_moment: Sliding a half-length window along the beads and watching the red count pass through exactly half.
biggest_problem: Cutting paper strips uses up the material and makes retrying slow, and the younger versions are thin.
one_change: Use reusable beads on a string with clothes-peg cut markers, and give K-1 longer two-colour strings so there is a real search.

title: Wobbly table and crumpled map

k1.why: Turning a rocking stool until it settles, and failing to make a three-legged stool rock, is hands-on and needs no reading; the map-on-map hunt is too abstract for this age and should be dropped for them.

g23.why: The stool and the two-figure monk puzzle are good concrete puzzles, but recording which diagonal rocks at every eighth of a turn is fiddly to judge and turns play into bookkeeping.

g45.why: The quarter-turn sign-swap argument and the shrinking map look-ups give real reasoning and an aha, but everything depends on a stool and sand tray that actually behave like the model, and pinning look-ups on two maps is fiddly.

best_moment: Nobody can make the three-legged stool rock, however hard they try.
biggest_problem: The core phenomenon rests on untested physical materials (worn stool legs, sand that gives way), and if the stool does not cooperate the session has nothing to stand on.
one_change: Replace the sand tray with a rigid, reusable bumpy board (e.g. a few glued wood shims) rehearsed in advance, and make the monk puzzle the main 2–3 task instead of the eighth-turn record.

title: Buffon's needle and noodle

k1.why: Dropping handfuls of toothpicks and sorting into two cups is pleasant hands-on play, and the ring always touching twice is a noticeable fact; but there is little for a 5-year-old to wonder about beyond sorting.

g23.why: Counting crossings per drop over 30 drops and comparing averages is tally work, average is not yet a meaningful idea, and the intended surprise (bent shapes cross the same on average) is a 'no difference' result buried in noise.

g45.why: Estimating pi from a class tally of toothpick drops is a genuine wow, and cutting the wire into pieces is an argument they can follow; it needs many drops and careful pooling.

best_moment: The class tally of toothpick drops comes out close to 3.14 and someone recognises pi.
biggest_problem: The headline discovery for younger children (shape does not matter) is a null effect that small, noisy samples cannot show convincingly.
one_change: For 2–3, keep only the toothpick drop with totals compared across tables, and make the pi reveal the shared ending rather than asking younger children to detect equal averages for bent wires.

title: Collecting every sticker

k1.why: Rolling a die and filling a sticker card is game-like and easy to do; the cube tower makes the run visible. Long runs of 25-plus rolls can drag, and the 'last one is slow' idea is felt more than understood.

g23.why: Circling new faces on a written roll strip and comparing gaps is a reasonable record, but writing every roll is a chore and the pattern needs many pooled runs.

g45.why: The stage-by-stage 6, 6/5, ... build to 14.7 matched against the class number line is a satisfying prediction-meets-data moment, though the math is mostly told and checked.

best_moment: Everyone stares at the last empty square on their card while the die keeps giving faces they already have.
biggest_problem: Repeated runs are dice-rolling with little decision-making, so after two or three runs the activity becomes waiting.
one_change: Turn it into a betting game: before each run every child bets a number of rolls on the class number line, and closest bet wins, so the long tail and the mean become things they care about.

title: Penney's coin-pattern races
