k1.why: Two-flip colour races with cubes for wins are simple and the 3-to-1 edge of blue-red over red-red can show up in ten races; spotting a two-box pattern on a track may need an adult eye.

g23.why: Picking a reply that beats whatever a partner chooses is a trick kids love to play on each other and on adults; the class who-beats-whom chart is some bookkeeping and the 2/3 edges need pooled races.

g45.why: The game plus the short 7/8 argument (HHH only wins if it comes first) is a real proof within reach, and waiting-time versus winning is a good second question.

best_moment: A child realises they can beat the adult whichever card the adult picks, and does it again.
biggest_problem: With only ten races per pair the 2/3 edges are often invisible, so 2–3 children may conclude there is no pattern.
one_change: Have each table race the same pairing and pool results onto one class chart before asking for the best reply.

title: Simpson's paradox with bags

k1.why: Choosing between an all-red bag and a mostly-red bag is obvious, and the reversal only means something if a child remembers and compares the earlier choices; drawing adds nothing for them.

g23.why: The pour-together reversal is a real surprise and building your own reversing set of bags is a good open challenge, though the main set (a one-counter bag) may feel like a trick.

g45.why: Fraction comparisons in the gentler set and the hunt for an equal-size reversal that never works give substantive reasoning; it is closer to arithmetic than play.

best_moment: After pouring, the side that won both pairs is suddenly the worse bag.
biggest_problem: The paradox is a comparison of earlier judgments with a later one, which needs memory and fraction sense the youngest lack, and the drawing ritual is luck that does not bear on the question.
one_change: Drop drawing entirely and make it a building challenge: 'make A win both pairs but lose after pouring', with the spare counters, scaffolded by the given set as an example.

title: Peg solitaire and Conway's soldiers

k1.why: Jumping counters to clear a row of 4 or 6 is a clear, satisfying puzzle; the 10-hole triangle is frustrating, and the colour-sticker chart means nothing to them.

g23.why: The 15-hole triangle is hard but compelling, and getting soldiers 1, 2 and 3 rows past the line with as few as possible is a classic absorbing challenge.

g45.why: The soldiers challenge plus the colour invariant and the weight argument for row 5 give real puzzles and a real impossibility proof; the infinite weight sum needs a good picture.

best_moment: Someone gets a soldier three rows past the line using only 8 soldiers.
biggest_problem: Counters on paper slide around and jumped counters are easy to confuse, so failed attempts are hard to retrace.
one_change: Use egg cartons or pegboards (or a hole-punched board) so pieces stay put and resets are fast.

title: Trust game (prisoner's dilemma)

k1.why: Choosing share or keep for beans is playable, but 5-year-olds mostly choose at random or take 'keep' as being mean, and watching strategy cards play each other is an adult moving beans.

g23.why: Discovering that keeping always pays more for you yet two keepers end poorer is a real aha, and the die ending is lively; social upset needs managing.

g45.why: Writing strategies and running a round robin is exciting, and copycat topping the table while never beating anyone is a great surprise, but scoring a tournament by hand is slow without a prepared sheet.

best_moment: Copycat wins the class tournament even though it never beat a single opponent.
biggest_problem: The hand-run round robin is long bookkeeping that adults end up doing, and 'keep' can feel like betrayal to young children.
one_change: Precompute or quickly score pairings with a printed match grid so children spend their time inventing and predicting strategies, and give K–1 a short fixed-length bean game only.

title: Sealed-bid auctions

k1.why: Value-minus-price with cube towers is abstract for 5-year-olds, who want to win the auction regardless of points, and an adult has to do the subtraction at each table.

g23.why: Bidding games are lively and the 'never-worse bid' table is a good discovery, though the points-not-prizes framing needs care.

g45.why: The case-by-case argument for bidding your value and the halve-your-bid puzzle are good reasoning; the payoff is clear once the rules land.

best_moment: A volunteer wins the auction and the class realises they actually lost points.
biggest_problem: Children instinctively play to win the auction, not to maximise value minus price, so the scoring has to be understood before any of the strategy makes sense.
one_change: Open with several quick demo rounds where winners visibly lose points, before any child bids, and leave K–1 out or give them only the tower-building comparison.

title: Game of Life

k1.why: Counting eight neighbours including diagonals is the hard part for 5-year-olds, so an adult counts aloud while they place counters, and the floor routine is likely to need adults running it.

g23.why: Small starts that blink, settle or vanish are fun to find and parent-finding is a good puzzle, but hand-updating larger shapes (the T for nine generations) is error-prone simulation.

g45.why: The glider and the Rule 90 ring are within reach, and the Sierpinski triangle emerging row by row is a real gasp; enumerating ring patterns is heavy.

best_moment: Rule 90 from a single coloured square draws the Sierpinski triangle on squared paper.
biggest_problem: Updating a grid by hand is slow and mistake-prone, so a single error derails a pattern and the whole-room floor version risks collapsing into adults operating it.
one_change: Keep the floor grid as a short demo, and give children small patterns (3–5 counters) on transparent overlays or a 'neighbour window' card, saving long evolutions for an app.

title: Busy beaver

k1.why: Following a two-state rule table needs a simultaneous lookup of colour and cup, so an adult reads and runs it while children move a toy; there is no surprise at this age.

g23.why: Designing cards means many simultaneous choices, most random cards stop at once or obviously run forever, the record of 6 cannot be beaten, and the key insight is told by the facilitator.

g45.why: Some 10-year-olds enjoy being the machine and writing short 'forever proofs', but the 21-step run is a long, error-prone simulation and the explosive growth is told, not felt.

best_moment: A child notices their card is bouncing between the same two cups forever and explains why it will never stop.
biggest_problem: The minute-to-minute activity is executing a rule table step by step, a simulation chore with an unbeatable record and a payoff that exists only as a story.
one_change: Reframe for 4–5 only as 'stops or forever?': hand out a deck of small ready-made cards to sort and prove, rather than long runs and record-chasing.

title: Secret messages and two padlocks

k1.why: Handling real padlocks and acting out the four trips is fun and physical, though why it is clever may not register; symbol counting on a short message is fine.

g23.why: Breaking a secret message with tallies and short words is a beloved activity, and the padlock trick is a genuine puzzle; the 183-letter tally needs splitting across a table.

g45.why: Catching the shift-padlock leak as an eavesdropper is a good aha, but the clock-power arithmetic mod 11 may swamp the reasoning without a printed power table.

best_moment: The class hands over the locked pencil case and works out how to get it there without ever sending a key.
biggest_problem: The 2–3 cipher is long to tally by hand, and the 4–5 modular powers risk becoming arithmetic practice.
one_change: Split the cipher text into table strips with a pooled tally chart, and give 4–5 a printed powers-of-2 clock table.

title: Proving without telling

k1.why: Running round a ring of chairs and seeing how long a bluffer survives is lively and the 'how many before you believe' idea is reachable; it needs two adults and much is luck.

g23.why: Hiding colourings under cups and lifting one border is a good game, and playing the cheater on the five-petal flower is fun; re-colouring behind a folder correctly and quickly may need an adult.

g45.why: The probability of a cheater surviving k rounds and the shuffle table make the ideas concrete; 'learns nothing' remains subtle and secret sharing is a separate topic.

best_moment: The bluffer survives one round, then two, and the room cheers until the streak breaks.
biggest_problem: The zero-knowledge part ('the verifier learns nothing') is the deep idea but is the hardest thing to feel, and the colour-swap step behind the folder is likely to break down.
one_change: Use a printed colour-swap card for re-colouring and make the cheater-on-five-petals game the centrepiece for 2–5, dropping secret sharing to the guide.

title: Leaning towers off the table

k1.why: Sliding blocks out until the top one hangs completely past the edge is pure physical play with a visible surprise, and toppling is part of the fun.

g23.why: Finding the fewest blocks to get past the edge is a clear, gripping goal; measuring the shrinking steps adds a pattern to notice.

g45.why: Centres of mass, the harmonic steps and the side-by-side stack beating one-per-level give deep math anchored in something they built.

best_moment: Four blocks: the top block hangs entirely beyond the table edge and doesn't fall.
biggest_problem: Knife-edge stacks topple easily, so the four-block milestone may need patience and identical blocks.
one_change: Rehearse with the actual blocks and provide a pillow plus a five-block target so children reliably experience the milestone.

title: Space-filling curves

k1.why: Walking a floor path and inventing one that steps on every square once is active and easy, but there is little surprise for this age.

g23.why: Rotating four cups to join them into the next stage is a good spatial puzzle and drawing stage 3 is satisfying, though reflections are tricky and the 8 × 8 drawing is fine-motor work.

g45.why: Numbering 64 cells is a chore before the payoff, and the limit argument is abstract; the cells-close-in-number-versus-close-in-space contrast is a good hook.

best_moment: Four copies of the little cup snap together into one path that visits every square.
biggest_problem: The real mathematics (the limit reaching every point) arrives after a long numbering task and may not land.
one_change: Give 4–5 a pre-numbered stage-3 board and spend the time on the quarter-of-time-in-a-quarter-of-space puzzle instead of numbering.

title: Domino computers

k1.why: Knocking down domino lines, forks and merges is pure joy for this age, but five-year-olds knock lines over while setting them up and a reliable fork takes adult help; the truth-table card is incidental to the fun.

g23.why: The 'make the cup fall only if both are pushed' challenge is a great hook but a domino AND is genuinely hard and may just end in rebuilds; the human-gate half adder is a fun skit that an adult choreographs while most children stand and wait.

g45.why: Fewest-NAND-card puzzles are real puzzles a 10-year-old can own, but they are paper-and-rule-card work detached from the dominoes, and the domino gates beyond OR may not work reliably at table scale.

best_moment: The cup toppling when two lines merge, and the moment someone gets a cup to fall only when both starts are pushed.
biggest_problem: Most of the session risks going to resetting fallen dominoes and to gates (AND, XOR, NOT) that do not work reliably at table scale, so the gate ideas never get tested.
one_change: Rehearse and supply printed placement templates or simple jigs for wire, fork, merge and one working AND so children rebuild in a minute and spend their time testing and predicting.

title: The MU puzzle

k1.why: Doubling a cube pile or taking away 3 is concrete, and seeing 3, 6, 9, 12 stay empty on the mat is a real noticing, but routes like 1-2-4-8-5-10-7 are long for a five-year-old and the adult will keep the goal in mind.

g23.why: Juggling four conditional rewriting rules (ends in I, double after M, III to U, drop UU) while copying ever-longer tile strings is heavy, and the I-count-mod-3 insight is unlikely to emerge at this age, so it becomes aimless string-making with no aha.

g45.why: Proving MU impossible by tracking the I count is a classic, satisfying invariant argument for 10-year-olds, though the letter game itself is dry and the converse route-building is fiddly tile bookkeeping.

best_moment: Realising that no pile of 3, 6, 9 or 12 ever shows up no matter how you double and subtract.
biggest_problem: The four letter rules plus string doubling overload grades 2-3 and the invariant pay-off arrives only after a long, unfocused search.
one_change: Lead every band with the cube-pile game (double or take 3) as the main puzzle and offer the MIU letter system only to grades 4-5 as the follow-up that has the same hidden invariant.

title: Fake coin and the balance

k1.why: A real balance and a secret heavy egg is a hands-on detective game children love, and three eggs in one weighing is a lovely find; nine in two needs planning most five-year-olds will not do unaided, and a bucket balance may not tip clearly.

g23.why: Faker-and-detective roles, the 'level means it's the one left off' trick, and the 3-9-27 pattern are concrete and surprising; a 7-year-old can plan and test a two-weighing strategy with real eggs, though drawing the tree may need an adult scribe.

g45.why: The heavy-or-light 12-coin problem is notoriously hard and many 10-year-olds will not crack it in a session, and the 13-coin first-weighing argument is abstract; the heavy-only part is a strong entry if allowed.

best_moment: Discovering that one weighing finds the heavy one among three because a level balance also gives an answer.
biggest_problem: It depends on a balance sensitive enough to show one extra washer, and the 4-5 heavy-or-light challenge may be too hard to land in one hour.
one_change: Use a heavier fake (two or three extra washers) and rehearse the balance, and give 4-5 the heavy-or-light version with 3, then 4, then 12 containers as an explicit ladder rather than jumping to 12.

title: Easy to check, hard to find

k1.why: Splitting cube sticks into two equal rows and checking by sliding them side by side is concrete, and being a puzzle maker who breaks a tower in half is fun; but the plan's example bag 1 to 6 totals 21 (odd) and has no split, and the check-versus-find idea is a meta point they won't feel.

g23.why: Finding the one split of the 7-stick bag, beating the greedy rule and wrestling with a no-split bag are real puzzles; it can feel like addition practice and the no bag may frustrate without an adult ending.

g45.why: Counting ways to share sticks, collecting reasons for 'no' and finding a no bag none of them explains is good reasoning, and the million-dollar open problem is a hook; the activity itself is subset-sum trial and error without a big gasp.

best_moment: Lifting the folder to check a hidden split in two seconds after struggling to find it, or making a bag that a friend can't crack.
biggest_problem: The core action is searching for equal-sum splits, which is mildly satisfying but has no strong surprise, and the K-1 example bag is unsolvable as written.
one_change: Turn it into a maker-versus-solver game: each child builds a secret solvable bag from a split tower and challenges a partner against a timer, so the check-is-fast, find-is-slow contrast is felt rather than told (and fix the K-1 bag to an even total).
