title: Pairing strategies

k1.why: The strip game is quick and replayable, and 'two in a row always wins' is easy to see, but finding or following a domino pairing plan is beyond most five-year-olds; they will play Breaker with dominoes an adult drew.

g23.why: Tic-tac-toe variants are instantly appealing and 'Maker first always wins on 3 by 3' is a good discovery; the 5 by 5 domino plan is a hard puzzle and checking 12 lines on a clear sleeve is fiddly, so many children will need the diagonal hint.

g45.why: Playing games, then proving Breaker always wins with a domino plan, plus the lovely counting argument that 4 by 4 (16 squares, 10 lines needing 20) has no plan, is exactly the game-to-proof arc 10-year-olds enjoy.

best_moment: Watching a pre-drawn domino plan shut down every attempt at three in a row, then discovering you can beat it on a board where it can't exist.
biggest_problem: The central pairing idea is a strategy someone else designs, so younger children mostly play a game whose clever part they don't see.
one_change: Give 2-3 a ladder of pairing puzzles on smaller boards (strips, 3 by 4 rectangles) before 5 by 5, so children design a working plan themselves before the hard one.

title: Guess two-thirds of the average

k1.why: Levelling eleven secret towers to find an average is slow and adult-run, five-year-olds can't reason about what others will guess, so each round is effectively a lottery with one winner and some upset losers.

g23.why: The class game with a chart of falling targets is lively and 'why would anyone guess over 67?' is reachable, but most 7-year-olds guess randomly and the adult does all the averaging.

g45.why: Ten-year-olds reason about other players' reasoning about as well as adults, the falling targets round to round produce real laughter and argument, and the crossing-out staircase is a satisfying explanation.

best_moment: Seeing the winning number drop sharply in round two as everyone tries to outthink everyone else.
biggest_problem: Only the oldest children can play the reasoning game; for younger ones and at a kitchen table with two or three players it degenerates (with two players the lower guess always wins).
one_change: Run it as a whole-room game aimed at 4-5 with a quick visual average (calculator or number line) and give K-1 a different task, and add a kitchen-table version with imaginary extra players or past-class data so it works with three people.

title: Racetrack

k1.why: Being the car on a floor road, hopping by a speed card and trying to stop exactly in the garage is physical and funny; tracking 'add 1, keep, take 1' while hopping needs a partner holding the card, and the planning is mostly adult-prompted.

g23.why: Racetrack races are a game children replay happily, but the ghost-arrow rule is hard for 7-year-olds to execute on 1 cm squares and crashes from miscopied arrows may cause disputes.

g45.why: Paper races in pairs with a real strategy (brake before the corner) are absorbing and replayable, and the 1-2-3-2-1 parking pattern and a why-no-faster argument give genuine mathematics.

best_moment: Overshooting the garage or crashing into the wall at full speed, then realising you have to brake early to win.
biggest_problem: For younger children the vector-copying rule on small squared paper is fiddly enough that adults end up checking or drawing moves.
one_change: Use a larger grid (2 cm squares or a printed dot board) and a transparent or cut-out 3-by-3 'steering card' placed at the tip of the copied arrow so younger children can execute moves without miscounting.

title: Same network or different

k1.why: Bead-and-string networks tangle, five-year-olds struggle to lay them out to match a drawing, and 'same network' is an abstract judgment they cannot make by themselves.

g23.why: Sorting a deck of drawings into families is a decent spot-the-same game and the pentagon-equals-star reveal is nice, but proving differences by counts gets dry and the equal-count different pair at 8 dots is likely too hard.

g45.why: Finding all six trees on six beads and writing renamings is solid reasoning for 10-year-olds, but checking renamings is bookkeeping and there is little surprise after the first reveal.

best_moment: Dropping the pentagon as a tangle and laying it out as a five-pointed star: it's the same network.
biggest_problem: After the first 'it's the same!' moment the activity becomes counting degrees and checking renamings, which is careful bookkeeping more than discovery.
one_change: Make it a game: one child secretly re-lays a bead network, the other must decide same or different and challenge, so the counts become weapons in a contest rather than a checklist.

title: Instant Insanity

k1.why: Folding paper cubes from nets is beyond five-year-old hands, and keeping four sides of a tower in mind while turning cubes overloads them; only the 'front shows four colours' goal is realistic.

g23.why: The ladder of goals gives some progress and the broken cube with four red faces is a good impossibility argument, but the full puzzle by trial is famously frustrating and most children won't solve it.

g45.why: The opposite-face graph is a beautiful trick, but drawing and reading it needs a long adult explanation and the pay-off arrives late, after children have likely spent their patience on trial and error.

best_moment: Proving the broken set is hopeless: one cube with four red faces must show red on two sides.
biggest_problem: The core puzzle is a mostly-blind search with a tiny solution set, so children face long frustration before the clever method appears.
one_change: Supply sturdy pre-made cubes (wooden with stickers), and introduce the 'only opposite pairs matter' idea early with a 2- or 3-cube version that kids can solve, so the graph method helps before patience runs out.

title: Who is most important?

k1.why: Walking between chairs and dropping counters is fun for a few minutes, but it is a coin-driven walk with no decisions, one floor setup means waiting turns, and the point (A beats C) only appears after pooling many steps.

g23.why: The vote-then-surprise is a good hook and the trap and die rule are memorable, but 26 coin-flip steps per pair and tallying are a simulation chore and results are noisy.

g45.why: Checking that the 4, 2, 3, 2, 1, 1 counter split survives a sharing round is a crisp aha and explains why C loses to A, though it comes after a long random walk.

best_moment: The class vote for C turning out wrong when the cups are lined up.
biggest_problem: Most of the time goes to executing random steps and tallying, and the surprising result only emerges after pooling, by which point younger children have lost interest.
one_change: Lead with the counter-sharing round (everyone at a chair passes counters along arrows simultaneously) so all children act at once and see the piles settle, keeping the random walk as a short confirmation.

title: Soap-film shortcuts

k1.why: Dipping a frame and seeing a soap network appear is magic for five-year-olds; drawing it and comparing string lengths is simple, even if the shortest-network idea stays light.

g23.why: The soap's surprising square network (two junctions, not an X) and the string comparisons give a real gasp; measuring 120 degrees is fiddly but a three-armed template helps.

g45.why: The sliding-junction argument for equal angles, predicting junctions then checking with soap, and catching soap in a worse network are rich and hands-on for 10-year-olds.

best_moment: Lifting the square frame out of the soap and seeing two junctions joined by a bridge instead of the expected X.
biggest_problem: Building reliable plate-and-peg frames is over the 30-minute prep budget for a parent volunteer and the frames may not work well first time.
one_change: Specify a no-drill frame design (e.g., two clear lids with pushpins or glued dowels) and rehearse it, with a fallback of printed photos of the soap networks if frames fail.

title: Bulgarian solitaire

k1.why: With 6 counters the move is concrete and the staircase appears in a few moves, which is a little magic, but 'one from every pile' is easy to fumble and it's a procedure rather than a puzzle.

g23.why: Discovering that some totals settle and some loop is a real surprise, but filling a class table for 3 to 10 is a simulation chore with careful recording.

g45.why: Finding both cycles for 8 and the shapes no move makes is good, but the tipped-diagram proof is abstract and may need a return visit.

best_moment: Every different start of 6 cards ending in the same 3-2-1 staircase.
biggest_problem: Children spend most of their time executing a fixed move and recording piles rather than making choices.
one_change: Make it a challenge: 'find the start that takes longest to reach the staircase' or 'make a pile shape that can never appear', so children choose starts and hunt rather than just repeat the move.

title: Weird dice

k1.why: Racing counters up a 2-to-12 track with dice is a game kids enjoy, but it's pure luck and the point (weird dice behave the same) is invisible to five-year-olds after a few rolls.

g23.why: Filling two addition tables and finding identical counts is a genuine surprise and good arithmetic, but designing a matching die from scratch is a hard, open search that can stall.

g45.why: Finding the four-sided weird pair is a nice puzzle, but the polynomial factoring is too abstract for most 10-year-olds without algebra.

best_moment: Filling both addition tables and realising the strange dice give exactly the same sums counts.
biggest_problem: The surprise lives in a table, not in play, and the deep explanation needs algebra beyond the band.
one_change: Make a game where knowing doubles matters (roll again on doubles), so children feel the one visible difference, and give 2-3 a guided search for the four-sided pair instead of the six-sided design.

title: Lining up by height

k1.why: Picking people 'in order but skipping some' is a subtle idea for five-year-olds, and checking all triples in a line of 5 needs an adult to drive.

g23.why: Building the longest line with no run of 3 or 4 is a good puzzle and patience sorting is a fun card game, but checking runs by hand is error-prone.

g45.why: Finding 3 2 1 6 5 4 9 8 7, discovering 10 always fails, and the label-pair pigeonhole proof are rich and accessible for 10-year-olds.

best_moment: Five volunteers trying every rearrangement and never escaping a run of three.
biggest_problem: Spotting non-adjacent rising or falling runs is error-prone, so younger children rely on an adult to check.
one_change: Add a quick check method (patience piles or step-forward routine) introduced early so children can verify runs themselves.

title: Remainders that repeat

k1.why: Dealing counters onto plates is fine for a round or two, but trading leftovers for ten smaller counters is a symbolic step a 5-year-old won't follow; the adult does the trading and recording while kids deal, and 'the cards repeat' after six rounds is mostly the adult's observation.

g23.why: Dealing then switching to the wheel is doable and 'the leftover came back, so it must repeat forever' is a real aha, but six to twelve rounds of deal-trade-record is a long procedure and the shift from counters to wheel needs a strong adult; without decimals the payoff (the digits 142857) is muted.

g45.why: The rotating digits of 142857 and 2/7 starting the same wheel at 2 are genuine surprises, but the route there is long division by hand and the period table for primes to 41 is bookkeeping shared across tables, with 17 and 19 needing 16-18 rounds.

best_moment: Multiplying 142857 by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and seeing the same digits come back rotated, then times 7 giving 999999.
biggest_problem: The concrete dealing is slow and repetitive and turns into a rote simulation before the interesting wheel and rotation patterns appear.
one_change: Move the counters to a 3-minute launch and have children work mainly on the remainder wheel (with the 'times 3 on the 7-wheel' shortcut available), saving time for the 142857 rotation hunt.

title: Squares from two squares

k1.why: Building small squares from tiles and adding two of them with an adult is real hands-on work, and colouring a class chart is satisfying, but the totals quickly need counting past 20 and the 'never works' pattern is mostly adult-noticed.

g23.why: A class hunt to fill a 1-50 chart is engaging and the leftover-after-fours sort is a concrete obstruction, but after the first 15 minutes it becomes mental addition of squares and chart bookkeeping; tiles help only for small cases.

g45.why: Proving 'leaves 3 after fours is impossible' with tile groups is a real proof children can own, and the prime split (5, 13, 17 work; 3, 7, 11 don't) is a striking pattern; windmills are fiddly but a good challenge with printed outlines.

best_moment: Discovering that every never-works number leaves exactly 3 when grouped in fours, so 43 and 47 can be ruled out without trying.
biggest_problem: For younger bands the chart hunt drifts into arithmetic of squares with a light payoff, and windmill building needs 29 tiles and careful orientation.
one_change: Give 2-3 a pre-printed table of square numbers to pair up so the hunt focuses on the pattern of failures, and give 4-5 printed windmill outlines.

title: Rectangles of a number

k1.why: Building every rectangle from 6, 7, 8 and 12 tiles is a good K-1 task and '7 only makes a line' is a small surprise; the tower comparison needs an adult to list sides, but kids can stack and compare towers.

g23.why: Rectangle galleries and the short/level/tall sort are concrete and finding 28 as the second 'level' number is a satisfying hunt, but tracing every rectangle onto squared paper is busywork and the material repeats familiar factor-rectangle work.

g45.why: Predicting 496 from the doubling sums and checking why 15 fails gives a real conjecture-and-test moment, and 'nobody knows if an odd one exists' lands well at this age.

best_moment: A tower of 1+2+3 standing exactly level with a tower of 6, then hunting for the next number that does it.
biggest_problem: Tracing galleries and stacking towers for many numbers is slow, and the rectangle gallery repeats Week 96-style material.
one_change: Drop the tracing; let tables share a wall list of side lengths and spend the time on the level-tower hunt and the doubling pattern.

title: Times tables on a circle

k1.why: Hooking yarn round a notched plate while an adult reads pairs is fiddly, the adult is operating the rule, and on 10 notches no striking shape appears.

g23.why: Watching a heart appear from straight lines is a real wow, but drawing 59 accurate chords with a ruler and computing 'times 2, keep the remainder past 60' is a long chore that many 7-8-year-olds won't finish; splitting dots within a table helps.

g45.why: Cusp counting across times 2 to 5 and the parallel chords of times 23 are good conjectures, but each picture is 10-15 minutes of ruler work, so comparing four multipliers needs pre-printed help; the return-to-1 question is good mental work.

best_moment: The cardioid emerging from a mess of straight chords on the 60-dot circle.
biggest_problem: The payoff depends on dozens of precise ruler chords, which is slow, fine-motor and error-prone.
one_change: Print dot circles with each dot's target number already labelled (or faint chords for half the circle) so children draw quickly and spend time comparing pictures.

title: Flexagons

k1.why: A pre-folded trihexaflexagon that magically shows a hidden colour delights young children and stickering new faces is easy, but the pinch flex itself is awkward for small hands and there is little to do after finding three faces.

g23.why: Folding a trihexa with help and hunting all six faces of a pre-folded hexahexa is absorbing play with a built-in mystery (rare faces), and the face map is a natural record.

g45.why: Folding the hexahexaflexagon is fiddly but doable at this age, and the traverse, the triangle map and predicting the hidden face from the strip give real reasoning tied to a toy kids want to keep playing with.

best_moment: Pinching open the flexagon and a colour nobody had seen appears in the middle.
biggest_problem: Folding, especially the hexahexa, is a known stumbling point and the face map depends on the printed strip matching the plan, which is untested on paper.
one_change: Rehearse and print a tested hexahexa strip and prepare enough pre-folded spares that no child waits on folding to start flexing.

title: Thirty coloured cubes

k1.why: Stickering red/blue cubes is fun and 'same after turning' is a real idea at this age, but reliably deciding whether two cubes match by turning is hard for 5-year-olds, so the table count of 10 will need heavy adult checking.

g23.why: Building a class museum is a motivating collective goal, but comparing six-colour cubes by turning is slow and error-prone, and duplicates or misses will creep in unless the sorting card system is given early.

g45.why: The 5 x 6 and 720 / 24 arguments, mirror twins and MacMahon's double-size puzzle are rich, but the puzzle needs a complete, correct set of 30, which the museum may not deliver in one session.

best_moment: Two cubes that look totally different turning slowly until they match, or a pair that can never be made to match (mirror twins).
biggest_problem: Every stage rests on children correctly judging cube sameness by mental or physical rotation, which is slow and unreliable.
one_change: Give the 'red on top, which colour below, read the sides from a fixed colour' card from the start and have a pre-made checked set of 30 ready for the MacMahon puzzle.

title: Arrow multiplication

k1.why: Quarter-turn floor games are fun movement but the mathematics is just counting turns, and naming a half turn 'minus 1' means nothing to children who haven't met negative numbers.

g23.why: Multiplying by 1 + i means placing an arrow and its turned copy nose to tail and recording points like -2 + 2i; children execute a rule they can't connect to anything, and the spiral payoff needs accurate long arrows off a table mat.

g45.why: Some 10-year-olds will enjoy that two tilted arrows multiply to land exactly on 5 and that 3 can never be made, but the nose-to-tail rule with backwards copies is abstract and needs a worked example and a strong adult.

best_moment: The child-arrow on the floor turning twice to face backwards and the room realising 'times i times i' is 'minus 1'.
biggest_problem: The concrete action (turning) is trivial while the real content (Gaussian multiplication) is an abstract rule pitched well above the bands.
one_change: Reserve it for 4-5 as a sequel to Week 158, built around one physical puzzle: which grid arrows can be combined to land exactly on 5, 13 or 3.

title: Borromean rings

k1.why: Hooking pipe-cleaner chains is easy fun and untwisting one ring so the other two fall free is a great magic moment, but the adult will build the magic three for them.

g23.why: Choosing who is on top at each crossing, lifting to test, and sorting 8 patterns into 'falls apart' and 'holds together' is a concrete, self-checking hunt with a surprise answer (only 2 hold).

g45.why: The four-loop Brunnian chain is a good challenge but unrehearsed, and scoring crossings with a hand rule to get 0 is abstract bookkeeping whose point (0 does not mean unlinked) needs careful adult talk.

best_moment: Three rings hang together from one hand, no two are hooked, and untwisting any one drops the other two.
biggest_problem: Weaving the third ring and the four-loop chain are fiddly and unrehearsed, and the 4-5 linking number is an abstract scoring exercise.
one_change: Give 4-5 more physical challenges (build a four- or five-ring Brunnian chain with rubber bands, design one) and keep the crossing-score as a short demo.

title: Inside or outside?

k1.why: Jumping in and out of rope loops and checking by walking without stepping over is joyful and physical, but the odd/even rule is something the adult tells them rather than something they find.

g23.why: Deciding quickly for bugs on tangle sheets, checking by colouring, and designing a trick loop for a partner is game-like, independent and has a satisfying shortcut to discover.

g45.why: Why each crossing switches and where the rule breaks (corners, edges, self-crossings, the star's centre) is good reasoning, but much of it is discussion, and it overlaps other self-crossing and winding drafts.

best_moment: A toy deep in the rope spiral: the room votes, one child walks out counting rope crossings, and the count settles it.
biggest_problem: The rope spiral needs floor space and rehearsal, and the 4-5 part leans on talk rather than doing.
one_change: Give 4-5 a concrete challenge, such as drawing a loop where some ray has to pass through a corner and fixing the count, or two-colouring a partner's self-crossing loop.

title: You can't comb a hairy ball

k1.why: Covering a ball with arrow stickers so 'neighbours point almost the same way' is fiddly and vague for 5-year-olds, and they can't tell whether their calm spot is forced or just a sticker mistake; the combing launch is the only clear moment.

g23.why: Trying for exactly one or two calm spots needs judging continuity of a hand-placed sticker field on a curved surface, which leads to disputes rather than discovery; the ring-versus-ball contrast is good but brief.

g45.why: Indices and the 'total is always 2' pattern are a real discovery for 10-year-olds, but the pointer walk is new and abstract, and the cube net with springs, saddles and drains is adult-guided.

best_moment: Combing a fluffy pompom and the tuft that always appears somewhere.
biggest_problem: The core activity, a field of stickers on a beach ball, is too imprecise for children to see what forces a calm spot.
one_change: Use printed sphere and torus nets with pre-placed dots so children draw arrows on a grid, keeping the combing and the swim ring as the physical hook.

title: Walking a loop

k1.why: Walking tape paths and dropping a peg on the left or right card at each turn is physical and kids can do it, but the 'always one full turn' comparison of piles needs adult help, and the turn dial is fiddly.

g23.why: Drawing a wild grid loop for a partner and predicting 'left minus right is always 4' is a crisp, checkable surprise, and crossing loops making 0 or 8 is a good follow-up.

g45.why: Turtle stars with 72, 144 and 135 degree turns are hard to draw by hand, so it becomes prediction on paper; the rule is good but the concrete action is thin without a turtle program or pre-printed paths.

best_moment: However wiggly the loop, left turns minus right turns always come out the same.
biggest_problem: Taping five floor paths is a lot of prep, and the 4-5 turtle part has little concrete action.
one_change: For 4-5, give angle cards for walking turtle stars on a big floor (or a simple Logo screen) so they act out the star before predicting.

title: Folding beats the compass

k1.why: Halves and quarters are fine, but the 'magic fold' and the equilateral triangle are copied step by step after an adult and need precise folds that 5-year-olds can't make.

g23.why: Haga's fold making exact thirds is a real trick and the pinch game converging to a third is satisfying, but folding accuracy limits what children see, and finding which fractions appear needs measuring.

g45.why: Abe's trisection is a striking fold, but it needs a precise simultaneous placement that many 10-year-olds will botch, and the 'why' of the equilateral fold is the stronger task.

best_moment: One fold makes exact thirds, checked by folding the paper so the pieces match one-to-two.
biggest_problem: Most moves are procedures copied from an adult and judged by folding precision rather than reasoning.
one_change: Centre 2-3 and 4-5 on open exploration of Haga's fold (fold a corner to any edge point and find what fractions appear), with the trisection as an optional demonstration.

title: Stacking oranges

k1.why: Stacking balls into pyramids is concrete and fun, and seeing a ball roll into a hollow is a good discovery, but ping-pong balls roll everywhere in a noisy room and need frames and non-slip mats.

g23.why: Predicting pyramid counts before building is a good pattern task, but the box comparison (64 vs 66) shows almost no difference, and counting the 12 touching balls in a big stack is hard to see.

g45.why: Finding triangular layers on the slanted face of a square pyramid is a nice 3D aha, but the cannonball part is a table lookup and the Kepler material is mostly story.

best_moment: Spotting that the slanted face of the square pyramid is a triangle of balls, the same stack seen another way.
biggest_problem: The headline comparison of stacking methods gives an unconvincing difference, and loose balls make building frustrating.
one_change: Use a taller box or count balls per layer area so the straight-up versus hollows difference is clear, and supply frames that keep balls from rolling.

title: Rep-tiles

k1.why: Making a bigger copy of a pattern block from copies of itself is easy to understand, self-checking and quick, and the hexagon refusing to double is a real surprise.

g23.why: Building the big L from four Ls and then from 16 is a satisfying puzzle with a countable pattern, and testing which tetrominoes double gives a clear yes/no hunt.

g45.why: The sphinx double needing flips is a genuinely tricky puzzle, and folding A4 against letter paper gives a nice real-world aha about the square root of 2 ratio.

best_moment: Four small sphinxes, three of them flipped, clicking into one big sphinx.
biggest_problem: Cutting about 70 L-trominoes and the sphinxes per table is well over a parent's 30-minute prep.
one_change: Make Ls from square tiles or snap cubes (or buy polyomino sets) and pre-tape 16-blocks, so cutting is limited to the sphinxes.

title: Shared birthdays

k1.why: Rolling a die for each teddy and seeing whether two land in the same box is easy and fun for a minute or two, and dropping cubes into two cups is a fine tally. But comparing the cup towers is a probability idea with no surprise for children who had no expectation in the first place, so after a few parties it turns into repetitive rolling.

g23.why: Rolling parties of 3 to 6 guests on a 12-box calendar is quick and children can run it themselves, and 'why are 13 always enough?' is a real pigeonhole aha. But separating 4 guests (43%) from 5 (62%) needs about 30 parties per size, so most of the hour is rolling and tallying for a margin the pooled chart may not show clearly.

g45.why: Counting pairs (10 in a party of 5, 253 in 23) and multiplying 11/12 x 10/12 x ... to get 38% is a real reason behind the data, and the 'someone shares MY birthday needs 253 people' contrast can produce a gasp. Multiplying fractions with a calculator is abstract, and the famous surprise lives on a 365-day calendar that the class never actually experiences.

best_moment: A party where children bet 'no match' and the fifth roll lands on an occupied box, again and again, until the class chart shows that shared boxes are winning.
biggest_problem: The surprise depends on a wrong intuition that young children don't have yet, and the evidence needs long repetitive rolling and pooling.
one_change: Open with a betting game in which each child stakes a counter on 'match' or 'no match' before each party, so the surprise is felt in their own wins and losses rather than read off a pooled tally.

title: First digits (Benford)

k1.why: Sorting cards with big printed numbers by their first digit shape and building towers is something children can do, but the numbers mean nothing to them, the deck is simply handed over, and 'one deck makes a staircase' has no reason they can reach. It is a sorting chore with a modest visual payoff.

g23.why: Doubling from a number they chose with a calculator and adding first-digit stickers to a class chart is quick, and the doubling map (anything starting with 5 to 9 doubles to a number starting with 1) is a genuine aha they can find themselves. Doubling by hand past 1000 turns into arithmetic practice, and the class chart needs many stickers before 1 clearly wins.

g45.why: Listing the powers of 2 by digit length and noticing that each group has exactly one starting with 1 is a pattern they can find and explain, and the unit-change extension is a nice twist. The explanation (3 or 4 powers per digit length, a share between 1/4 and 1/3) is good but a little dry, and the real-data hook is unchecked.

best_moment: Discovering that every number starting with 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 doubles to a number starting with 1, so the 1 column has to win.
biggest_problem: The core activity is generating and sorting long numbers, which feels like processing data more than playing, and the joy depends on an anticipation of 'all digits equal' that children may not have.
one_change: Build the session around the doubling-map arrows as a board game (a token moves along first digits as you double) so children feel why 1 keeps being visited, with the sticker chart as confirmation.

title: How long does Snakes and Ladders last?

k1.why: Playing Snakes and Ladders on a short board and adding a cube for every roll is something young children love and can do alone; lining up towers from shortest to tallest makes the spread visible. The mathematical question is light (shortest game, snakes covered), but they will happily replay it.

g23.why: Asking which square is best or worst and whether removing a snake helps is a real question, but games average about 7 rolls with a wide spread, so the few games a pair can play give noisy answers and the class may draw the wrong conclusion. It is a pure luck game with no decisions, so the thinking happens only in prediction.

g45.why: Working backwards on the coin strip is a beautiful idea, and 'a ladder that makes the game longer' is a real surprise. But the computation is fractions like 9/4, 23/8 and 153/64 with no physical action, so many 10-year-olds will need an adult to carry it, and the classic-board surprises need a computer.

best_moment: Finding that adding a ladder can make the game take longer.
biggest_problem: The fun part (playing) and the mathematical part (working back with fractions) are disconnected, and noisy small samples can mislead the middle band.
one_change: Give 4-5 the backward computation in 'out of 16 games' whole numbers on the board itself, and choose a small board where a harmful ladder changes the class's own game lengths visibly.

title: Shrinking piles

k1.why: Pouring a cup of two-colour counters, taking away the reds and building a tower of what is left is hands-on and gives a satisfying staircase. Counting and building a tower each round is slow for 5-year-olds, and comparing staircases with neighbours is a mild observation rather than a surprise.

g23.why: Predicting what is left after each pour is engaging, and 'doubling the pile adds only about one pour' is a real idea. But time-to-empty varies a lot (a spread of nearly 2 rounds) while doubling adds only one, so the pooled sticky notes from a few pairs may not show the pattern.

g45.why: The mystery cup (a partner pours 64 counters secretly and shows what is left, you guess how many pours) is a genuine guessing game with a reasoning payoff that children can replay, and the dice-sixes half-life extension gives a fresh twist. The radiocarbon story adds a real-world wow.

best_moment: Guessing from a handful of counters left in the mystery cup that the partner poured exactly four times.
biggest_problem: The 2-3 headline pattern (one extra pour per doubling) is statistically too noisy to emerge from the data one class can generate.
one_change: Lead 2-3 with the predict-the-pile and mystery-cup games, and keep 'how many pours does a doubled pile last?' as a whole-class pooled question with many trials or an app run.

title: The chaos game

k1.why: Marking halfway points with a stretched rubber band, 10 to 15 times, needs fine-motor accuracy that 5-year-olds lack, and every dot depends on the last, so errors compound. The payoff (holes in a stack of transparencies) only arrives at the end and may not appear at all with imprecise dots.

g23.why: Thirty halfway measurements with a ruler along slanted lines (halving non-whole centimetres) is a long, error-prone chore for 7- and 8-year-olds. The stacked reveal could be a real gasp, but it arrives late and depends on accuracy they are unlikely to keep.

g45.why: Ten-year-olds can measure reasonably and will get absorbed in why a dot can never land in the middle triangle, which is a lovely argument. The measuring is still a slog, and the picture is only convincing if the class stack is accurate enough.

best_moment: Stacking every table's transparencies on a window and watching the empty triangles appear.
biggest_problem: The activity's success depends on many precise measured dots, which is exactly what children are worst at, and the payoff comes only at the end.
one_change: Have children do a handful of hand jumps to learn the rule, then reveal the full picture with an app or projector run, and spend the main time on 'why can't a dot land here?' with half-size triangle cut-outs.

title: Hide the bean (mixed strategies)

k1.why: Hiding a bean under cups and trying to outguess a partner is a game young children will play happily for a long time, and noticing that 'always blue' gets caught is within reach. The die recipe will mostly be an adult's idea, but the core play is theirs.

g23.why: Testing recipes such as 'red on 1 to 4' against a seeker who knows the recipe is a good question, but comparing pooled cube totals from noisy random play is slow and may not separate the recipes clearly. Professor Swindle adds a nice 'looks fair but isn't' moment.

g45.why: The equalising argument (make the seeker's two guesses equally good) is something ten-year-olds can reach, and Morra's 7/12 deck plus the adult mind-reader round give real surprises. But mixed-strategy reasoning is abstract and the long-run claims rest on averages they can't see in a few rounds.

best_moment: The adult 'mind reader' predicting a child's supposedly random hiding again and again, then failing against a die.
biggest_problem: The mathematics (a best random mix) is only visible in long-run averages, which children's few noisy rounds won't reveal.
one_change: Make the mind-reader round the launch, so children feel why a die beats their own 'random' choices before they look for the best mix.

title: Pirates share the gold

k1.why: Wearing rank cards and holding gold coins is fun, but the voting rule (thumbs up only for more than you'd get after the captain walks) needs backward reasoning that 5-year-olds can't hold, so the adult does all the logic and children just vote by feeling.

g23.why: Building up from small ships on a strip and finding the 1, 0, 1, 0 pattern works with a capable adult, and the captain keeping almost everything is a real gasp. The tie-break preferences (enjoying a splash, the proposer's casting vote) are a lot of rules, and children acting as pirates will vote out of fairness or spite rather than by the logic.

g45.why: This is a classic puzzle with a shocking answer that ten-year-olds can reach themselves by working up from small ships, and acting it out makes the argument concrete. The power-of-two survivors for few coins is a deep extension for keen children.

best_moment: Realising that the five-pirate captain keeps 98 coins and everyone still votes yes.
biggest_problem: Children playing the pirates bring real feelings about fairness, which clashes with the cold self-interest the logic assumes, and the tie-break rules are easy to lose.
one_change: Put the three preferences (survive, then coins, then enjoy a splash) on one picture card, and have children predict each pirate's vote from the ship strip rather than voting as themselves.

title: Bidding for turns

k1.why: Hiding chips in a fist and opening together is fun, but the rule that the winner pays the loser is counterintuitive and the star tie rule is beyond 5-year-olds. They will bid at random, so the 'spending everything hands it over' idea will have to be pointed out by an adult.

g23.why: The flag race with 10 chips gives a real puzzle (how many chips guarantee a win?), and bidding tic-tac-toe is a fresh game children like. The star rule is the hardest part and will need rehearsed adult help, and the analysis of splits needs careful record-keeping.

g45.why: Finding that 1 chip out of 10 wins a 1-against-3 race and that this matches the coin-flip chance of 1/8 is a striking surprise. But it rests on working back probabilities and an averaging argument that most children will test rather than understand, and the discrete star rule complicates the clean picture.

best_moment: Winning the bidding race with just 1 chip against 9.
biggest_problem: The rules (hidden bids, paying the opponent, the star tie-break) take most of the attention before any strategy can develop.
one_change: Drop the star for younger bands with a simple 'tie means both bid again' rule, and save the star for 4-5 once the race is familiar.

title: Sharing the taxi fare

k1.why: Driving a toy taxi and laying cubes is pleasant, but the stretch-sharing rule is given by the adult and children only carry it out, square by square. There is no puzzle or surprise for them to find.

g23.why: Arguing about what's fair is engaging for this age, and testing rules (equal split, by distance, by stretch) on new trips gives them something to check. Without a sharp script, the 'fair' argument may stall in opinions, and the payoff is a quiet conclusion rather than an aha.

g45.why: Playing all six arrival orders and finding that the average equals the stretch rule is a genuine surprise, and testing which rules break which condition is good reasoning. Shapley's conditions, especially additivity, are abstract, and averaging six orders is somewhat procedural.

best_moment: Averaging the six arrival orders and finding that the far friend pays exactly 3, the same as the stretch rule.
biggest_problem: Most of the activity is carrying out sharing rules, with little tension or game, so the joy depends on a fairness debate that may not take off.
one_change: Open with a case where an obvious rule (equal split) makes a near neighbour pay more than a taxi of their own, so the class has an injustice to fix before comparing rules.

title: Who holds the power?

k1.why: Three voters with 4, 3 and 2 cubes snapping towers to reach a line, and finding that any two win, is concrete and gives a small surprise (unequal stacks, equal power). It works with adults acting it out, but the 'needed' idea will mostly be shown by an adult stepping away.

g23.why: Four voters and four quota lines mean listing up to 15 teams per line and checking each member for criticality, which is heavy bookkeeping for 7- and 8-year-olds. The discoveries (a 2-cube voter as weak as a 1-cube voter) are good but buried under the listing.

g45.why: The Nassau board, where the 7-vote member equals each 9 and three members have no power at all, is a surprise ten-year-olds can argue for without listing everything, and the 'hunt for a dummy' is a good puzzle. The link to Week 179's arrival order is a nice extra.

best_moment: Discovering that a voter holding cubes can never change the result.
biggest_problem: The core method (list every team, test each member) is exhaustive bookkeeping that overwhelms the middle band.
one_change: For 2-3, use three voters on two or three quota lines and frame the dummy hunt as a challenge ('make a vote where someone with cubes never matters') instead of complete team listings.

title: A new road makes traffic worse

k1.why: Being a car on a taped floor map and seeing that the new road made everyone slower is physical and memorable. But the switching rule and adding up trip times will be run by the adult, so 5-year-olds mostly walk where they're told and hear the result.

g23.why: Moving counters on a map for 2 to 5 cars, finding settled arrangements and discovering that the shortcut helps 3 cars and hurts 4, is a real surprise children can find with small sums. Several equilibria from 5 cars on may need adult care.

g45.why: Explaining why nobody leaves the shortcut (9 minutes against 8) and why 2 and 2 is still better for the group gives a satisfying argument, and Braess's and Pigou's numbers extend it. The paradox is a genuine 'wait, what?' that ten-year-olds will want to retell.

best_moment: Opening the free shortcut, everyone taking it, and everyone arriving later than before.
biggest_problem: Acting out one-at-a-time selfish switching on the floor needs strict turn-taking, and children may cooperate instead of acting selfishly, blurring the equilibrium.
one_change: Give each driver a personal goal card ('get home fastest, you win a sticker if you beat your old time') and a clear one-at-a-time switch turn, so selfish switching is part of the game.

title: Passing secrets by phone

k1.why: Acting out calls with coloured cubes is concrete, and beating the adult's 6-call plan with fewer calls for four animals is a nice challenge. Taking the right cubes from the tray and following a call list needs adult support, so K-1 will partly watch.

g23.why: Finding 4 calls for 4 people is a satisfying puzzle with a clear aha, and pushing to 5 in 6 and 6 in 8, beating the hub plan, keeps them going. The cube exchange can get slow with 6 people, but the call list is a light record.

g45.why: Generalising the 4-chief plan and proving that 3 calls can't work for 4 people gives real reasoning, and the honest open gap (7 vs 8 for six people) is a good end. It is puzzle-driven with little bookkeeping.

best_moment: Finding the 4-call trick (AB, CD, AC, BD) after trying and failing with more calls.
biggest_problem: Physical cube exchanges with many colours get slow and error-prone as groups grow.
one_change: Use a printed strip of colour boxes to tick for groups of 5 or more, keeping cubes only for the first acted-out calls.

title: Can everyone get a partner?

k1.why: Placing clips on lines to pair faces with animals on small mats is a manageable puzzle, and pointing to 'these three only like these two' is a nice idea. Crowded mats and clips on lines may be fiddly, and the stuck-group idea will need an adult to bring out.

g23.why: Sorting mats into 'works' and 'cannot' and fixing a pairing by swaps is good puzzle work, and designing a failing mat where everyone has two lines is a nice challenge. Finding the short group on 5-face mats without prompting is hard, and tangled lines make scanning tiring.

g45.why: The rook grid, where the most rooks always matches the fewest covering lines, is a clean surprise that ten-year-olds can test and check themselves, and the cover as proof is satisfying. Low reading and no bookkeeping.

best_moment: Finding that the most rooks and the fewest lines always match, so the cover proves you can't do better.
biggest_problem: On crowded mats, finding the group that blocks a pairing is a visual search that middle-band children may not manage without adult hints.
one_change: Draw the mats with few, clearly separated lines and colour-coded animals so the short group stands out, and grow mat size gradually.

title: Your friends have more friends

k1.why: Yarn between animals is fun to set up, but comparing one's own tower with a group of friends' towers is an averaging idea 5-year-olds can't handle, and an adult ties and runs everything.

g23.why: Passing sticky notes along yarn is physical and fun, and inventing a town where the piles tie is a good challenge. But computing averages like 20/8 and each animal's friends' average is beyond many 7- and 8-year-olds, and tangled yarn slows the activity.

g45.why: The 4-friend animal writing 16 notes, hence the sum of squares, is a nice reason children can explain, and the result is surprising. Averages and fractions dominate, and the yarn set-up takes time before any thinking starts.

best_moment: Seeing that the notes pile has a bigger average than the animals pile and realising popular animals write the most notes.
biggest_problem: The core comparison is between averages, which is arithmetic-heavy and abstract for the younger bands, and the yarn network is slow to set up.
one_change: Use a printed network board with tokens instead of yarn, and compare piles by levelling cube towers instead of computing averages.

title: One-way streets

k1.why: Putting arrow cards on a ring and driving a toy car round is concrete and fun, and the dead-end lane that always traps the car is findable. Checking both 'reach every house' and 'get back to school' is a lot to hold in mind, so an adult will run the second check.

g23.why: Finding a good plan on the 3-by-3 town is a real puzzle and the Manhattan rule failing at a corner is a nice surprise. Testing all 12 roads by driving the car from every crossing and back is slow, and errors are easy to miss without a systematic check.

g45.why: Why one lifeline road ruins every plan is an argument they can make with the car, and building a plan loop by loop is a satisfying constructive idea. The even-streets rule for alternating grids gives a checkable conjecture.

best_moment: Flipping one arrow on the ring and finding a house the car can leave but never get back to.
biggest_problem: Checking that a plan works needs two full reachability sweeps, which turns into slow car-driving bookkeeping on the bigger maps.
one_change: Give the two-way test a physical shortcut, such as a 'leaving' car and a 'returning' car, or a single round-trip loop that has to pass every house, so checking a plan takes one quick drive.

title: Counting trees on numbered pegs

k1.why: Building straw networks is fine for the hands, but deciding when two labelled trees are 'different' (a different pair joined, not just turned) is a subtle convention for 5-year-olds, and drawing each tree on a recording card is fiddly.

g23.why: Hunting all 16 four-peg trees as a pooled class collection has a nice target and the 12-lines-4-stars split is satisfying. Spotting duplicates and recording accurately will take adult help.

g45.why: Counting numberings of a shape as 4! or 5! divided by its symmetries and seeing the shapes add to 125 is a real aha. It overlaps heavily with existing AD-04 and draft 150, so it is a return visit rather than fresh joy.

best_moment: Adding up the shape counts on 5 pegs (60 + 60 + 5) and landing exactly on 125 = 5 x 5 x 5.
biggest_problem: The core activity is listing and deduplicating labelled trees, which is bookkeeping-heavy and depends on a sameness convention young children find arbitrary.
one_change: Drop it as a separate week and run the symmetry-counting hour as a 4-5 return visit to AD-04, giving K-1 only the 3-cup sort.

title: Coin forests (percolation)

k1.why: Flipping 25 coins and placing 25 stickers is a long chore governed by luck, and a crossed-or-stuck pile has no decision in it. Finger-tracing the fire is fun but brief.

g23.why: The class tally landing near a half, and the die rules shifting it sharply, can surprise them, and hex against square is a good question. Most of the time is spent flipping and stickering, and the payoff only appears once boards are pooled.

g45.why: The exact-half argument via Hex (one crossing always happens, then colour swap) is a real aha if they have played Hex first. Filling 49- or 81-cell boards by coin is tedious; colouring boards by choice would be faster.

best_moment: Trying to colour a hex board so that nobody crosses and finding it is impossible, while on squares it is easy.
biggest_problem: Minute-to-minute work is coin flipping and sticker placing with no choices, and the interesting pattern only appears after a class tally.
one_change: Lead with the deliberate challenge (colour a board so neither side crosses, on hexes and squares), and fill the random boards fast with a die per row or a pre-printed random deck.

title: Small worlds and shortcuts

k1.why: Standing in a yarn ring and passing a bean bag is lively, and seeing one shortcut cut the passes is easy to feel. Counting passes is all they do, and it needs a whole room of children, so it fails at a kitchen table.

g23.why: Finding the farthest pair on a 16-dot ring, and discovering that a shortcut straight across leaves it unchanged, is a genuine surprise. Placing 2 shortcuts to minimise the farthest distance is a good puzzle, but average distance means a lot of tallying.

g45.why: Comparing planned with random shortcuts and guessing the 1000-person distance is interesting. Computing distances on many pooled random rings is a bookkeeping chore, and the log2 n theorem can only be told, not found.

best_moment: Adding a shortcut straight across the ring and finding the two people farthest apart are still exactly as far apart as before.
biggest_problem: The physical ring needs many children, and the paper version quickly becomes distance-counting tables.
one_change: Centre the paper work on the 'farthest pair' optimisation puzzle (best spots for 1, 2, 3 shortcuts) and drop average distance to a guide-only note.

title: Guessing your own hat

k1.why: Wearing headbands and revealing on three is fun, but the outcome is pure luck to them, and sorting the 8 hat-row cards under a rule is adult-led abstraction they will watch rather than do.

g23.why: Hunting a three-player rule that wins as many of the 8 rows as possible is a crisp puzzle with a record (6 of 8). The bridge from the played game to the 8-card sort needs careful adult framing.

g45.why: The pass-if-different rule winning 3 out of 4 when each guess is still a coin flip is a real surprise, and the dot-balance argument for why 7 of 8 is impossible is within reach with the cards.

best_moment: Finding that a team can win 6 of 8 rows even though every single guess is still right only half the time.
biggest_problem: For young children the game is all luck, and the counting tool that reveals the mathematics is abstract.
one_change: Make the 8-card deck the game board from the start (deal a row card, each player covers their own face and decides), so play and counting are the same action.

title: Follow the loop (prisoners and boxes)

k1.why: Lifting a cup, reading the number and going to that cup until you find your own is a lovely, doable chase with numbers to 6. The team game with cup resets between players is slow and the win/lose rule may feel unfair.

g23.why: The loop rule winning far more often than random lifting is a striking result. Shuffling 10 cups many times and recording the longest loop is repetitive simulation.

g45.why: Counting the 24 orders of 4 cups by loop pattern to get 10 wins, why only one loop can be too long, and the helper's one-swap rescue are crisp, checkable arguments with a big payoff.

best_moment: Realising that with the loop rule the whole team either all wins or all loses together, and wins about 4 times in 10 instead of almost never.
biggest_problem: The team game needs an adult to reset hidden cups between players, and the 10-cup statistics turn into repeated simulation.
one_change: Play the team game with each player's lifts checked on one shared laid-out shuffle (look at the arrows, not the cups) so no reset is needed and kids see the loops directly.

title: Look-and-say

k1.why: Saying a short row aloud and building it is a fun riddle for the first five rows, and discovering 22 never changes is delightful. Mixing count cards with colour cubes is a confusing double representation for 5-year-olds, and rows soon get too long.

g23.why: Spotting 'only 1, 2, 3 ever appear' and 'every row ends in 1' is a real pattern hunt. Ten rows by hand means transcribing 20-plus digits with compounding errors.

g45.why: Explaining why a 4 never appears, finding the row before 312211 and deciding that 1111 can never be a reading are short, satisfying puzzles. The backward game is checkable without long rows.

best_moment: Cracking the 1, 11, 21, 1211 riddle and then finding that the start 22 just reads itself forever.
biggest_problem: Rows grow fast, so after a few minutes the activity becomes error-prone copying of long digit strings.
one_change: Keep forward rows short (first six) and make the backward game, 'which strings can be readings', the main task for 2-3 as well as 4-5.

title: Short codes for common letters

k1.why: Walking turn messages on a taped floor tree and calling out pictures is physical and fun. Comparing two trees by counting turns is fine with cubes, though 'jump back to the root' needs a clear marker.

g23.why: Designing a tree that makes ABRACADABRA as short as possible with a class record is a good competitive puzzle. Counting 11 letters' worth of turns per attempt is tedious; a shorter message would help.

g45.why: Discovering 'join the two rarest' and seeing it beat everyone's hand-made trees is a real aha. The tree-budget reason why lengths 1, 1, 2 are impossible is graspable.

best_moment: Finding a gap-free message on a badly built code that can be read two different ways.
biggest_problem: Counting the total message length for each candidate tree is arithmetic bookkeeping, and the topic largely duplicates atlas AP-29.
one_change: Use a shorter message with a 4-letter alphabet for 2-3 and have each letter's count printed on its card, so a tree's cost is count times depth summed quickly.

title: Langton's ant

k1.why: Being the ant on a floor of plates is fun for a few steps, but left and right turns are unreliable at 5, one error ruins everything after it, and most children are waiting while one walks.

g23.why: Running 50 to 100 steps by hand is a long error-prone procedure, but the computer showing chaos and then the highway near step 10,000 is a genuine gasp. The run-backward game is a nice puzzle.

g45.why: Why moves alternate and why the rule can run backward are graspable, but the unboundedness proof is a facilitator story they follow rather than find. The honest 'nobody knows' open question is appealing.

best_moment: Watching the computer ant scribble chaotically for 10,000 steps and then suddenly build a straight highway.
biggest_problem: The hands-on part is a long rote simulation where one mistake spoils everything, and the real surprise only comes from watching a computer.
one_change: Keep hand simulation to about 20 steps with a partner checker, and give children the computer for experiments of their own (add one black square, predict, run).

title: Hilbert's hotel and the diagonal

k1.why: With three rows of three, making a row that is not on the list is trivial by trial, and the diagonal recipe is handed to them as a procedure, so there is nothing to discover and no infinity.

g23.why: The 'everyone move up a room' stories are fun to act out, and finding a method that beats any list a partner makes is a good two-player challenge. 'Same size' for endless collections is slippery at 7 or 8.

g45.why: Ten-year-olds love infinity paradoxes, and the diagonal move that beats any list is a short, famous argument they can actually make with counters.

best_moment: A full endless hotel fits a busload of endlessly many new guests when everyone moves to double their room number.
biggest_problem: The concrete counter game is weak at small sizes, because any missing row is easy to find without the diagonal, so the power of the idea only shows abstractly.
one_change: Play the diagonal as a race on longer lists (6 or 8 rows of 6 or 8) where trial and error is hopeless and the diagonal wins instantly, and drop the K-1 version.

title: Ordering stones with a balance

k1.why: A balance and mystery containers are irresistible, and a knockout to find the heaviest is easy to run. 'Sometimes 2 weighings, sometimes 3' is noticeable, but worst-case thinking is beyond most 5-year-olds.

g23.why: Ordering 4 in the fewest weighings is a good challenge, but with real containers the outcomes are fixed, so a lucky child 'wins' in fewer and 'always works' stays abstract. Drawing a method as a branching tree will need an adult scribe.

g45.why: The counting bound (64 endings are too few for 120 orders) is a nice argument, but the 5-in-7 plan is intricate and will mostly be fed through guide hints.

best_moment: Realising that 6 weighings can never be enough for 5 stones, because there are more orders than possible weighing stories.
biggest_problem: Fixed physical weights cannot play the tricky worst case, so the central idea of a method that always works is hard to experience, and the balance kit needs careful preparation.
one_change: Have a partner or adult secretly decide each weighing's answer as an adversary (or reshuffle contents between tries) so children face the worst case directly.

title: Change ringing

k1.why: Children as bells swapping places with neighbours is lively and physical, and 6 line-ups of 3 is a manageable target. Spotting repeats and laying the ladder record will need an adult.

g23.why: Plain hunt coming home after 8 rows instead of 24 is a real surprise, and flipping printed row cards on a wall chart makes repeats visible. A 24-row extent is long for bodies on the floor, so it moves to cards.

g45.why: Building the 4-bell extent by letting bell 4 weave through the 3-bell rows is a satisfying construction. The coset reason why Plain Bob never repeats will mostly be adult explanation.

best_moment: The plain-hunt dance on four bells unexpectedly arriving back home after only 8 of the 24 line-ups.
biggest_problem: The 24-row extent is a long sequence where one slip spoils the record, so it risks becoming a procedure the group follows rather than a puzzle.
one_change: Make the 4-bell task a card puzzle on a 24-card wall chart with a ready-made partial ladder to complete or fix, keeping bodies for 3 bells and plain hunt.

title: Star patterns from crossing lines

k1.why: Turning one paper square on another to make an eight-pointed star works, but most of the plan needs extending ruled lines on dot paper until they meet, which is beyond 5-year-old fine motor control.

g23.why: Drawing X's and watching stars appear when the grid is erased is a real visual payoff, and comparing dot-step rules is a good question. Accurate ruler work across a whole grid is slow and error-prone.

g45.why: Linking contact angle to joining midpoints and hunting the pattern's symmetry with tracing paper is rich. The 22.5- and 67.5-degree angle strips and the 'star has 8-fold but the pattern doesn't' argument need adult support.

best_moment: Erasing the plain grid and seeing a field of stars appear from lines they drew themselves.
biggest_problem: The core action is precise ruled drawing over many cells, so young children spend their energy on fine motor work rather than on noticing.
one_change: Provide printed sheets with all candidate lines drawn faintly so children choose and trace or colour lines, keeping the angle choice and the discovery without the precision drawing.

title: Nibble a tile

k1.why: Cutting a nibble, taping it across and decorating a creature is a craft they will enjoy, and the flipped-nibble row that will not close is visible. Cutting and aligned tracing will need help.

g23.why: On grid card, 'where can the nibble go so the floor still slides together' has clear, checkable answers and a surprise (anywhere along the bottom works, never a side). The pentomino sliding hunt is a good pooled task.

g45.why: Matching opposite boundary pieces, the Conway half-turn spin, and which pentominoes need turning give real design-and-explain problems built on a hands-on craft.

best_moment: Sticking the nibble somewhere else along the bottom edge and finding the floor still works, with the rows sliding sideways.
biggest_problem: K-1 tracing and cutting accuracy may be too rough for a fit or a clash to show clearly.
one_change: Give K-1 pre-cut grid-square tiles with nibbles that snap to the grid, so whether the floor works is unambiguous.

title: Steering a card with perfect shuffles

k1.why: Every shuffle means moving all eight cards at once along an arrow mat to a second mat. A five-year-old will lose cards or mix up arrows, so an adult ends up doing the shuffles. The mirror-colour observation means little at this age.

g23.why: Hunting for the in/out word that sends the star card to each spot is a real puzzle with a pattern to notice (1, 2, 4). Counting places from 0 is unnatural, and every trial costs a full eight-card shuffle, so it needs a steady adult and patience.

g45.why: The realisation that the steering word is the place written in binary is a genuine aha, and '8 of 24 orders with 4 cards' is a nice impossibility. Whole-deck shuffling is slow and error-prone, and the material overlaps Week 3 heavily for returning children.

best_moment: A 4-5 child predicts 'in, out, in' for spot 5, shuffles, and the star card lands exactly there.
biggest_problem: The core move, a whole-deck shuffle done by hand or by arrow mat, is slow and error-prone, so experiments get buried in card handling.
one_change: Let children track only the star card's position with the rules 'double' and 'double and add one' on a number strip, and save whole-deck shuffles for checking a prediction. Fold the week into a Week 3 return visit.

title: Kaprekar's sorting machine

k1.why: The two-digit version hands children a gap chart that turns the gap into two mystery cards. They follow a lookup procedure without seeing why, so the loop they walk is an adult-made circuit rather than something they discover.

g23.why: Landing on 495 from every start is a real surprise, but getting there takes several three-digit subtractions with regrouping, which can make the hour feel like arithmetic drill. Pooling the nine first answers is a good collective proof if a calculator or subtraction strip carries the arithmetic.

g45.why: With a calculator every start mysteriously falls to 6174, children race to find a 7-step start, and the question of why 3524 and 5432 give the same answer leads to a proof by 54 shared cases they can actually finish.

best_moment: A whole table discovers that everyone's different four-digit number ended at the same 6174.
biggest_problem: Below grade 4 the machine is either long hand subtraction or an opaque lookup chart, so younger children run a procedure instead of exploring.
one_change: Allow calculators for 2–3 after one hand-worked step, and give K–1 a sorting and comparing task with digit cards rather than the gap-chart lookup.

title: Prime pairs (Goldbach)

k1.why: Standing two ready-made towers beside a target to match its height is a clear, hands-on matching puzzle. Finding that 11 can't be made is a small surprise. The towers being 'prime' means nothing to them, so it's light number play.

g23.why: Filling a chart of even numbers to 50 is mostly addition-fact listing. The questions about which numbers have the most ways, and why odd numbers need a 2, give it some point. Pooling keeps the load down, but the excitement is modest.

g45.why: The odd-number proof and the 'nobody has proved it, but it's checked to 4 × 10¹⁸' story give older kids a thrill. Still, the minute-to-minute work is filling in a chart of sums up to 100.

best_moment: Learning that a statement a child can check in a minute has defeated every mathematician for 280 years.
biggest_problem: The hands-on work is listing prime sums, which gets repetitive. The interesting part, an open problem, is something to talk about rather than something to do.
one_change: Make it a hunt: teams race to find an even number with exactly one way, or the number below 100 with the most ways, rather than filling every row of a chart.

title: Halfway to the wall

k1.why: The halfway walk is a fun body launch, and folding and colouring a strip is concrete. After four or five folds the pieces are too small to colour, and 'is there always white left?' needs an adult to make it land.

g23.why: Shading one of four corners again and again and finding that the shaded part is one third is a real surprise. Cutting and stacking ever-smaller bands is fiddly, so pre-printed nested squares would help.

g45.why: The 'three equal squares' picture proof, Achilles catching the tortoise, and 'is 0.999… really 1?' reliably spark argument and conviction at this age. Each child can draw and defend a proof.

best_moment: The child walking halfway ends up shuffling heel-to-toe while the room shouts about whether they'll ever touch the wall.
biggest_problem: After the first few folds or cuts the pieces are too small for small hands, so younger bands lose the concrete action just as the idea gets interesting.
one_change: Give K–3 large pre-printed strips and squares with the nested pieces already outlined, so they colour and compare rather than fold and cut tiny regions.

title: Press it again

k1.why: Clips crowding together on the ribbon and then flipping it to find the hidden marks is a real magic moment. The two-step fold-and-move rule is a lot to repeat accurately, so an adult will often do the folding.

g23.why: Pressing √ over and over is irresistible, and a million collapsing to 1 is a laugh. Children this age can't read the long decimals, though, so 'where does it settle' becomes 'when does the screen stop changing', and the extra machines need typed keystrokes each round.

g45.why: Sorting machines into 'settles', 'flips' and 'runs away' by pressing buttons is fast, physical experimentation with surprises (cos always reaches 0.739). The race against averaging gives a vivid sense of speed, provided there are scientific calculators.

best_moment: Flipping the ribbon over to find that every clip ended on the hidden one-third and two-thirds marks.
biggest_problem: It depends on materials: cheap calculators lack cos and radian mode, and the ribbon fold rule needs careful repetition, so the experiment can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the math.
one_change: Use machines on cards (halve and add 1, double and subtract 3, and so on) worked on a simple calculator or a number line, so 2–3 can sort machines without needing decimals or scientific keys.

title: The fastest slide

k1.why: Marble races between a straight ramp and a bent one, with a vote first, are pure joy. Bending a track to beat the straight one is something a five-year-old can try again and again.

g23.why: Changing only the shape and finding that the shortest ramp loses, and that a dip below the finish can still win, is a genuine 'wait, what?' backed by children's own races.

g45.why: The same racing plus 'speed comes only from dropping' gives older kids a reason they can state. The tautochrone (different heights arriving together) is a showstopper if it works on homemade track.

best_moment: The marble on the curved track that dips below the finish beats the straight one, against nearly every vote.
biggest_problem: Homemade flexible track or cardboard channels may not hold a smooth curve or keep marbles on, and the time differences on a short course may be too small to see.
one_change: Rehearse and fix one reliable 1 m-wide course (for example foam pipe insulation cut in half on a cycloid template) before running the session.

title: Pi from polygons

k1.why: Wrapping string round cans and marking off 'three and a bit' across-lengths is concrete, and fanning plate wedges into a strip is satisfying. Cutting and handling string accurately needs an adult, and the payoff is a mild observation.

g23.why: Measuring several objects and finding the same 'three and a bit' every time is a nice constant to discover. Measurement error, comparing lengths and counting about 300 grid squares can make it feel like a measuring and counting chore.

g45.why: Trapping π between hexagon and 12-gon perimeters and explaining the wedge rectangle is good reasoning. Most of the time goes to careful measuring, the gasp is limited, and some children will already 'know 3.14'.

best_moment: A bucket, a coin and a plate all give 'three and a bit' when children lay out the across-lengths.
biggest_problem: The core action is accurate measuring and counting, which is slow and error-prone, and the surprise that every circle gives the same number is a quiet one.
one_change: Drop the grid-square count and frame the string task as a challenge: find a round thing that is NOT three and a bit, using big hoops and buckets so measurement is reliable.

title: Folding the square root of two

k1.why: Cutting the biggest square repeatedly from A-paper needs precise folds and cuts on ever-thinner strips. The 1, 2, 2, 2 versus 1, 3 counts mean nothing to a five-year-old, so an adult does the cutting.

g23.why: Building two equal tile squares and trying to make one big square, then finding near-misses (5+5 against 7×7), is a concrete hunt with a surprise. The 12-and-17 case needs nearly 300 tiles and a lot of counting.

g45.why: The overlap picture and the endless 'two again' square-cutting can give a real 'it can never stop' moment. Infinite descent is abstract, though, the fold argument involves an impossible square, and paper precision fails after a few rounds.

best_moment: Laying 49 tiles beside two 5-by-5 squares and finding it is off by exactly one, then finding it happens again with 12 and 17.
biggest_problem: The proof is the point, and it is abstract, while the physical square-cutting that should make it concrete breaks down from paper imprecision after three or four rounds.
one_change: Centre the hands-on work on the tile near-miss hunt with a grid sheet instead of loose tiles, and present square-cutting on a pre-drawn large diagram rather than real paper.

title: Random walks home

k1.why: Flipping a coin and stepping on a floor number line is active and fun for a few walks. Some walks drag on for 30 or more flips with nothing to decide, and 'did everyone get home' is all they take away.

g23.why: Odd-flip impossibility and listing the four-flip paths are good puzzles. The class average shifting as long walks arrive is interesting, but it takes many walks and a lot of recording.

g45.why: The real ideas (a certain return with an infinite average, recurrence depending on dimension) can't be seen from a class chart, and the road argument assumes Week 91. Children mostly flip and wait while the punchline stays an adult's claim.

best_moment: A walker who drifted out to +9 finally stumbles back to 0 and the room cheers.
biggest_problem: The activity is long luck-driven simulation, and the surprising theorems (infinite average time, 3D transience) are not visible at the scale children can simulate.
one_change: Run short capped walks for the launch, then shift the main work to the four- and six-flip path-counting puzzle, and leave the infinite-average and dimension story to a brief adult demonstration or the app.

title: Long runs

k1.why: Building a red-and-blue cube tower by coin flips is fun and easy. Many five-year-olds won't grasp making a 'pretend random' tower, so the detective contrast needs adult framing.

g23.why: Making a real and a fake 20-flip strip and trying to fool another pair is a game kids want to replay. Spotting that real strips have surprisingly long runs is an aha they find themselves.

g45.why: The detective game plus predicting the longest run in 100 flips, and the '1 in 64' explanation, give real reasoning on top of a fun hook. 100 flips is tedious unless shared or done with a cup of coins.

best_moment: The detectives point at a strip with five heads in a row and declare it fake, and it turns out to be the real one.
biggest_problem: The 100-flip recording for 4–5 can become a tedious transcription chore that eats time.
one_change: Use the tip-a-cup-of-10-coins method for the 100-flip grid, so recording takes minutes and the time goes to predicting and detecting.
